cases.title: Distributed GPT-2 evaluation discarded its final 128 predictions

findings.observation: Two A100 GPUs ran the posted GPT-2 program on 512 identical prompts. Accelerate 0.15.0 and the fix parent returned 128 predictions in each of the first three batches and zero in the fourth. The fixed revision returned all four batches. A neighboring run with 513 inputs also retained the last prediction.
findings.interpretation: Both ranks generated 64 predictions in the fourth batch. The NCCL gather delivered all 128 to each rank. In gather_for_metrics, the affected _adjust_samples sliced the gathered tensor at a remainder of zero. The fix retained the complete batch when division was exact. A separate test with numbered samples verified the missing row identities at input sizes 128, 256 and 512.
findings.limits: The replay used the original model name, pinned public GPT-2 weights, Python 3.10.11, PyTorch 1.13.1, Transformers 4.25.1 and CUDA 11.7. The reporter used Python 3.7.15 and CUDA 10.2. A single-GPU run independently checked all 20 generated tokens. The evidence records synchronous function calls in two distributed processes.

cases.title: Accelerate keeps padding duplicates from a sized iterable dataset

findings.observation: Across two CPU ranks, a ten-sample map-style dataset returned ten items in both configurations, while the sized iterable with dispatch disabled returned 16 or 12, duplicating items 0–5 or 0–1.
findings.interpretation: Using shard length 8 and local batch size 4 gave a zero remainder and kept the whole final batch. Neither correction alone worked across inputs, but together they returned the original sequence in all 56 configurations.
findings.limits: The two changes were a local implementation of the author’s proposal. The Linux CPU runs used synchronous ranks. The report used macOS arm64.

cases.title: Uneven batches inflate a metric gathered across four GPUs

findings.observation: With batch size 17 per rank, both four-GPU runs counted 636/10,064 (0.063196) instead of 572/10,000 (0.057200). Evenly divisible batches returned the expected score.
findings.interpretation: The caller reduced each rank to scalars before gather_for_metrics trimmed the final batch, so it kept all four subtotals, including 64 duplicate IDs that were all hits.
findings.limits: This matches the maintainer’s explanation of API usage. The replay used Ubuntu 22.04 instead of 20.04. The unpadded control was stopped while ranks waited.

cases.title: A sharded data loader counts a final batch that one rank never receives

findings.observation: With two CPU/Gloo ranks, rank 0 read [0] and [2], while rank 1 read only [1], yet both loaders reported two batches. Each of two releases overcounted by one in 50 of 171 rank configurations.
findings.interpretation: With split_batches enabled and even_batches disabled, the length calculation counted the final batch even for an empty rank slice. Applying the proposed length change alone made all counts agree with the samples.
findings.limits: Sequential CPU sampling only. The reported main revision was unspecified, and PR #4127 closed without merging.

cases.title: Repeated token-ID lookups rebuild the added-token map

findings.observation: In the author’s Chinese BERT example, 100 conversions of 360 tokens with 5,005 added tokens took 87.045 seconds on 5.9.0 and 0.018 seconds on 5.12.1.
findings.interpretation: Traces showed the membership check and the subsequent lookup both rebuilding the map; removing 5,000 extra entries while preserving the output also sharply reduced conversion time.
findings.limits: The local run used Python 3.12.4 rather than the reported 3.12.13. Detailed request traces used six tokens each and cover token conversion only.

cases.title: Ray Serve processes ready batches serially by default

findings.observation: One real Serve replica received 24 integers and correctly doubled them in three batches of eight, but three one-second waits took 3.05 seconds in total.
findings.interpretation: The batch queue waited for model I/O even with more requests ready, whereas setting the new concurrency limit to three let the three waits overlap.
findings.limits: The reporter’s model used NumPy and a bounded sleep to represent async I/O. The new setting is optional and defaults to serial execution.

cases.title: A Ray Serve handle touches another thread’s event loop

findings.observation: On 2.48.0 the main-loop handle.remote call raised a cross-thread error with asyncio debugging on and returned the string “1” with it off, while 2.54.0 returned “1” with debugging on.
findings.interpretation: The failed Task, target loop and two thread identities explained the call-site dependency and allowed comparison with Task creation in the fixed version.
findings.limits: The debug-mode error was reproducible. Its relationship to two reported production stalls in roughly 90 days remains unconfirmed.

cases.title: Batched Ray Serve requests can select the wrong multiplexed model

findings.observation: In each request order, three of six batched requests returned the wrong model while ordinary calls stayed correct. The fixed version answered all 12 batched requests correctly.
findings.interpretation: Reversing the first request reversed the wrong answer. The fix carried each model ID into the queue and split the batch so each processing task read its own ID.
findings.limits: The reported deployments used strings as model objects. Graphs cover the model replica. Sequential request logs link it to clients and other actors.

cases.title: The reported cold model-load delay did not recur locally

findings.observation: With the author’s Serve app and an empty OS page cache, the first requests took 54.4 and 56.7 ms, and Serve logged 8.0 and 7.8 ms for loading versus 9,543.2 ms in the report.
findings.interpretation: The replica task read the file through predict → load_model → get_model, reusing it for the same model ID and evicting it for a new ID; prewarming the file or visiting Swagger first did not reproduce the delay.
findings.limits: The public attachment reads ONNX bytes on local Linux storage. Docker Desktop shared-mount performance and the private MLflow model remain unknown.

cases.title: Default shuffling leaves three of four DataLoader workers idle

findings.observation: Across 19 Parquet files, Datasets 5.0.1 delivered 152/0/0/0 rows to four workers, versus 40/40/40/32 on 5.1.0, with all 152 unique rows delivered in both cases.
findings.interpretation: Disabling shuffle or limiting the input buffer to one shard restored a 5/5/5/4 file split, and the fix constructs each worker’s interleaved reader after assigning its source shards.
findings.limits: The data run used small local files and one CPU node. Only CelebA metadata was tested, with no multi-rank or sustained resource measurements.

cases.title: gather_for_metrics trims a full batch when drop_last is set

findings.observation: With batch size 5, the author’s 9-item example returned only 0–3, and the 11-item example returned only 5 from the full batch 5–9; the fix returned 0–4 and 5–9 respectively.
findings.interpretation: The input batches and collective results were unchanged, and preserving _drop_last on the prepared loader prevented a second, incorrect trim for metrics.
findings.limits: Tested with PyTorch 1.13.1 on CPU and two local Gloo processes. GPU training and NCCL were outside the comparison.

cases.title: Custom keys are encoded twice by multi_cached

findings.observation: Transformed keys reached the wrapped function and appeared in its results, and a repeated request for the same two Redis keys ran the function again.
findings.interpretation: The write task passed doubly prefixed keys to _multi_set while the reader looked up singly prefixed keys; aligning the two made overlapping requests fetch only new items.
findings.limits: The report used an in-memory cache and gave no version. Redis was a separate control for 0.12.3 and a development-branch change.

cases.title: A renewed cache entry disappears at its original expiry time

findings.observation: The reporter wrote 100 with a two-second TTL, read it after one second, then replaced it with 200 and renewed the TTL. A second read returned None on aiocache 0.10.0 and the fix parent. It returned 200 on the fix and on 0.10.1. Redis retained 200 in all four runs.
findings.interpretation: The timeout wrapper created the read task. Its _get sample returned the missing value between the old and new deadlines. The timer observations explain why. On the affected build, the first timer fired, deleted the replacement and cancelled its timer. The fix cancelled the first timer during the replacement write.
findings.limits: The report did not specify a release. The two published versions bracket the identified fix. The expiry callback runs synchronously on the event loop. The matched coroutine is the second cache read.

cases.title: aiocsv splits a quoted multiline field into separate records

findings.observation: Version 1.1.1 printed six rows for the input’s two records, including a new row for “nuff: 1”. Versions 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 printed two complete records. All three batches produced identical stdout with the recorder enabled and disabled on each build.
findings.interpretation: The creation stack and the _read_until sample identify the task that cut the first quoted field. The same reader passed a buffer ending at that newline to the standard-library parser. The truncated dictionary returned by the reader is the same object the reporter’s print call received.
findings.limits: The report gave no version pins. The local measurements run from task creation through the first malformed dictionary at print. The fixed capture observes the compiled parser’s returned fields.

cases.title: An LF-terminated airport file yielded its header and no data

findings.observation: The author supplied a two-line file. Running the maintainer’s complete program with the author’s LF endings returned only the header. With CRLF endings the same program also returned the data row, including the quoted JSON field. On an airport CSV, the old dictionary reader returned zero of 3,376 airports. Setting the dialect’s line terminator to LF recovered every field in every record.
findings.interpretation: The stack follows the main task into AsyncReader.__anext__ and _read_until. The reader looked for CRLF and passed the entire LF file to a single iteration. The standard CSV reader consumed 71 characters for the header, leaving the 122-character data line unread. The async reader then cleared its buffer. In a separate run, two concurrent imports of identical airport records had distinct creation sites. The LF task lost the records while the CRLF task read all 3,376.
findings.limits: The issue closed with a documentation change. The later parser change and release 1.2.1 both read LF correctly by default. The author’s initial snippet passed fieldnames to AsyncReader, which raised TypeError. The documented AsyncDictReader variant reproduced the posted dictionary output. The unchanged executable example came from the maintainer. The local run used Linux and CPython 3.9.25. The author used macOS and CPython 3.9.1.

cases.title: A leap-day file disappears from an FTP directory listing

findings.observation: A local FTP server listed three files, including a readable February 29 file. aioftp 0.15.0 and the fix parent exited successfully but returned only the February 28 and March 1 entries.
findings.interpretation: The listing task received the February 29 line and hit ValueError in both date-parsing paths. The iterator skipped the entry. The fix parsed the same timestamp as 20200229092400.
findings.limits: The original server and Python patch release were unspecified. The test used a read-only loopback FTP server and an English UNIX listing with the client clock set to March 1, 2020. The traced task was the top-level task in the posted client.

cases.title: Why did the FTP listing date a 2017 file to 1900?

findings.observation: The reporter used await client.list(path) on an anonymous FTP server. On a loopback server with the same recent-file date, aioftp 0.10.1 and the immediate fix parent printed 19000927232500. The correcting commit and 0.11.0 printed 20170927232500. The filesystem timestamp was September 27, 2017 at 23:25 UTC. The older file and machine-readable directory listing gave the right year in all four builds.
findings.interpretation: The legacy listing sent “Sep 27 23:25”. A separate FTP client read the same bytes. At parse_ls_date the old client held a struct_time whose year was 1900. The corrected parser held a datetime with year 2017. CPython caught the library creating its internal _to_list coroutine and matched the retained object to the frame returning the rows to the reporter.
findings.limits: The reporter’s get_info function ran unchanged with a local endpoint and Linux event loop. The server used a small synthetic ZIP under the reported filename. Its read-only directory and both client processes used October 10, 2017 UTC as their wall clock. Coverage comprises these two files, two listings and four builds. The upstream test file accompanying the patch is included as source.

cases.title: Why did the third GET return an empty stream from a full cache?

findings.observation: A single client requested the same 42-byte document three times. All three responses had HTTP status 200 and declared a 42-byte body. The server received one GET. On 0.8.2 and the immediate fix parent, the third stream read returned zero bytes while the cached response still held all 42. On the fix and 0.9.0, every stream read returned the full document. Plain aiohttp and standard-library clients each made three origin requests and returned all 42 bytes every time.
findings.interpretation: On 0.8.2, DictCache.read (segment 22) returned the same cached response. Its content getter (24) returned the exhausted reader. The third read started at cursor 42 with zero bytes buffered (26). CPython recorded the application creating StreamReader.read (25). The same coroutine frame was running when _read_nowait returned empty bytes (30). On 0.9.0, DictCache.read called CachedResponse.reset, which cleared the reader on the same response (25). The content getter called CachedStreamReader.__init__ (33) and returned the new reader (34). The third read started at cursor 0 with 42 bytes buffered (36) and returned all 42 (47).
findings.limits: The observer followed sequential GETs through the in-memory backend on the two release wheels. The loopback fixture replaces the reporter’s public URL and corrects a repeated variable name in the interactive transcript. Both adjacent source builds identify themselves as 0.8.3, so the table labels them by commit. The landed regression uses response.read() and passed on all four builds. Switching the two cached reads to response.content.read() reproduced the reported difference. The CSV table uses a separate 15-byte document and measures what the next cache hit could parse.

cases.title: Trailing whitespace makes aiohttp reject a valid disposition type

findings.observation: The reporter’s program warned and returned (None, {}) on 3.14.1 but parsed form-data and the field name “field” on 3.14.2. Every version delivered “hello” with HTTP 200.
findings.interpretation: The old parser checked the token with its trailing space intact, while the fix strips whitespace before validation.
findings.limits: The original parser call was synchronous. Task attribution covers only the end-to-end HTTP test.

cases.title: A precompressed file receives a second layer of HTTP compression

findings.observation: On aiohttp 3.9.1, a GET for a precompressed file with dynamic compression enabled advertised deflate. Decoding the response once left 38 bytes of gzip data. The fixed server advertised gzip and returned the original 18 bytes after one decode. Serving the precompressed file alone and enabling compression on a plain file both produced the expected contents.
findings.interpretation: RequestHandler.start created the task that selected the gzip file. In that same request, _do_start_compression selected deflate. The client port, request object and task identity connect that decision to the raw HTTP response. Repeating the request with a second TCP client and a byte-identical file confirmed the result.
findings.limits: The reported release ran locally on Python 3.12.13. The report used 3.12.0. The parent and fix ran with aiohttp’s Python implementation. The reporter’s test explicitly expects the old deflate header, so its assertion fails on the corrected header. A separate check decodes and compares the complete body.

cases.title: A partial download contained the right bytes but could not be resumed

findings.observation: A request for bytes 500 onward in a 10,000-byte file returned HTTP 206 and the correct 9,500 bytes on aiohttp 3.0.9. The Content-Range header was missing. curl and Wget each left the original 500-byte file in place. After the fix, both produced the complete 10,000-byte file with the expected digest.
findings.interpretation: The creation and execution records identify the same request task in FileResponse.prepare(). In the affected source-parent capture, 679.371 µs elapsed from the recorded create_task return to the stack immediately before sendfile. The archived recorder uses the same monotonic clock and thread for both records. The range calculation and payload length agreed with the actual response bytes. In a separate replay, adding Content-Range alone let both clients finish. Adding only Accept-Ranges left both downloads incomplete.
findings.limits: The experiment used the reported aiohttp version and the framework’s real static route on loopback. The tested download clients were curl and Wget. The browser download behavior comes from the upstream report.

cases.title: A multipart upload arrives under the wrong form field name

findings.observation: aiohttp 3.5.4 sent the file in the reporter’s example. The receiver stored it under files%5B%5D, so looking it up under files[] returned an empty list. aiohttp 3.8.0 preserved the brackets and the lookup found the file. When two island data files were uploaded together, both releases delivered both files in the submitted order.
findings.interpretation: The encoder’s return value already contained the escaped name. The creation stack in ClientRequest.send identifies the writer task that later sent those exact header bytes. Independent parsing of the saved body and replay through a second server reproduced the field lookup. The file hashes matched across builds.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied an async client fragment on Python 3.6.8. The local run supplied an upload URL, files and a Werkzeug receiver. Its HTTP 200 receipt exposed what the parser received. The creation and write samples come from the source builds on Python 3.8.20.

cases.title: A two-byte separator split CSV records one byte too early

findings.observation: The original client read 14 bytes from the reporter’s public example using ab as a delimiter. aiohttp 3.8.1 and the fix parent ended records at bytes 3, 8, 13 and 14. The fix returned records ending at bytes 4, 9 and 14. In a CSV transfer with 244 restaurant checks, Python’s CSV reader consumed the header and then rejected the next record on both affected builds. The fix delivered all 244 data rows.
findings.interpretation: StreamReader.readuntil found the delimiter, but consumed only its first byte. The trace paired the first partial record with the original main Task created by run_until_complete at line 17 of the reporter’s script. The nested reads and their return sizes explain the observed split. The fix consumed the full delimiter. Concatenating the returned pieces recovered the original body on every build.
findings.limits: The report used macOS and Python 3.8.9. The local runs used Linux and Python 3.10.12. The reporter’s original client, a URL-only loopback replay and eight stream controls ran with and without instrumentation. The restaurant data was served with CRLF endings using Content-Length and chunked transfer. Both deliveries kept each delimiter together in the server’s writes. The coroutine origin belongs to the original client.

cases.title: aiohttp traces the whole request across middleware retries

findings.observation: Three GET attempts that returned 500 produced one start, one end and no exception signal. A 503 followed by a 200 exposed only the 200 at the end.
findings.interpretation: The signals surround ClientSession._request, while retries run inside the middleware. Two explicit GETs produced two signal pairs, and raise_for_status reported one exception after the middleware finished.
findings.limits: Loopback HTTP responses only. Transport retries and OpenTelemetry spans were untested, and upstream had not settled the intended semantics.

cases.title: aiohttp returned a prefix slice for an HTTP suffix range

findings.observation: The report requested the last 5,678 bytes of a resource. On a 10,000-byte file, aiohttp 1.2.0 and the fix parent returned slice(None, -5678, 1). An application using that slice sent the first 4,322 bytes. The fix returned slice(-5678, None, 1) and the application sent exactly the last 5,678 bytes.
findings.interpretation: The range parser put the negative offset in the slice's stop field. The fix moved it to the start field and left the stop open. The built-in static handler understood the old representation and served the correct tail on all five runs. The parent and fixed captures connect each property return to the exact RequestHandler.start task created by aiohttp, its request and its TCP connection. In the affected source-parent capture, 1.220375 ms elapsed from the recorded create_task return to the http_range return for the reported request. Both timestamps come from the same process's archived monotonic clock.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied the header, the aiohttp version and both slice values. The resource follows the fix's regression fixture. The byte-returning application, static route and additional ranges are local controls. Each measured connection carried one successful GET. The upstream regression tests ran separately with their original mocked request helper.

cases.title: aioitertools.zip delivers raised exceptions as batch values

findings.observation: After nine successful pairs, 0.11.0 delivered two AssertionError objects in the tenth list, producing a blank space in one example and a TypeError during nested unpacking in the other. 0.12.0 used a tuple.
findings.interpretation: A failed child task held the same exception object as the batch, while a task that yielded a ValueError as data had no exception. The proposed type check confused those cases.
findings.limits: PR #157 was unmerged. The Linux replay traced each __anext__ task separately. The gather completion callback had no coroutine identity.

cases.title: Batched Kafka sends skip the configured key and value serializers

findings.observation: The affected release and fix parent raised TypeError on the first batch record and left the topic at offset zero, while individual sends wrote all three records.
findings.interpretation: BatchBuilder.append passed inputs straight to the builder. With byte inputs it stored alpha/raw unchanged, while individual sends and the fixed batch stored ALPHA/encoded:raw, as an independent consumer verified.
findings.limits: Used local Kafka 2.2.1, supplied a JSON-encodable input and corrected an incomplete log statement in the example.

cases.title: aiokafka treats positional message headers as a partition key

findings.observation: All three reported versions failed with positional headers, while passing headers= let an independent Java consumer read back the bytes for the test header (12).
findings.interpretation: Object identities showed the headers list reaching murmur2 as the serialized key, where partition selection failed before record construction, and 0.10.0 reproduced all four reported client stack locations in order.
findings.limits: The test used the published method and a real local Kafka broker. The original application, certificates, and Debian image were unavailable.

cases.title: Redis transactions return bytes despite a UTF-8 setting

findings.observation: The stored list contained ab and cd throughout, but 0.2.4 returned bytes from EXEC with either inherited or explicit UTF-8, while a direct read returned strings.
findings.interpretation: Both versions received identical EXEC bytes. The closing commit decoded each queued command’s results with its own encoding before completing its Future.
findings.limits: The report pinned only Python. The fix’s parent raised a separate TypeError, and release 0.2.5 still decoded a nested list explicitly requested as bytes.

cases.title: Row-by-row async SQLite iteration makes one worker handoff per row

findings.observation: For 120,000 rows, median iteration took 4.733 s on the old build, 0.123 s in batches of 250, and 0.071 s with sqlite3. On 0.16.0 iteration took 0.203 s but explicit fetchone still took 4.667 s.
findings.interpretation: The slow task repeatedly entered __anext__ → fetchone → _execute, and independent worker counts fell from 120,001 handoffs to 1,876 or 481 with chunks of 64 or 250, preserving the checksum.
findings.limits: The original schema and data were unavailable. These are local Linux timings on a disk database. The reported 15× ratio came from macOS.

cases.title: Committing through an aiosqlite cursor exposes the underlying connection

findings.observation: The original con.commit() succeeded, but cur.connection.commit() raised a cross-thread SQLite ProgrammingError on both 0.20.0 and 0.22.1. Both commits succeeded with the proposed change.
findings.interpretation: The cursor property returned the raw handle, so the Task committed on the event-loop thread. Returning the async wrapper sent the same handle’s second commit back to its owning worker thread.
findings.limits: Used the reported interpreter and package versions. PR #384 was tested separately as a proposal, and worker operations were matched by handle identity.

cases.title: Setting row_factory on an aiosqlite cursor still returns a tuple

findings.observation: The three original SELECT 1 examples returned Row, Row and tuple on both 0.17.0 and 0.18.0; the fix and 0.19.0 returned Row when requested on either connection or cursor.
findings.interpretation: The old wrapper held the setting while the worker’s sqlite3.Cursor still had row_factory=None, and object identity confirmed that the same tuple passed through the Future to the caller.
findings.limits: The report gave no version or platform. Task creation evidence came only from an additional two-cursor control.

cases.title: Awaiting an empty aiostream stream reported an extra exception

findings.observation: Under 0.4.3 and the merge parent, awaiting either an empty stream or an exhausted one-shot iterator raised StreamEmpty with an UnboundLocalError context. The merge and 0.4.4 raised StreamEmpty directly.
findings.interpretation: CoroPerf links the real await-wrapper coroutine and its allocation stack to both exceptions in the same wait_stream frame. The first exception came from reading an unassigned local. The fix tracks whether the iterator yielded any item. Every build accepts None as a last item, repeats a repeatable stream and preserves NameError from a user callback.
findings.limits: The reported application was private. The runs reproduce the library behavior with a standalone example. The local timings include the start of the prepared component process.

cases.title: aiostream flatmap checked a coroutine before awaiting it

findings.observation: On aiostream 0.6.4 and the fix parent, the original example hit AssertionError on the first batch and consumed zero items. The merged fix and 0.7.2 delivered all 25 values in order in every stock and traced run.
findings.interpretation: smap created the async_processor coroutine and yielded it to base_combine. The failing assertion and native warning identify the same object and frame in CORO_CREATED state. The fixed path awaited the callback and iterated its return value. CoroPerf also found the smap allocation stack with its transparent --capture-unawaited mode on every affected run of the unchanged example. The fixed runs had no such warning.
findings.limits: The reporter had already identified the assertion in the issue description. The archive includes the full local stacks. The extended origin count includes this never-started object. Timings use three prepared local processes per build and include process startup.

cases.title: A synchronous iterator stalls the event-loop heartbeat

findings.observation: All ten inputs were yielded, but the 100 ms heartbeat paused for seconds; using the posted async iterator or running next in an executor restored the heartbeat.
findings.interpretation: An independent thread stack caught the consuming task in time.sleep while from_iterable advanced the generator, and the executor control placed that same line on a worker thread.
findings.limits: Upstream described synchronous iteration semantics and proposed no fix. The named task origin came from a separate two-input control.

cases.title: Simultaneous iterator failures leave one task exception unread

findings.observation: When the two posted iterators failed together, the consumer received one exception and asyncio warned about the other. Staggering the failures produced only the consumer exception.
findings.interpretation: wait_any returned both completed tasks, but cleanup removed the second without reading its exception. The fix calls exception() on that same task, clearing the unread flag.
findings.limits: The report omitted the version. Task and exception identity came from instrumented runs. Plain runs kept asyncio’s default exception handler.

cases.title: A shielded AnyIO host left its sibling waiting for cancellation

findings.observation: The unchanged reporter timed out on AnyIO 4.1.0 and the merge parent. The landed fix and AnyIO 4.2.0 exited normally in every stock and traced run.
findings.interpretation: The outer cancellation loop saw a host in a shielded scope. Its sibling was in an unshielded child scope, suspended in wait_cancel with no cancellation requests at the observation deadline. The fix traverses child scopes and delivers cancellation to that same task role. The graph matches the stalled coroutine to the exact instance created by func.
findings.limits: The watchdog observes 1.4 seconds of pending work. It snapshots the sibling before cancelling the process. Each timing is a median of three local runs on prepared CPython 3.11.

cases.title: Cancelling task startup bypasses an active asyncio shield

findings.observation: On Python 3.10, the reporter’s shield assertion failed on AnyIO 4.7.0 and 4.13.0, and only the targeted connection missed its cleanup acknowledgement in a two-connection test.
findings.interpretation: After the readiness Future was cancelled, TaskGroup.start called cancel() directly on the child observed inside the shield. 4.14.0 routed cancellation through TaskHandle’s cancel scope and shielded I/O completed.
findings.limits: The fixed-version checks used the upstream release-event test and bounded loopback I/O because the shielded original waits indefinitely.

cases.title: PostgreSQL sent the schedule notification, but the scheduler stayed asleep

findings.observation: The released broker received three distinct PostgreSQL notifications on two listening connections. All six callbacks raised NoEventLoopError. A scheduled job also missed its due time during the four-second observation. After a PostgreSQL restart, the schedule still carried its original due time and the job had written zero completion receipts. With the upstream one-line listener change, the job wrote its receipt in both batches.
findings.interpretation: asyncpg dispatched the synchronous listener on a running loop with no current task. Under an unmarked context, sniffio could not identify the backend when the listener asked AnyIO to start a delivery task. The exception stacks show the call through TaskGroup.start_soon and TaskHandle to get_async_backend. coroPerf also matched the specific scheduler coroutine created by AsyncScheduler.run_until_stopped to its Event.wait after the job was due. The same wait appears after a successful job, so the SQL receipt and schedule times establish which outcome occurred.
findings.limits: The local test corrected two API calls in the posted snippet. PostgreSQL 14.13 ran on a Unix socket. Explicitly marking the context as asyncio restored delivery on the released code. Removing sniffio restored delivery for the standalone broker. This version of the SQLAlchemy data store imports sniffio and raised ModuleNotFoundError in that environment.

cases.title: CronTrigger scheduled its first run before the start time

findings.observation: The start was 11:16 in the trigger’s time zone, but the old scheduler chose 11:00, 16 minutes early, while the fix chose 11:20.
findings.interpretation: CronTrigger.next read the hour as 10 in the source zone and applied the target zone only when setting the field. Converting first yields the correct five-minute boundary.
findings.limits: Fixed-offset and named-zone tests checked the stored schedule and cursor, without waiting for the historical job to run.

cases.title: APScheduler records job failures without printing the exception

findings.observation: Two ticks ten seconds apart each printed a timestamp and JobOutcome.error, with nothing on stderr. Both jobs raised NameError in frak() before reaching the explicit raise.
findings.interpretation: The task trace followed each exception from tg.start_soon through _run_job to release_job: JobResult retained the exception object, while JobReleased exposed only the failure status.
findings.limits: The report gave no commit hash. The replay used master from the posting date and stopped the example after observing the failures.

cases.title: A job on the default queue waits while a custom worker is idle

findings.observation: The custom-queue worker completed a probe job, but a submission without _queue_name remained pending until a default-queue worker started and completed the same job without resubmission.
findings.interpretation: The worker’s ZRANGEBYSCORE read the custom queue while the waiter’s ZSCORE polled the same job ID on the default queue, confirming the configuration mismatch.
findings.limits: The producer and worker were reconstructed from the report. The verified task origin belongs to the polling worker.

cases.title: An arq quarterly schedule loses its time zone at a month boundary

findings.observation: With the reported schedule, 0.25.0 and the fix parent raised TypeError on the next heartbeat after crossing a month boundary. The fix commit, 0.26.0 and 0.26.1 retained the time zone.
findings.interpretation: Inside the same worker.main Task, the month-end branch produced a naive datetime that run_cron compared with an aware deadline before the job started. The fix preserved tzinfo.
findings.limits: The reporter corrected the version to an unspecified older release. The local worker used the published schedule and a placeholder job.

cases.title: Arrow returned a positive running maximum for a negative first value

findings.observation: The reporter passed −2.5 and 2.5 to PyArrow and to a pandas Series backed by Arrow. The first prefix contains only −2.5. Both calls on 25.0.1 returned 2.2250738585072014e-308 for that prefix. Both calls on 26.0.0 returned −2.5. In a separate five-row IPC job the affected release produced four wrong prefixes. Supplying the first observation as the explicit start restored both values on the original fixture.
findings.interpretation: GDB stopped before and after the float64 maximum instruction in the shipped compute library. The accumulator on 25.0.1 started at the smallest positive normal double and retained it when compared with −2.5. On 26.0.0 the accumulator started at negative infinity and took the observed value −2.5. The direct and chunked paths reached the same Max accumulator through Arrow’s vector executor. The landed change replaced the floating-point default maximum seed with negative infinity.
findings.limits: The physical samples come from the synchronous reporter program. The Fairbanks job ran separately on NOAA’s 366 daily highs for 2024. Its three float64 paths gave the same wrong year-to-date high for 43 dates, through February 12. The correct high on January 1 was −19.3 °C. On February 13 the daily high reached +5.0 °C and all paths agreed. Integer tenths matched every date on both releases. A fresh extracted replay reproduced every weather IPC file and result JSON byte for byte against both independently supplied batches.

cases.title: Parquet footer statistics undercount nulls in a repeated column

findings.observation: For [[0, 1], None, [2, None, 3]], the old footer reported one null and five non-null values instead of two and four. Both versions read back all three rows with the same minimum and maximum.
findings.interpretation: The old calculation subtracted four non-null values from five leaf slots, overlooking the outer None. The fix used all six level entries, and replacing the outer None with [None] also corrected the old count.
findings.limits: Checked column-chunk statistics and decoded values, with synchronous native stacks. Query pruning was untested.
