cases.title: Cache eviction leaves callers waiting after their work finishes

findings.observation: With 20 concurrent keys, capacity 5 and a 60-second TTL, all 20 computations finished but 15 Futures remained pending on 2.0.2 and the fix’s parent. The fix delivered all 20 values.
findings.interpretation: Each of the 15 KeyErrors came from a completion callback looking up an evicted key, while the corresponding caller was still awaiting shield(fut).
findings.limits: Each affected build was run twice with an external timeout. Future identities came from extra probes. The callbacks ran on the event loop.

cases.title: A cached async call loses its caller from the live stack

findings.observation: On 2.0.4 and the experimental branch’s parent, inspect.stack() showed only bar. Directly awaiting it also showed foo and main, as did the propagated exception traceback in the second example.
findings.interpretation: A cache miss created a child Task for bar, whose creation stack identified foo and main and distinguished its first caller from four other waiters sharing the result.
findings.limits: The issue concerned logging, and the experimental direct-await branch had a separate cleanup error.

cases.title: Descending async merge reverses source order for equal keys

findings.observation: For tied keys, descending merge yielded the second source first, while heapq.merge yielded the first, and correcting the order also changed which SQLite partition supplied both top results.
findings.interpretation: Equal keys carried source indices 0 and −1, so the second source left the heap first, and changing only the key comparator preserved the error, while correcting the source indices resolved it.
findings.limits: The original example and upstream regression test ran locally. The three-partition SQLite selection was a separate control.

cases.title: Async max selects the last item tied for first

findings.observation: For two records tied at the maximum key of 1, asyncstdlib selected second while Python’s max kept first. The fix also kept the earlier record in a 14-row database control.
findings.interpretation: The old _min_max combined invert with a less-than comparison using XOR, so equality executed best = item. The fixed version skipped that assignment.
findings.limits: The posted example and upstream regression ran locally. The task origin belongs to the example’s main task, and the database cursor was a separate ordering check.

cases.title: Cursor prefetch delays delivery of rows that are already available

findings.observation: With row three held on PostgreSQL 14, asyncpg 0.29.0 delivered nothing before release at prefetch 4 or 50 and delivered rows 1 and 2 at prefetch 1, while the other cursor returned all five.
findings.interpretation: Task stacks distinguished the initial batch fetch from the next single-row fetch, and protocol records showed a complete large DataRow could arrive before the application saw any row.
findings.limits: The report supplied no SQL or versions. A local cooperative lock controlled readiness, and stacks alone could not distinguish buffering from batch delivery.

cases.title: Why did a PostgreSQL date range raise an error, and December 31 become year 1?

findings.observation: PostgreSQL stored the inclusive range [-infinity,infinity]. Reading it with asyncpg 0.8.3 raised ValueError: ordinal must be >= 1. A finite date exposed the same bug silently. PostgreSQL returned 1999-12-31, and the old driver delivered 0001-01-01. The 0.8.4 wheel and its exact source commit read the infinite endpoints as Python’s minimum and maximum dates and returned the finite date correctly. The reporter’s minimal script produced the same outcome in both trials of each build. The first table also shows the reverse direction, binding Python date.min and reading PostgreSQL’s text for that value. In 24 comparisons the received binary fields agreed byte for byte with independent libpq and PostgreSQL COPY reads.
findings.interpretation:
PostgreSQL encodes a date as a signed count of days from 2000-01-01. Its bytes for 1999-12-31 are ffffffff (−1). Its negative-infinity sentinel is 80000000 (−2147483648). The loaded 0.8.3 decoder compared against −1. When the actual infinity arrived, the decoder added −2147483648 to the epoch ordinal 730120 and passed −2146753528 to date.fromordinal. GDB recorded that argument and the decoder’s failed return. The fix uses the signed 32-bit minimum for DATE. On the finite −1 input the corrected decoder passed 730119 to date.fromordinal and returned December 31.

Inside Connection.fetch, asyncpg/connection.py line 268 created _get_statement. CPython sampled that same coroutine object and frame at line 233 as it returned the prepared statement (0.8.3 graph segments 3 and 21). GDB found the same statement and waiting Future on the active protocol while the receive callback decoded the row. The reporter had created the outer fetch at reporter.py line 12. That fetch resumed with the ValueError (segments 1 and 29). On 0.8.4 it returned the inclusive range (segments 1 and 31).

In a separate finite-only test, PostgreSQL evaluated its range-containment operator for four windows and nine probe dates. Python evaluated lower ≤ day < upper using the returned endpoints. Moving a lower bound from 1999-12-31 to year 1 admitted five extra dates, including 1900-01-01. Moving an upper bound to year 1 excluded two valid dates. Each affected build disagreed on seven of 36 checks in each trial. Both corrected builds agreed on all 36.
findings.limits: The opening report queried the author’s application table and described 0.7.0 as working. This replay uses the author’s later self-contained test_62 script, CPython 3.6.5 and a local PostgreSQL 10.23 server. The four builds represent two commits, each tested as a released wheel and a source build. Explicit infinite DATE endpoints are inclusive values here. The separate unbounded-range control returned absent endpoints on every build. Cases with finite December 30, the epoch date and positive infinity also agreed. For timestamp one microsecond before the epoch, 0.8.4 still returned 2000-01-01 00:00:00.999999, one second late. That fractional-timestamp behavior belongs to separate issue #363. The coroutine-origin count for #62 is one. GDB stops describe ordinary native callback frames.

cases.title: Reading an enum array changes later scalar enum handling

findings.observation: Reading the array first returned strings, the next scalar came back as the plain string paper, and querying row 2 with Choice.paper raised DataError.
findings.interpretation: The array codec was built with CODEC_C/BINARY in the affected release and CODEC_PY/TEXT after the fix, pinpointing the format selection during codec construction.
findings.limits: The local PostgreSQL 10.23 baseline used Python 3.7.6. The GDB and asyncio evidence came from separate processes.

cases.title: asyncpg added one second to fractional timestamps before 2000

findings.observation: The reporter queried 1970-01-01 20:31:23.648000. PostgreSQL returned the correct bytes. On asyncpg 0.17.0 the application read 20:31:24.648000. The fix and release 0.18.0 returned the original timestamp. Two independent USGS earthquake times from 1989 and 1994 also gained one second in the affected builds. An interval of minus one microsecond came back as positive 999,999 microseconds.
findings.interpretation: A native stack reached timestamp_decode from the PostgreSQL row decoder. For the posted value, the affected helper split −946,610,916,352,000 microseconds into −946,610,916 seconds and a positive remainder of 648,000 microseconds. That quotient was one second too large. The fixed helper rounded the quotient down to −946,610,917 and kept the same remainder. A separate coroutine capture linked the main task created in the reporter’s script to fetchval returning the shifted time.
findings.limits: The original Python 3.6.5 program ran against local PostgreSQL 10.23 with the connection port substituted. The report used PostgreSQL 10.3. The published wheel supplied the native decoder stack. Debug builds at the parent and fixing commits supplied the local integer values. The protocol callback and the application task were captured in separate runs.

cases.title: Why did an eight-place PostgreSQL decimal come back with twelve places?

findings.observation: The reporter stored 0.00003000 in a NUMERIC(1000,8) column. The original script returned 0.000030000000 on asyncpg 0.18.3 and 0.20.0, and 0.00003000 on 0.20.1. PostgreSQL sent the same numerical value and a display scale of eight. On each release we also ran one read-only query three times on the same connection. Selecting the text decoder removed the four extra places on both affected releases. Restoring the default binary decoder brought them back. The last two columns count scale mismatches across 22 stored rows in each column type.
findings.interpretation: The affected fetchrow coroutine returned the same Record and Decimal later read by the caller. Its creation and return stacks identify where that query originated. PostgreSQL encoded the number as one base-10,000 group containing 3000 at weight −2. The old decoder’s fractional-digit calculation omitted the leading zero group and added four trailing zeros. In the fixed decoder the native stack recorded eight fractional digits and zero adjustment. This explains why the numerical value stayed equal while the Decimal exponent changed. Copying the actual result into an unconstrained NUMERIC column three times persisted the extra places at each step.
findings.limits: The stock release runs used Linux, CPython 3.7.6, asyncio and PostgreSQL 11.5. The creation stack comes from a separate observed run of the reported SELECT. It follows one physical fetchrow coroutine. Protocol decoding ran in an event-loop callback. Native decoder locals were measured on a debug build of the fixed release. The affected release’s arithmetic is inferred from its shipped source, the wire values and the same-connection codec switch.

cases.title: An extra None in an asynchronous running total

findings.observation: The reporter summed three items, 1, 2 and 3, with initial=None. Both 3.13.1 and the immediate parent of PR #178 returned [None, 1, 3, 6]. The merged fix and 3.13.2 returned [1, 3, 6], matching itertools in the same program. All four calls completed successfully.
findings.interpretation: On the affected build the first yield occurred before the input generator supplied 1. The reducer then received (None, 1). The fixed build read 1 before its first yield and first called the reducer with (1, 2). The captured caller created the reporter’s collector coroutine at line 32. That identical object returned the measured list at line 30.
findings.limits: Each build ran in two plain and two instrumented processes on a local asyncio event loop. Coroutine identity covers the reporter’s collector. The library’s async generator has physical yield samples. This experiment uses finite streams in one process.

cases.title: asyncstdlib.heapq.merge reverses the source order of equal keys

findings.observation: The example yielded uvw, abc, xyz, def, while the stable standard-library merge yielded abc, uvw, def, xyz.
findings.interpretation: Distinct heap wrappers inherited identity-based equality, so equal keys never reached the tuple’s source-order tiebreaker. Changing only equality produced the expected order and matched the observed comparisons.
findings.limits: The report did not pin versions. Python probes captured the comparisons around the C tuple operation, and Task attribution covers the merge’s main Task.

cases.title: A nested async tee skips records when its parent advances

findings.observation: Two branches created at different positions returned 6, 7, 8 and 9 on 3.13.1 and the fix parent. The fixed commit, 3.13.2 and the synchronous itertools reference returned 1, 4, 2 and 5. Three of ten file-backed controls lost records on the old builds.
findings.interpretation: On the old build, advancing either child entered tee_peer twice and fetched a new source value. The child had its own buffer and wrapped its parent. On the fixed build, each child inherited the buffer position at its fork, and all four reads were served without another source read.
findings.limits: The report runs on a single top-level async execution. The evidence identifies iterators and their buffers. All eleven selected upstream tests passed on all four builds; the original reproduction and independent file controls distinguish the faulty behavior.

cases.title: Beam rejects duplicated() on a deferred Series

findings.observation: On Beam 2.77.0 and 2.78.0, duplicated() on the named Series [1, 2, 1] raised WontImplementError for keep=False and keep='any', while the DataFrame control succeeded.
findings.interpretation: The aggregation already returned a Boolean mask. Removing the extra column lookup and restoring the name yielded [true, false, true] for keep=False across three partitions.
findings.limits: The failure occurred during driver-side planning. The successful control used the merged production module.

cases.title: RunInference’s file watcher can publish an older model after a newer one

findings.observation: A single poll published two new model files, separate polls could publish the older file last, and replaying the two same-poll outputs made the first inference batch reject a singleton input of size two.
findings.interpretation: Both paths began with the same initial timestamp and each key’s singleton counter started at zero, allowing both models through the per-path state checks.
findings.limits: Prism required separate jobs for live file polling and inference replay. The control used the proposed PR and a local multiplier model.

cases.title: A Bolt reader waiting for a writer can block a database remap

findings.observation: The reporter’s on-disk test blocked in all four runs and passed in all four when the read transaction returned before waiting for the writer.
findings.interpretation: The reader held the mapping lock the writer needed at the 32,768-byte remap boundary; reopening the same-size file let the writer reuse pages 2 and 3 and commit.
findings.limits: The report gave no Bolt revision, so the test used a contemporary commit. Cross-device index exchange was outside the test.

cases.title: Why did a yearly date range skip every other December?

findings.observation:
The reporter iterated from December 25, 2012 to January 1, 2023 with a one-year step and an exclusive stop. boltons 21.0.0 yielded six dates, all in even years. The immediate source parent returned the same sequence. The landed commit and 23.0.0 yielded December 25 in all eleven years. A recursive SQLite query independently advanced each date by one calendar year.

A separate SQLite table held one record per December 25, with quantities 1 through 11. Joining the generator’s dates to those records selected six records totaling 36 units on the affected builds. The corrected builds selected eleven records totaling 66 units.
findings.interpretation:
The first physical yield in the reporter’s loop returned December 25, 2012. In the 21.0.0 graph, segments 2 and 3 sample the multi-line date.replace expression at timeutils.py line 393. The year step was 1, the month step 0, and divmod(12, 12) gave a year carry of 1 with remainder 0. The expression added both the explicit year step and the carry. Segment 4 records the next yield, December 25, 2014. In 23.0.0 the code converts the year step to 12 months and computes from a zero-based month index. The carry is 1 with remainder 11, which maps back to December. Line 395 adds only that carry. Segment 4 records December 25, 2013.

The landed upstream test uses a shorter stop date, January 1, 2016. Its annual assertion expected four dates and found two on the affected builds. Both assertions in the landed test passed on the corrected builds. The thirteen-month example also passed independently on every build.
findings.limits: The December 2022 report supplied the loop and its date bounds without a release number or imports. The replay prepends imports for date and daterange to those statements. The 21.0.0 and 23.0.0 controls are official PyPI wheels. The source comparison uses complete boltons packages from the adjacent Git commits. These runs used CPython 3.10.12 and date values without time zones. The table and quantities are a separate local application control. The execution samples belong to a synchronous generator and the coroutine-origin count is zero.

cases.title: Cassandra SELECT JSON displayed empty text as null

findings.observation: Cassandra 3.11.2 returned null in two of the four JSON rows from the reported queries. One held an empty text column. The other had an empty clustering key and age 42. Ordinary SELECT returned zero bytes for both text values. Apache releases 3.0.8 and 3.11.3 rendered both as the JSON string "".
findings.interpretation: The parent renderer received a present buffer with zero remaining bytes and appended the four characters null. The fix appended two double quotes. The observed return bytes matched the native protocol response for each row. After a flush and clean restart, the same reads reproduced the discrepancy. Offline SSTable export recovered the empty values in all seven databases.
findings.limits: Each build ran on one healthy node. The client replayed the successful CQL from the report over native protocol v4. Omitted-column and absent-partition reads, direct clustering-key lookup, and the persistence checks are supplemental. The exact parent and fix runs compiled their Selection.java against the same 3.11.2 distribution. The physical stacks identify native request workers. Coroutine creation was unobserved.

cases.title: A failed conditional delete omitted a null static column

findings.observation: Cassandra 3.0.9 sent the same one-column reply for an existing partition with a null s2 and for an absent partition. The fix included the integer column s2 with a null value for the existing partition. Six three-node clusters produced 60 conditional results and 216 table readbacks.
findings.interpretation: Coordinator stacks identify the read filter, the failed predicate and the result builder. The parent read zero rows from the existing partition. The fix read one clustering row, giving the result builder enough information to include s2. Both versions returned its value 7 in the non-null control and reported success when the condition matched.
findings.limits: The report compared Cassandra 2.x and 3.x. Local runs covered stock 3.0.9 and 3.0.10 and the exact changed production class on 3.0.9. One- and three-replica controls checked data and Paxos ballots. The captured JVM stacks identify worker threads.

cases.title: CatBoost accuracy changes when labels are reshaped to a single column

findings.observation: On the posted classifier, the same labels scored 1.0 as a vector and 0.5 as a column in CatBoost 1.2.10, the reported source revision and the fix parent. Inverting every label still gave 0.5 for the column. The fix returned 1.0 for the correct labels and 0.0 for the inverted labels.
findings.interpretation: The captured comparison paired each one-dimensional prediction with every row of the label column. The fix flattened the single-column labels before comparing. For a reordered five-row sample, the old score counted 13 of 25 pairs and the fixed score counted the three correct rows out of five.
findings.limits: The experiment covers single-target CPU classification on Linux x86-64. The reporter used macOS arm64. The source comparisons shared the same release native extension, and the traced scoring calls ran synchronously.

cases.title: Why did a Celery chord return ten results in reverse order?

findings.observation: A Celery 5.3.1 producer submitted ten tasks numbered 0 through 9. All ten completed successfully. We released them in a known, nonsequential order. With descending task IDs the callback received 9 through 0. Independently reading the Redis sorted set after each of the first nine writes showed that every stored result had the same score.
findings.interpretation: The producer stack shows group._prepared calling Signature.freeze without a group index for generator tasks. All ten broker messages carried a null index. On the worker, RedisBackend.on_chord_part_return converted each missing index to positive infinity. Redis then sorted equal-scored members by their encoded bytes, which include the task ID. The gevent creation stack and the result-write stack identify the same worker greenlet. Changing just the producer to 5.3.4 restored input order with the 5.3.1 worker.
findings.limits: The experiment used Redis for message transport and results. The reporter used RabbitMQ for transport. The generated-ID case ran freely. Controlled IDs and completion gates distinguish submission order, completion order and Redis ordering. Function stacks were captured in separate runs of the released Python packages using observer callbacks.

cases.title: Chroma matched a stored integer of 2 against a filter for 2.5

findings.observation: Chroma 1.5.9 returned both int2 and float2_5 for equality with 2.5. It also omitted int2 when asked for values below 2.5. On 178 Wine measurements with mixed numeric types, 30 of 56 filters returned incorrect ID sets. Across those filters, 288 record memberships differed from direct numeric comparisons.
findings.interpretation: The native Rust stack reached the helper that builds one SQL branch per storage type. On the parent build, the integer threshold read 2 and the floating-point threshold read 2.5. The SQLite worker bound those values and executed the union. In the proposed build the integer equality branch evaluated to false. For the greater-than-or-equal filter its threshold was 3. Replaying the same statements and bindings against the saved databases returned the same IDs.
findings.limits: The reported wheel and two Rust source builds ran on Linux x86_64. The reporter used macOS ARM64. Membership comparisons ignore the order of IDs. The Wine workload uses ordinary finite measurements. The comparison build is the head of an open proposal. Each native capture identifies the executing thread.

cases.title: The CockroachDB CLI displays CHAR text as escaped bytes

findings.observation: With the reporter’s six SQL statements, the v22.1.0 client escaped the six UTF-8 bytes for the Chinese greeting “hello” in CHAR(10) but displayed the two characters correctly in VARCHAR(10).
findings.interpretation: Type comparisons, encoder arguments and return values isolated the old CLI formatter’s byte branch, while the linked fix switched the CLI driver to pgx.
findings.limits: The report omitted the version. Independent libpq reads and GDB checked padding that the table display trims.

cases.title: Why did skipping one conflicting row also discard the next valid row?

findings.observation: The table already contained (1, 1, 1). The batch proposed (1, 2, 1) and (3, 2, 2). The first candidate reused primary key 1. The second could use secondary key 2 because the first candidate never entered the table. Both affected releases reported INSERT 0. Every gateway in each three-node cluster returned only the seed row, including reads forced through the primary and secondary indexes. The January alpha and v19.1.0 reported INSERT 1 and stored (3, 2, 2). Splitting the batch or reversing the two candidates recovered the valid row on the affected releases.
findings.interpretation: The sampled SQL connection goroutine reached strictTableUpserter.getConflictingRows. On the December alpha it reserved the first candidate’s secondary key while preparing the storage reads. Its next lookup found the same key in the same Go map and marked the second candidate for omission. Both releases then read the same four keys from storage. Only the first primary key existed. The January alpha checked storage first, omitted the first row and reached row.Inserter.InsertRow with the values (3, 2, 2). The creation stack and scheduler observation match the goroutine performing these decisions.
findings.limits: The report gives the SQL and expected PostgreSQL result. Its CockroachDB version is unspecified. Native stacks come from the two dated alpha releases on opposite sides of the fix. The table below the original result covers 24 extra candidate orders. Each family has six orders and the counts include any statement error. The six errors on v19.1.0 occurred when proposed rows conflicted with each other. Its default plan used two index lookups and an inserter. Switching the same release to its strict upserter handled all six orders. Both plans passed the original reported SQL.

cases.title: Followers reject pre-votes from their former leader

findings.observation: After a brief AppendEntries interruption ended, two followers that still recognized the former leader repeatedly rejected its pre-votes and delayed a new election.
findings.interpretation: The requestPreVote rejection stack and RPC records exposed an incorrectly decoded candidate address. PR #605 read it from the RPC header and eliminated rejections under the same interruption.
findings.limits: Three nodes shared one Go process and communicated over loopback TCP. Different election timeouts made the lease-expiry order repeatable.

cases.title: A re-elected Raft leader keeps rejecting writes after leadership transfer

findings.observation: After two leadership transfers with one follower’s replication delayed, the original leader stepped down, won re-election and still rejected new writes after the follower caught up.
findings.interpretation: The affected run showed the channel waits described in proposed PR #708, where a blocked replication trigger could leave the transfer flag set. With the proposal, the first write after recovery committed.
findings.limits: Three local nodes and five observed write attempts per failure. The proposal was unmerged, and the observation window does not establish a permanent stall.

cases.title: Idle KRaft controllers report five seconds of queue time

findings.observation: In a three-controller KRaft cluster, a five-second idle-write interval drove the active controller’s EventQueueTimeMs p99 to 5,000 ms in both affected runs, versus 0 ms in both patched runs and both 3.3.0 runs.
findings.interpretation: Changing only QuorumController removed the timing call for the scheduled write while replication continued and ordinary createTopics requests still updated the metric.
findings.limits: The test covers the idle-controller false positive. Production backlog, failover, and other delayed events were outside its scope.

cases.title: A successful Consul transaction returns the wrong index for an unchanged key

findings.observation: A same-value CAS returned HTTP 200, but reusing its reported index returned 409 in both trials on each affected release, while all three replicas retained the same value.
findings.interpretation: The Raft apply stack traced the wrong response index to the unchanged-value branch, while the isolated fix and 1.8.0 preserved the original index and advanced only keys that changed.
findings.limits: The test used ordinary KV transactions on three healthy local voters. The identified FSM goroutine belonged to the replay.

cases.title: Why did a longer prompt return no new tokens in a mixed batch?

findings.observation: The reporter’s asynchronous Python program submitted six translation prompts to CTranslate2. With GPT-2 on CPU, the longest input had 204 tokens and the shortest had 56. The requested maximum was 80 new tokens. The 3.15.1 worker called the decoder 80 times and returned an empty sequence for the longest input. The 3.16.0 worker called it 191 times and returned 43 tokens for that input. The same output list passed from the executor thread through the generate coroutine to run_test.
findings.interpretation: The maintainer’s deterministic regression isolates the length calculation. After processing the common prompt length, the longer row still had two supplied tokens to consume. In both greedy and beam search, the affected decoder ran at positions 2 and 3, consumed those tokens, and returned an empty continuation from native search. The first fixed wheel also ran at positions 4 and 5 and returned [2497, 262] (“ saw the”), matching independent PyTorch inference. Reversing input order moved the empty result with the longer prompt. The archived native stacks place the positional decoder inside search. CPython recorded run_test creating the generate coroutine at line 99 and observed the same frame resume with the affected result at line 69.
findings.limits: The original deployment used a 13B Vicuna-family model, CUDA, and int8/float16. This replay used GPT-2, its tokenizer and float32 on CPU. It retained the posted run_test and generate definitions, prompt text and generation arguments, selected six inputs with a recorded seed, and stopped after one batch. The first table gives the sampled run’s actual lengths. The pytest table uses deterministic generation. Only the Python generate coroutine contributes an origin. The executor and native worker have their own recorded thread identities.

cases.title: Dask assigned accident counts to the wrong year during aggregation

findings.observation: The input contained 2,845,342 accidents. Dask 2023.4.1 kept that total but reported 78,677 severity-2 accidents for 2021. A row-by-row count found 1,487,713. The fixed version returned the independent counts for every year and severity. A single-partition read also returned the correct counts on the parent.
findings.interpretation: In one captured _value_counts_aggregate call, a severity-2 subtotal of 324,582 was labeled 2020 before Dask reassigned the MultiIndex levels and 2018 afterward. The integer codes and counts stayed identical across that line. The parent copied the year labels from the input in a different order. The fixed build kept the result labels in their original order across all six recorded aggregation calls.
findings.limits: The report linked to a dataset with multiple releases. The archived December 2021 CSV differs from the reporter’s copy in all 18 published reference cells. The table separates the two sets of counts. The maintainer’s pandas 1.5.3 example ran with its local file path replaced. The stock runs used the default scheduler. The two stack captures used the synchronous scheduler and reproduced the same totals and groups.

cases.title: The Dask dashboard counts the same keys under two task names

findings.observation: Two workers held three keys and returned [3, 2, 7], yet the dashboard showed sum=3 and len=3. Adding one sum returned 17 and raised both counts to 4.
findings.interpretation: An empty fallback group name made both prefixes count all the same keys, and changing that fallback alone corrected the displayed counts.
findings.limits: The original tasks ran on two local TCP workers. Chromium independently confirmed the rendered dashboard counts.

cases.title: A Dask bag built from zero files lost its dataframe schema

findings.observation: In the two posted examples, filtering four records down to zero produced an empty pandas DataFrame with an integer column named a. Starting from an empty list returned an empty tuple. The two fixed builds produced the typed DataFrame in both cases.
findings.interpretation: The from_sequence call recorded zero input partitions on the affected builds. Bag.to_dataframe had the column metadata, but it scheduled zero conversion tasks. The finalizer called _concat with no partition results and returned the empty tuple. The fix created one empty partition. The worker converted it to a typed DataFrame, which the finalizer returned.
findings.limits: The public example ran on the reported Python 3.6.5, Dask 0.19.3 and pandas 0.23.4. The directory experiment used local monthly files from the Seattle weather dataset. A calendar join checked 191 rainy days in 2012 and 1,461 dates in total against the source CSV under both synchronous and threaded scheduling. These traces cover ordinary calls and worker tasks.

cases.title: Dask returned the first column twice when computing grouped cumulative sums

findings.observation: The six-row program from the issue asks for the cumulative sums of ones and twos. Dask 0.18.1 returned the name ones and values 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2 twice. On 731 days of bike rentals, all 731 registered-rider totals were wrong when casual riders were requested first. Reversing the arguments reversed which column was lost. Computing the columns separately returned the correct totals.
findings.interpretation: The captured _GroupBy._cum_agg calls assign identical output task names to the two columns. During dask.compute, _unpack assigns both to slot 0 and retains the first collection. The merged graph has one output. Separating only the output names restored both slots but exposed a second collision in the carry tasks. On February 13, the casual-rider calculation added 397 to the registered carry of 16,932, returning 17,329. The correct casual carry was 1,443. The upstream fix distinguishes both sets of names. Its results match independent integer sums in all 15 settings.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied the six-row program and did not name a Dask release. We selected releases on either side of the fix and added the UCI Bike Sharing daily dataset to test partition boundaries. The captures show synchronous Python calls. The coroutine-origin count is unchanged.

cases.title: A groupby shift assigns values to the wrong rows after a shuffle

findings.observation: On the six-row example, Dask 2022.2.0 failed 48 of 48 runs: rows indexed 1 and 2 received 30 and 40 where both should have been missing.
findings.interpretation: The disk shuffle delivered one group in index order 5, 1, 3 before pandas shifted it. Sorting the index in the fix also eliminated 20 lag and 18 lead errors in a reversed-partition control.
findings.limits: The original used macOS. The Linux replay pinned pandas 1.4.1. Partition order was controlled only in the separate 96-row experiment.

cases.title: Dask Series.map loses lookups across partition boundaries

findings.observation: Dask 2026.3.0 failed all 55 of the reporter’s Series tests. Mapping destinations to states for 2,000 flight records exposed a second symptom. The airport directory contained every destination, yet 1,804 results were missing. Dask 2026.6.0 passed all 55 tests and returned every state.
findings.interpretation: The failing test reaches Map._divisions with the expected pandas Series in the slot for a Boolean flag. In the flight run, the old scheduler plan split the airport directory by row index. The pandas.Series.map call for one Albuquerque flight had 81 airport keys and lacked LAS. After the fix, each worker call saw all 3,376 keys and returned the state for every destination.
findings.limits: The replay used Dask’s local threaded scheduler. SQLite and a separate Python dictionary agreed on every reference value. Removing LAX erased exactly the 94 flights to that airport on the fixed build. The separate Index tests still had 25 failures on that build. The recorded frames cover synchronous worker calls.

cases.title: Dask dropped the month-end count when the last input fell on January 31

findings.observation: The reporter supplied two January rows. Dask 2023.10.1 returned an empty tuple for month end when the second date was January 31. Changing only that date to January 30 returned the January 31 count of 2. Month start returned 2 in both cases. The full January and quarter inputs also lost their expected end-labeled counts of 31 and 90.
findings.interpretation: The planner retained one output boundary when the final input date equaled the period label. Forming intervals from adjacent output boundaries produced zero aggregation keys. The finalizer received zero partitions and returned an empty tuple. With January 30 as the last input, the planner produced two boundaries and a thread-pool worker counted both rows. Independent calendar counts and pandas agree across the measured inputs.
findings.limits: The original examples use one partition. The local run used Linux and the reported Python, Dask and pandas versions. The taxi input consists of December 2024 pickups before 00:05 each day, grouped by pickup date. The release comparison uses each version’s default execution path. Dask 2025.12.0 with pandas 2.2.3 raised IndexError on the January 31 input. The issue was open when checked. The capture records local Python stacks and supplies no coroutine creation identity.

cases.title: Dask undercounts replicated task data and can report negative bytes

findings.observation: Five 160-byte chunks replicated across two workers occupied 1,600 bytes, but TaskGroup.nbytes_in_memory reported 800 and fell to −800 after release.
findings.interpretation: Separate handle_comm tasks handled replication and release for the same key and TaskState. The retained task group exposed the accounting discrepancy across those operations.
findings.limits: The measurement covers array payloads on two local workers. A downstream dependency kept the group observable. The fix removed the counter.

cases.title: Why did sorting a three-row Dask DataFrame return zero rows?

findings.observation: The reporter set the index to b = [3, 1, 3] across two partitions, sorted by a, and asked for the length. Dask 2023.9.0 and the fix parent returned 0 in both trials. Computing the rows separately returned an empty frame. The fix and 2023.9.1 returned all three (a, b-index) pairs in order. Both a direct sort of the input and pandas gave (1, 3), (2, 1), (3, 3). Each build also returned three rows with the reporter’s ordered keys, unique keys and one-partition controls.
findings.interpretation: Both workers’ saved Arrow files together contained all three rows. The affected workers wrote files named 0.0 and 1.0. The output coroutines asked for 0 and 1, handled the lookup misses, and returned empty partitions. On 2023.9.1 the filenames matched and the reads returned both partitions. For partition 0 the runtime links creation in distributed.utils.sync (segment 16) to the disk read (22) by the same task and coroutine frame. The metadata was built earlier on the driver. In rearrange_by_divisions the example index was [1, 2]. The affected partition metadata used [0] and the assigned column was float64. The fix aligned it to [1] and the column stayed int64. Applying the landed index assignment in both metadata builders on the old release restored three rows. Removing it from both on the newer release triggered the integer-column check while planning the final shuffle.
findings.limits: The posted length and the ordered rows came from separate evaluations on the same indexed frame. Worker disk traces cover the two releases. The paired Dask source runs held distributed at 2023.9.0. The matched coroutine explains the empty partition returned by the worker. The link to the driver’s metadata decision comes from comparing the driver measurements, landed source and separate alignment experiment across runs. Both landed dtype tests failed on the affected builds and passed on the corrected builds. The task-shuffle and fractional-index controls each returned three rows in all four alignment runs. The second table uses a separate synthetic input of eight records totaling 44 units. Units are summed from the rows each computation actually returned.

cases.title: Reading only the SQL index discarded every populated Dask partition

findings.observation: SQLite returned 3,503 track IDs across four partitions. Dask 2021.02.0 returned zero of them when asked for the index alone. Selecting the track name as well returned all 3,503 IDs. The same index-only read lost all 50 rows in a single-column table. Both affected reads returned every ID on the fixed build.
findings.interpretation: Each sampled _read_sql_chunk return on the parent showed a fetched DataFrame with hundreds of IDs and zero ordinary columns alongside a metadata template with zero IDs. The pandas empty property was true for the fetched frame. Dask returned the metadata template. The fixed branch measured the number of rows and returned the fetched frame. Independent SQLite reads reproduced the exact index digest of each recorded chunk.
findings.limits: The posted call omitted the partition setting required with head_rows=0 and explicit metadata. Running it as written raised the same validation error on all four builds. The partitioned runs supplied this parameter. The catalog is the public Chinook sample database. The CPython stack samples cover synchronous computation. Both synchronous and threaded reads produced the same user-visible results with pandas 1.2.5 and SQLAlchemy 1.3.24.

cases.title: Dask reverses contraction axes when calculating tensordot chunks

findings.observation: The reported 4×5 input produced chunks ((5,), (5,)) and a ValueError before the fix, while afterward it returned 20, matching NumPy.
findings.interpretation: The old path expanded axes=2 as (1,0) on the left and (0,1) on the right, while correcting the order also changed a square control’s sum from 69 to 70.
findings.limits: The reporter did not pin Dask. Tests covered 2.5.2 and the commits around the merge. The block-product control used synchronous scheduling.

cases.title: Worker log requests return the oldest entries first

findings.observation: The reporter’s one- and two-worker programs returned the two oldest startup records on both affected releases, while 2023.1.1 and the fix returned the newest first.
findings.interpretation: The worker’s RPC task scanned the log queue from the head and stopped at the requested limit. Reversing iteration also restored the time-filtered results.
findings.limits: Local Linux TCP workers ran in separate processes. The two nannies shared a process and logger, so their broadcast results were checked individually.

cases.title: Cancelling a timed acquire leaves an asyncpg pool slot occupied

findings.observation: The application never entered the connection context, yet the pool’s only slot remained occupied and close() did not return within 150 ms.
findings.interpretation: Cancellation discarded an already-completed acquire result before cleanup could run. 0.22.0 retained the result and released the same connection through the context manager.
findings.limits: The test used one slot, CPython 3.7 and PostgreSQL 11. The wait was bounded, and uvloop was not tested.

cases.title: An asyncpg backend survives cancellation after its pool entry is invalidated

findings.observation: After AnyIO cancelled a transaction task, the pool reported zero checked-out connections, yet the original PostgreSQL backend was still alive after a new connection opened and dispose() completed.
findings.interpretation: The hard-close stack reached driver cleanup that could itself be cancelled. Shielding close in 2.0.38 removed the old PID by context exit, while asyncio.TaskGroup on 2.0.36 allowed normal reuse and disposal.
findings.limits: Each local process cancelled once, with an independent observer connection. The final PID check establishes liveness only at that instant.

cases.title: A UNION selecting only an annotation returns integers instead of booleans

findings.observation: On two independent PostgreSQL clusters, the upstream test returned [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4] on the fix parent and [False, True] after the fix.
findings.interpretation: Selecting only the outer annotation left values_select empty, so UNION deduplicated full five-column rows. The fix passed is_creator to both branches, and projecting it inside each old branch also returned the two booleans.
findings.limits: Synchronous PostgreSQL regression test with the original OuterRef(pk). No async Task identity was recorded.

cases.title: A nested RETURNING clause shifted PostgreSQL result columns

findings.observation: The database returned object ID 901 and event ID 101. Reading the result by name returned 101 for the object ID on the report-era client. A positional lookup returned 901. All 412 invoice inserts from the Chinook sample database produced incorrectly mapped records on the proposal parent. Restoring each database recovered every expected object and event.
findings.interpretation: The captured backend coroutine compiled the inner event ID first, then appended the four outer RETURNING fields. Record.__init__ received five column descriptions for four driver values. It assigned the outer ID to position one, which held the event ID. Two replays linked the unstarted coroutine returned to Connection.fetch_one to the mapping stack after 4.370 ms and 5.778 ms. The same Record was then used for the incorrect named lookup.
findings.limits: The historical run used releases available when the issue was filed. A test-only wrapper observed the unstarted coroutine before returning it unchanged to the caller. The contributor proposal passed the submitted test. A control with distinct note and article IDs exposed a remaining column-object lookup error on that branch. The later release comparison changed both databases and SQLAlchemy.

cases.title: A PostgreSQL row turns into an empty dictionary after a raw SQL query

findings.observation: Using databases 0.2.2 and asyncpg 0.18.3, reading row['id'] returned 101. The same row converted to an empty dictionary and tested false. A SQLAlchemy expression selecting the same four fields returned all four. The error also reproduced on 0.2.4. Version 0.2.5 returned four fields for both queries.
findings.interpretation: The same returned row reached Record.__iter__ and Record.__len__. For raw SQL the compiler supplied zero column names, even though the driver held four values. The old methods used the compiler’s column list. The fix reads the underlying asyncpg record. In the two-depot run, each task’s creation in dispatch_snapshot was matched to the iteration of the rows that task actually fetched.
findings.limits: The original report supplies the API calls and dependency versions. The local run used a PostgreSQL 10.23 server with four inventory rows. The paired task origins come from the concurrent depot reads. Restoring the database dump and changing one quantity from 0 to 9 independently confirmed the driver and fixed mapping returned the new value.

cases.title: An expanding SQLAlchemy IN parameter reaches PostgreSQL unrendered

findings.observation: The reported IN query for IDs 1, 3 and 4 failed at a literal square bracket with SQLSTATE 42601, while the fix commit and 0.5.1 returned all three IDs.
findings.interpretation: Enabling render_postcompile changed one list parameter into three scalars, as confirmed by the server log; reversing submission order left the error with the IN query.
findings.limits: The local aiopg/psycopg2 fixture supplied five rows. Only the additional concurrent control gave the read its own task.

cases.title: DataFusion placed exact pre-epoch timestamps in the previous time bin

findings.observation: The two reported SQL queries used 19:00:00 and 19:00:30 on December 31, 1969. Both lost 30 seconds at the parent revision. Among 6,347 historical USGS earthquake times, the same build misclassified all 11 events on a 30-second boundary. It also misclassified all 88 events on a one-second boundary. The fixed CLI matched integer floor division for every event.
findings.interpretation: At an exact negative boundary, the remainder is zero. GDB observed compute_distance subtract an extra stride on the parent and keep the original delta on the fix. The two posted constants reached this code during optimizer constant folding. An actual earthquake row reached it during physical projection. For that row the reader’s spawn stack, allocated Tokio task ID and header address match the poll that executed the incorrect branch on a worker thread.
findings.limits: The report supplied SQL without a binary version. The local runs compare the upstream fix with its direct parent in unmodified Linux/amd64 debug builds. The earthquake catalogue and the nanosecond controls are additional workloads. The verified task origin belongs to the physical record-batch scan. The two literal queries were evaluated on the CLI main thread.

cases.title: Batched Dataset.map drops rows at each worker boundary

findings.observation: For 10 rows and batches of three, two workers kept only rows 0–2 and 5–7 with drop_last_batch enabled, while one worker kept rows 0–8.
findings.interpretation: Each worker rounded its five-row shard down to three, dropping four rows in total instead of one. The proposal assigned six and three rows, and reopening the Arrow output confirmed all nine survived.
findings.limits: Tested two multiprocessing start methods on Linux with Python 3.13. The report used macOS, and the proposed fix was still open.

cases.title: Joining two sorted datasets by column pairs sentences with the wrong tags

findings.observation: In the reporter’s example, Datasets 1.15.1 returned the second column in the order [3, 1, 2]. Two independently sorted views of the English Web Treebank produced 2,077 mismatched sentence and annotation IDs, one for every sentence checked. Datasets 1.16.0 returned [1, 2, 3] for the example and matched every sentence to its original tag sequence.
findings.interpretation: The stack records concatenate_datasets building a single six-entry index for two three-row inputs. Reading the first three rows then applies the left input’s order to both columns. The fixed build calls flatten_indices on each input to put it in its own logical order before joining columns. Explicitly materializing both inputs also restores the correct pairs on the older release.
findings.limits: The issue gives no exact version. The comparison covers the 1.15.1 and 1.16.0 wheels, the issue-day revision and both sides of the fix. The treebank follow-up checked the first 2,077 rows against an independent SQLite join on sentence ID. All captured functions ran synchronously.

cases.title: Interleaving datasets loses the shuffled shard order

findings.observation: Two uninstrumented 3.0.0 runs matched the posted 11 batches, including worker 0’s first batch of [0,8,16,24,0,8,16,24] from 25 shards and eight workers.
findings.interpretation: Parent-process frames located the lost shuffle state at interleave construction, and worker records matched delivered batches. In the 5.1.0 control both copies retained the shuffled input order.
findings.limits: The bounded replay used shuffle buffer 1, probabilities [1,0] and a CPU PyTorch 2.1.0 DataLoader. Task numbers and receipt in the parent established delivery order independently of worker completion order.

cases.title: Skipping a row after a distributed split sends the same data to both ranks

findings.observation: In the posted program both ranks returned the same 15 rows after skip(1). In an independent run with 2,000 flight records, each rank read 1,999 flights and every row overlapped. On the fix each rank read 999 flights and the two sets were disjoint.
findings.interpretation: The stack from the original example reaches shard_data_sources in the skip wrapper. Asked to split four sources across two ranks, the affected method returned its own object with all four sources. The fix passed two sources to each rank. In an async feature calculation, the task created by iter_outputs on rank 1 processed row 1, which also appeared on rank 0. Its fixed counterpart began at row 501.
findings.limits: The original script uses two logical ranks. A separate two-process run independently checked their full outputs against the source files. The coroutine creation and sample come from the supplementary async feature calculation.

cases.title: Resuming a mapped streaming dataset skips 800 examples

findings.observation: After saving just after ID 199, the old version resumed at 1000, while the fix and 4.8.5 resumed at 200.
findings.interpretation: Arrow had advanced to the end of a 1,000-row table after map delivered only 200 rows. The fix retained the table start and per-row progress for replay.
findings.limits: The original report compared five IDs on either side. Full-sequence and cross-process controls used local Parquet data.

cases.title: Resuming a filtered IterableDataset skips part of an Arrow table

findings.observation: Checkpointing after 1,500 rows on the reported commit yielded 9,500 of 10,000 rows in total, missing IDs 1500–1999. The fix and 5.0.1 returned all 10,000.
findings.interpretation: Prefetch had advanced the source cursor to 2000. The fix saved the second table’s start at 1000 and its 500 delivered rows, so iteration resumed at ID 1500.
findings.limits: The replay covers synchronous filter iteration. A separately reported map issue shared the table-prefetch mechanism.

cases.title: Hugging Face Datasets drops records from longer inputs during round-robin interleaving

findings.observation: The reporter interleaved three datasets of lengths 3, 4, and 3 without replacement. Datasets 4.5.0 and the fix parent returned nine values, omitting 13 from the second dataset. The fix commit and release 4.6.0 returned all ten in order. On 344 Palmer Penguins records grouped by species, the affected loader delivered 204 records. It omitted 84 Adelie and 56 Gentoo records. The fixed loader delivered all 344, in the order independently reconstructed from the CSV.
findings.interpretation: The captured call to _interleave_map_style_datasets shows how the rows disappeared. With no sampling probabilities and the all_exhausted_without_replacement strategy, the affected code used the shortest input length to build the selection indices. It selected three rounds from the reported example. The fix added a fourth round for the second input alone. In both runs, the indices stored in the returned Arrow dataset matched the indices selected by that function.
findings.limits: The result applies to round-robin interleaving of map-style datasets with unequal lengths. Equal-length inputs and the seeded weighted control retained every record on all four builds. The captured selection ran synchronously. Separate PyTorch runs with zero and two loader workers confirmed batch delivery on both sides of the fix.

cases.title: An implicit pipeline transaction reaches SAVEPOINT too early

findings.observation: The original synchronous session and upstream sync and async tests returned PostgreSQL 25P01 on 3.1.1. A separate insert rolled back before the transaction body ran, leaving zero rows after restart.
findings.interpretation: The protocol trace showed no Sync between SELECT and SAVEPOINT. The fix synchronized before BEGIN, and explicitly syncing or fetching the first result also worked.
findings.limits: The original report omitted server and libpq versions. Task provenance came from the upstream async test and server stacks were captured separately.

cases.title: An exhausted cursor prevents a schema change in the same transaction

findings.observation: Both posted functions printed row 1, but the 0.27.0 and 0.28.0 cursor runs failed with 55006 and rolled back. Fetch and the 0.29.0 cursor committed the row and new column, which survived restart.
findings.interpretation: After iteration, pg_cursors still listed a non-holdable portal for the SELECT, and explicitly closing just that portal allowed ALTER in the same transaction.
findings.limits: The host differed from the reporter’s Fedora 36 system. Portal state came from a separate run. Client and backend evidence was linked by connection PID and logs.

cases.title: Concurrent UPDATE … RETURNING calls can map a value to the wrong column

findings.observation: The author’s program read nft_id='C2' for a row whose stored nft_id was 1002. An independent database read confirmed that all 80 rows across both tables had been updated correctly.
findings.interpretation: A cache hit could override the column mapping by position and share its getter across executions. Scheduling it first gave 3/3 wrong results on each fix parent and 0/3 after either fix or with caching disabled.
findings.limits: Python 3.12 as confirmed by the reporter. Uncontrolled timing varied, and some 40-run batches on the affected parents had no errors.

cases.title: A Kafka Streams left join can emit an unmatched order before its payment arrives

findings.observation: With a 100 ms join window, the legacy API in 2.6.1 and 3.1.0 emitted both unpaid and paid for order A when payment followed by 5 ms, but only paid when payment arrived first.
findings.interpretation: On the same 3.1.0 build, the new window API buffered A until its payment arrived. It emitted the genuinely unpaid order B only when a later record advanced event time, preserving B’s original timestamp.
findings.limits: The upstream change introduced new semantics and retained the legacy API. Tested a single-partition left join with zero grace.

cases.title: Counting ten hourly groups returned zero in Django

findings.observation: The reporter inserted five rows in each of ten hours. On PostgreSQL 14.13, Django 4.2 and the fix parent returned zero from QuerySet.count(). Materializing the same queryset yielded ten groups. The fix and Django 4.2.1 returned ten through both paths.
findings.interpretation: Query.get_aggregation dropped the hour annotation from the selected columns of the counting subquery. The affected compiler included the primary key in the grouping. PostgreSQL then rejected all 50 singleton groups at the five-row threshold. The fix kept the hour annotation, and all ten hourly groups passed. The function trace identifies the compiler path and the executed query plan shows its effect.
findings.limits: The original ORM query runs synchronously. The replay used UTC and supplied the timedelta import missing from the report. Each revision ran against two fresh databases without instrumentation. On a second fixture with uneven group sizes, affected builds disagreed with direct SQL on 28 of 32 threshold checks. Both fixed builds matched on all 32.

cases.title: Why did an ASOF join lose the earlier non-NULL match?

findings.observation: The reporter inserted two observations: time 0 with value 0, and time 1 with a NULL value. The right-hand subquery kept only non-NULL values. Each left time should therefore match right time 0. DuckDB 0.10.0 and 0.10.1 returned only the first row. Both returned the second row when the eligible right input was materialized before the join. DuckDB 0.10.2 returned both rows for the original SQL. Independent Python and SQLite computations agree.
findings.interpretation: The native optimizer resolved the predicate to the right-hand value column on both versions. On 0.10.1, FilterPushdown::PushdownInnerJoin returned a filter above the ASOF join. PhysicalAsOfJoin::Sink received both right rows. The native join matched left time 1 to right time 1, and PhysicalFilter::ExecuteInternal then discarded its NULL value. On 0.10.2, the filter ran on the right input. Only time 0 reached the sink, so both left times matched it. The regression test failed on the parent commit and passed on the merge.
findings.limits: The reporter used 0.10.1-dev397 on Linux. We ran the posted SQL on three stock release wheels and the upstream test on the immediate source parent and merge. The debugger sampled the reporter query and controls on 0.10.1 and 0.10.2. The second table uses a separate transaction with tagged quotes to show which lookups lose a valid price as NULL records arrive. The captured native stacks show optimizer and execution functions. This case has no verified coroutine origin.

cases.title: DuckDB returned a primary key that did not identify the updated row

findings.observation: The reporter inserted abc with count 20, then upserted the same name with count 30. On DuckDB 1.2.2 and 1.3.2, the second statement returned ID 2 while the reopened table contained just (1, abc, 30). DuckDB 1.4.0 and a live PostgreSQL 14.13 server returned ID 1 and persisted the same row. All four engines advanced the sequence to 2. The posted programs and the on-disk comparison repeated in independent batches.
findings.interpretation: The conflicting insert generated candidate ID 2. GDB observed that value at the return instruction of the sequence function in all three release wheels. On the affected releases, the conflict handler built its return row from the proposed insert and replaced the count. The output collection received a dictionary vector whose selected BIGINT was 2. On 1.4.0 the same SQL ran through the merge and update operators, and the output collection received a flat BIGINT of 1. The native values agree with the unsampled client results.
findings.limits: A separate DuckDB application used the upsert result as a foreign key for a receipt. On both affected releases ID 2 found zero stations, the database rejected the receipt, and rollback left Fairbanks at count 20 with zero receipts. DuckDB 1.4.0 committed count 30 and one receipt. Reading the key by unique name worked on all three releases, as did inserting a new name. All 18 original transaction databases were reopened and checked. The PostgreSQL comparison covers the reporter’s original workload with two LONG spellings changed to BIGINT. The report spells the affected version “1.22”. The tested releases establish the operator change, while the first corrected commit remains unbisected. The native stacks establish synchronous execution only.

cases.title: Why did DuckDB return a decimal sum exactly 100 times too large?

findings.observation: The reporter created 100 balances from 0.25 to 99.25. Each balance joined to four rows, and the left join matched none. All 400 rows fell into one group. The balances sum to 4975.00 before the join, so the answer is 19900.00. The two reported PyPI builds, stable 2.0.1 and the PR parent returned 1990000.00. The landed source returned 19900.00. Every build described its output as DECIMAL(38,2). Turning off any one of the three optimizer passes in the table, or disabling the entire optimizer, restored the expected sum. The reporter also supplied a TPC-H query. Its 1,500 customers, 100 suppliers and 25 nations produced 5,929 joined rows. Weighting each customer balance by its matching supplier count gave 26492209.10. SQLite independently returned 2649220910 integer cents.
findings.interpretation: The reporter cast the input to DECIMAL(15,2) before adding 0.25. The resulting balance column was DECIMAL(16,2). In the parent trace, FilterStatisticsOptimizer called into SumPropagateStats, which specialized sum to sum_no_overflow. Its bound signature changed from DECIMAL(16,2) → DECIMAL(38,2) to BIGINT → HUGEINT (segments 2 and 5). The expression still declared a decimal result. Under TryDoubleEagerPushdown, SetStateExport received the integer signature (segment 6). Finalization wrote the integer 1990000, the correct number of cents, into a HUGEINT vector. The cast then wrote 199000000 to the scale-two result vector (segment 11), displayed as 1990000.00. The landed fix preserved the decimal signature at export. Its finalizer wrote the same 128-bit integer 1990000 into a DECIMAL(38,2) vector (landed segment 11), which represents 19900.00. The parent also returned 19900.00 with partial aggregate pushdown disabled. That trace still saw the integer specialization. Direct finalization wrote the sum into a scale-two decimal vector.
findings.limits: The fix was verified on the merged source build. All three published wheels tested here were affected. The reporter used Python on Windows. The local runs used Python wheels and source-built CLIs on Linux. One variation distinguishes the parent from the three wheels. With n.nk < 3 the parent inflated all four groups to 382000.00, 390000.00, 398000.00 and 820000.00. The wheels and landed source returned 3820.00, 3900.00, 3980.00 and 8200.00. The query has no ORDER BY, so the comparison uses the complete multiset. The TPC-H measurements use generated scale-factor 0.01 data. Native stack and vector observations cover 2.0.0, 2.0.1 and both source revisions. Each ran the minimal query, the pushdown-disabled control and the TPC-H query twice.

cases.title: Filtered COUNT DISTINCT depends on input order

findings.observation: For two rows with the same group and value 7, DuckDB 0.5.1 twice counted zero instead of one. Reversing the rows produced one.
findings.interpretation: Deduplication claimed the key before testing the type filter, so the first ineligible row excluded the later eligible row. The fix counted one in either order.
findings.limits: The original used Windows. The Linux CLI replay used GDB to inspect row indices and return values on this small query.

cases.title: A range LEFT JOIN against a newly created empty table dropped every left row

findings.observation: With two timestamps on the left and a new empty table on the right, the reported DuckDB build returned zero rows for both < and >. Equality returned the expected two rows with nulls. The fix returned both rows for all three comparisons. With 12 earthquake records, both affected comparisons omitted all 12.
findings.interpretation: The captured native stack reached StatisticsPropagator while optimizing the comparison join. EXPLAIN showed a cross product on the parent. Disabling statistics propagation alone restored the left join and both rows. The old optimizer treated the comparison as always true and rewrote the outer join to a cross product. A cross product with an empty table returns zero rows.
findings.limits: The native sample identifies the optimizer branch. The operator rewrite is inferred from the plan, the single-optimizer control and the parent-to-fix change. The tests also covered a populated right input and an input emptied by deletion. The synchronous C++ engine contributed no coroutine origin.

cases.title: Year-end pickups moved into the wrong ISO reporting week

findings.observation: The reporter’s pandas query classified December 31, 2024 as week 53 of 2024 on DuckDB 0.6.1. Python, pandas and DuckDB 0.7.0 returned week 1 of 2025. In the December NYC yellow taxi file, 170,718 pickups on December 30 and 31 changed weekly reporting groups after the fix.
findings.interpretation: The native stacks follow both SQL extractors into GetISOYearWeek. For December 31 the parent divided a zero-based day index of 365 by seven and added one, leaving the year at 2024. The fixed helper recognized that the next ISO year had begun, advanced the year and reset the zero-based week to zero. Across a complete 400-year calendar cycle, 343 dates had incorrect results in the parent. The fixed engine agreed with Python on every date.
findings.limits: The original report used macOS. These Linux runs use the published Python packages for the pandas example. The debugger captured the equivalent timestamp projection from a real SQL table. The taxi study is a separate workload. It includes 3,668,337 December pickups and excludes 34 records whose pickup dates fall outside the month. The C API engines read the timestamp column exported through Arrow. The Python releases read the original Parquet file. The observed calendar operations ran synchronously.

cases.title: DuckDB drops ORDER BY from a PIVOT without an ON clause

findings.observation: The reporter’s four-row query came back out of order in 47 of 64 eight-thread runs on 1.1.3 and in none of 64 runs in either round on 1.2.0. Timestamps and grouped sums agreed.
findings.interpretation: The old syntax tree lacked the modifiers and the plan lacked sorting or pagination. Adding the upstream TransformModifiers call and rebuilding that file restored both ordering and pagination.
findings.limits: Linux releases and source builds replaced the reporter’s Windows build. Hash-group output order varied between runs.

cases.title: DuckDB kept a rolled-up join key in two subtotal rows

findings.observation: The reporter joined two one-row tables and requested a three-column ROLLUP. DuckDB 1.2.2 returned the detail row (1, 1, 1) twice. Both subtotal rows retained 1 in their third column, where SQL requires NULL. DuckDB 1.3.0 and an independent PostgreSQL 14.13 run returned all four expected rows. On 1.2.2, disabling either optimizer pass separately restored both missing subtotals.
findings.interpretation: The join made the first and third columns equal in the detail row. ROLLUP still needs to clear the third column while retaining the first at two subtotal levels. On the affected native stack, the unused-column visitor changed the third binding to the first, and the duplicate-group visitor then reduced three grouping expressions to two. EXPLAIN showed two physical group keys. On 1.3.0, both visitors preserved three distinct bindings and EXPLAIN showed three keys. CLI builds of the immediate parent and merged fix isolated the change. On the parent, two of four ordered ROLLUP rows differed from the oracle. Changing only ROLLUP to CUBE gave six differences in eight ordered rows. The merged build matched both oracles.
findings.limits: GDB sampled synchronous C++ optimizer calls on the posted synthetic input. Function names establish the call path. Entry and return memory reads establish the binding changes. SQL responses and an independent prefix calculation establish which rows were wrong. A separate Palmer penguin workload used 344 observations. On 1.2.2, eight of fourteen rows had incorrect island labels, including the 168-observation Biscoe subtotal. The counts were correct. The published-data reference and its six result sets are documented in upstream/penguins/verification.json.

cases.title: DuckDB returned a group total for every row of a running sum

findings.observation: The five-row query returned 6, 6, 6 for one group and 3, 3 for the other in DuckDB 1.5.0 and 1.5.1. With positive inputs, each group can reach its total only once. In a second query each invoice had a frame containing just itself. Invoice 1 was for 198 cents and returned its customer's total of 3,762 cents. All 412 invoices returned incorrect amounts.
findings.interpretation: The native stack reached WindowSelfJoinOptimizer::CanOptimize from OptimizeInternal. Both release CLIs read the same window boundaries. Version 1.5.1 accepted the running frame, and its plan grouped by customer and joined the total back to every row. Version 1.5.2 rejected it and retained the window operator. Disabling only this optimization on 1.5.1 also restored the row-specific results.
findings.limits: The reporter used macOS ARM64. These four release CLIs ran on Linux x86_64 with one execution thread. The original frame leaves the order within a group unspecified. The verifier checks whether any order of those rows could produce the returned sums. The invoice data is the Chinook sample database. The native captures observe synchronous optimizer decisions.

cases.title: Window ranks reuse the first window’s NULL ordering

findings.observation: For three ones and a NULL, both ranks followed the first window’s NULL ordering. Swapping the windows reversed both, and all 11 second-column ranks were wrong in a separate two-partition case.
findings.interpretation: The old comparison ignored null_order and EXPLAIN showed one WINDOW. The fix compared NULL placement, produced two WINDOW operators and restored the ranks.
findings.limits: The real engine ran on Linux x86-64 rather than the reported macOS ARM system. The captured stacks were synchronous.
