cases.title: Why did the compaction counter stay at zero after nine revisions disappeared?

findings.observation: On a three-voter etcd 3.4.3 cluster, compacting through revision 5 reduced each backend snapshot from 15 historical records to 6. All three current keys were still readable. Every member reported zero additional compacted records. The 3.4.4 release reported nine on the same workload.
findings.interpretation: Go recorded the MVCC worker being created at schedule.go line 70. On that same goroutine the compaction loop deleted the nine verified revision tuples. The deferred update passed 0 to the Prometheus counter. The fix increments the local count after each delete. A mixed cluster replicated the same writes and compactions to all three builds, allowing the one-line correction to be tested against the original 3.4.3 implementation.
findings.limits: The reported symptom was reproduced with the upstream Linux releases. Native goroutine creation and compaction operands were captured in same-tag observed builds. The experiment measures historical MVCC records per member. Each physical snapshot and scrape belongs to the member named in its archive path.

cases.title: etcd returned key order for a range sorted by creation revision

findings.observation: The reporter wrote foo3, foo1 and foo2, then requested creation order without specifying a direction. etcd 3.0.12 and all three members on the fix parent returned foo1val first. The fixed servers returned foo3val first. Every member’s stored creation revisions placed foo3 first at revision 2, followed by foo1 at 3 and foo2 at 4. Explicit ascending order returned foo3val on every build.
findings.interpretation: The range backend received CREATE with the order field set to NONE. On the parent, the rows entered and left the sort branch in key order. On the fix, the backend selected ascending order and returned the rows in creation-revision order. Capture segments 0, 1, 2 and 3 follow one gRPC request goroutine from its creation through both observations to its exit. A separate replay of each member’s committed WAL and MVCC versions establishes the expected order.
findings.limits: The original workload used one v3.0.12 member. The three-member clusters, overwrite, historical read and explicit sort directions are additional controls. The keys have distinct creation revisions. The stack capture covers the original read on member 0 of each observed three-member cluster. The debugger and baseline runs used the same server binaries.

cases.title: etcd raises a one-second lease to the cluster minimum

findings.observation: After Grant(1) on a fresh three-node cluster, etcdctl on another member reported a two-second TTL with one second remaining, while a six-second grant stayed at six.
findings.interpretation: The lease ID and runtime worker linked Raft application to lessor.Grant, where the server enforced the minimum derived from election and heartbeat settings.
findings.limits: The report omitted the version and timing settings. This replay used 3.5.5 and checked the observed policy. The archived debugger recorded the scheduler launch and the sample in order. Both records lack timestamps.

cases.title: Why did etcdctl print 10 when the Raft term was 16?

findings.observation:
The reporter ran etcdctl member list --hex -w json on 3.5.1. We repeated the command against three local etcd members, transferring leadership with move-leader to reach each sampled term. At term 11 the client exited successfully and wrote the bare letter b. A JSON reader rejected the output at that letter. At term 16 the same client wrote 10. The reader accepted the entire document and returned the integer ten. The gateway returned 16, and all three members agreed on term 16 before and after the reads. Both behaviors followed the client when the server version changed.

Across 6 primary clusters and 336 completed member-list calls, all 168 plain JSON reads returned the cluster term. With --hex, 42 outputs failed to parse, 28 parsed to the wrong integer and 98 agreed with the cluster. Term 9 was a useful control because both bases printed 9.
findings.interpretation:
Hardware breakpoints caught the member-list command calling (*jsonPrinter).MemberList, then printMemberListWithHexJSON, then strconv.AppendUint. At term 16 the response header in the 3.5.1 client already held 16. At printer_json.go line 70 the formatter received 16 and base 16, and its returned bytes spelled 10. The separately run stock client printed those same bytes. At the same term the 3.5.3 client passed base 10 and returned the digits 16. At term 11 the two conversions returned b and 11. Only raft_term used the wrong base. All 80 observed conversions of identifiers used base 16. The two header IDs and the three membership IDs were correctly quoted hexadecimal strings, and each decoded to the ID returned by the gateway.

The published stacks use term 11. Segment 1 records the header at printer entry, segment 6 records the formatter arguments, and segment 7 records the returned byte slice. The second table gives both terms for the release and backport clients. For the stripped release binaries, the recorder resolved the sampled addresses using the executable’s own Go function and line tables. The source-built pair also provided named debug arguments for a second check of the value and base.
findings.limits:
The affected releases tested were 3.5.1 and 3.5.2. Release 3.5.3 is the first corrected 3.5 release tested, and 3.6.0 also agreed with the gateway. PR #13711 changed the main branch. The executed source boundary was its 3.5 backport, PR #13727, from 1eb8b6a75c to 3c2ef71358. The official 3.5.1 Linux server identified itself as e8732fb5f. Its printer source and the printer at the 3.5.1 tag (d42e8589) have the same Git blob.

The primary matrix read the member list from one endpoint per cluster and checked status and health on all three. The additional observer clusters used 3.5.1 and 3.5.3 servers at terms 11 and 16. The debugger captured 208 physical stops across 16 client invocations. The stacks cover 3.5.1, 3.5.3 and the two backport builds. Evidence for 3.5.2 and 3.6.0 comes from stock CLI output. The samples show synchronous client calls and supply zero matched goroutine origins.

cases.title: An etcd range page returns the correct keys and the wrong count

findings.observation: The posted etcdctl range query requested two keys from key1 up to the exclusive bound key5. Each of three servers returned key1 and key2. The affected response reported three matches although four keys matched. The fixed response reported four. Across the four clusters, 12 of 26 affected reads and none of 26 fixed reads reported a wrong total.
findings.interpretation: The trace links the FIFO scheduler’s creation of the Raft apply worker to rangeKeys handling this committed request. The index found four matches. To decide whether another page existed, the range read fetched three values. The affected result used that fetch length for its total. The fixed result used the index count while still fetching only three values. The retained WALs identify the requests and revisions on all three replicas.
findings.limits: The report did not specify a revision or cluster topology. The local clusters used the first parent and the merged fix. Native goroutine traces cover the first node of each observed cluster. Stock runs independently verified the visible command output.

cases.title: A limited etcd range returned the second-oldest key

findings.observation: After c, b and a were created in that order, etcdctl returned c, b, a for the unlimited creation-order query. A limit of one returned b on the reported revision. Explicit ascending order returned c. In a 412-invoice workload the earliest invoice was 0001 from Germany. The same limited query returned invoice 0119 from Argentina.
findings.interpretation: The gRPC server created the observed stream goroutine at go f(). The trace follows that instance into rangeLimit, where a request for one selected a two-key storage read. The storage scan produced a and b. Sorting those candidates put b first, after c had already been excluded. The proposed change resolved the default sort direction before choosing the read limit. It read all three keys and returned c.
findings.limits: The original workload ran on a single voter. The two three-voter clusters are an additional comparison with unique sort values at revision 431. Each cluster served 60 reads per voter. The Go trace probes observed one invocation of the original limited query on each source build. The source comparison uses the branch linked by the reporter.

cases.title: etcd snapshot status counts internal entries and old revisions

findings.observation: As the live user-key count changed from 0 to 1 to 1 to 2, the old tool reported 6, 7, 9 and 10, while the fixed tool matched every count.
findings.interpretation: An independent bbolt scan found three revisions in the key bucket and six internal entries; the old counter incremented for each entry, while the fix counted distinct user keys.
findings.limits: One healthy Linux/amd64 member and offline snapshots were tested. The six internal entries were specific to this initialization.

cases.title: etcd counted a completed one-shot watch twice on removal

findings.observation: Two one-shot watches on /message delivered the committed values goodbye world and sup, world. After each delivery, the official 2.0.0 and 2.0.8 releases reported 18446744073709551615 and 18446744073709551614 active watchers. Version 2.0.9 returned zero both times. Two fresh batches reproduced the sequence.
findings.interpretation: Go recorded the creation of the apply goroutine at EtcdServer.start. That same GoID reached notifyWatchers while applying the committed PUT. The parent decremented the signed count and left the watcher’s removed flag false. The watch connection then cleaned up the same watcher and decremented the count again. The stats endpoint serialized −1 and −2 as unsigned integers. The fix sets the flag in the notification path. HTTP cleanup then leaves the count alone.
findings.limits: The reported 2.0.0 binary and the adjacent release binaries ran unmodified on Linux/amd64. Physical stacks came from the release-branch parent and fix built with Go 1.23.0. The three-voter source runs opened the watches on n0 and submitted the writes on n1. Each member reported its own count and all three members read back each committed change.

cases.title: An etcd progress notification can overtake watch history

findings.observation: Across 16 of 16 trials on the reported build and the fix’s parent, an immediate progress notification preceded 24 committed updates. Resuming at that checkpoint delivered a newer write first.
findings.interpretation: The send goroutine delivered control revision 97 before an MVCC event at revision 87 on the same stream. The fix routed progress through MVCC so lagging watches could defer it.
findings.limits: Event revisions were checked separately from response headers, which can match. The production client’s incident trace was unavailable.

cases.title: etcd sent file-only Zap logs to standard error

findings.observation: With the reporter’s command, the official Linux 3.4.0-rc.2 binary wrote the same 40 JSON records to ./etcd.log and descriptor 2. The two complete streams were byte-identical at 8,732 bytes each. The 3.4.0 binary wrote 39 records to the file and zero bytes to stderr. Both kept stdout empty. Every CLI server successfully stored and returned abc. In two separate embedded-host runs per side with file-only output, the parent copied all 34 etcd records to stderr alongside two host diagnostics. At the fix, stderr contained just the two host diagnostics. The fixed log file had 35 records in the first run and 34 in the repeat.
findings.interpretation: The parent received one requested path and combined it with the default stderr sink. Zap opened both for normal log entries. For the first startup warning the same two os.File receivers appeared at syscall.Write, which returned 155 bytes on the file descriptor and 155 on descriptor 2. The fix replaced both destination lists before merging. Only the normal file sink received the warning. The verifier matches the opened objects, live descriptor identities and returned byte buffers to the captured files.
findings.limits: The reporter used Darwin amd64 and showed an initialized data directory. Our Linux runs used fresh directories and separate output descriptors. The first four startup records give a bounded comparison. Whole-process counts also include normal shutdown and can vary between runs. The source builds identify as 3.5.0-pre on master. The six stock pilot runs, eight new release processes and twelve source-built CLI processes are reported separately. The six native captures establish synchronous CLI startup routing and writes. The reporter also mentioned using the embed package. A separately written host exercised that API and read back stored-value in twelve additional processes.

cases.title: etcdctl prints plain text when endpoint health requests JSON

findings.observation: Both uninstrumented runs of endpoint health -w json exited successfully but printed plain text, while cluster discovery printed one line per healthy member.
findings.interpretation: The old health worker printed directly, bypassing the selected formatter, while the fixed stack entered the printer, and all three responding member IDs matched endpoint status.
findings.limits: The merge and its parent were tested against healthy 3.5.5 servers. The fixed printer’s main goroutine was not linked to individual workers.

cases.title: etcdctl v3 omits the settings needed to start a new cluster member

findings.observation: The v3 member add command registered the fourth member but printed only its ID and the cluster ID. API v2 printed three join variables. With the fix, the v3 text output also included ETCD_NAME, ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER and ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER_STATE. All four members subsequently served quorum reads.
findings.interpretation: At registration the server knew the new member’s ID and peer address. Its name remained empty until the process joined. The corrected CLI matched the ID in the response to the CLI argument newMember and printed a complete peer list. After startup, the four membership views confirmed that name and address.
findings.limits: The original report compared v2 and v3 without specifying an exact topology or version. The replay used the command from the merged documentation with three initial voters and a fourth process started from independently prepared configuration. Eight cluster runs covered both client revisions, text and JSON output, and GDB observation. The observed stacks belong to the synchronous CLI.

cases.title: etcdctl stored the quote characters around transaction values

findings.observation: The released 3.0.6 client wrote 14 bytes for the 12-byte value created-key1. Repeating the posted transaction took the success branch and added the same two quote bytes to overwrote-key1. In a 249-entry country catalog, all 80 names submitted in quotes acquired the extra characters. All 169 unquoted names were correct. Reads on three distinct members agreed before and after a cluster restart in both batches.
findings.interpretation: The physical Go stack reaches argify through parseRequestUnion and readOps. On the released parser, argify returned the quoted text as a token. The put handler then passed the same bytes into the client operation. Changing only argify to the upstream implementation removed the extra characters at both observation points and in persistent storage. The released 3.1.0 client independently produced the same correct values.
findings.limits: The report omitted the client version. The reproduction used a 3.0.6 client available before the report and a local three-member 3.5.33 cluster. Stack capture used two 3.0.6 source builds with Go 1.9.2. The observed parser calls ran synchronously. The evidence establishes the value conversion in the client.

cases.title: Splitting CRLF across chunks turned one server-sent event into two

findings.observation: The reporter's five chunks carry three data lines belonging to a single event. The fix parent emitted two callback values: the first contained A and B on separate lines, and the second contained C. The fixed parser and native Chromium EventSource emitted one value with A, B and C on three lines. The old and fixed parsers both produced one event when receiving the same 28 bytes in one chunk.
findings.interpretation: The parent completed the B line when its chunk ended in CR. The following LF became an empty line and triggered early dispatch. The fix retained the B line and its CR until the next chunk supplied the LF. V8 recorded both line-splitting results and the exact pending data at dispatch. Two of the 27 possible single cuts of the reported payload changed the parent's output. All 27 produced the expected value on the fix.
findings.limits: The original program feeds text chunks directly. The HTTP and browser runs are separate local controls. The Node client records the exact text chunks passed to the library; native Chromium exposes only dispatched events. Its extra named completion event terminates the browser control. The library parser runs synchronously inside a Web Streams callback.

cases.title: Why did moving the query and both candidates change the nearest neighbor?

findings.observation: In Faiss CPU 1.14.2 and 1.16.0, adding the same two-dimensional offset changed the Panorama result from ID 1 to ID 0. Direct squared Euclidean distance on the translated float32 inputs still selected ID 1. Both candidates received a Panorama score of zero. A radius search also admitted the farther vector.
findings.interpretation: The native search stack reaches Panorama::progressive_filter_batch and prune_kernel. For ID 0 the accumulated squared norms were 41522.28515625 and twice the dot product was exactly the same float. Subtraction produced zero. ID 1 also rounded to zero, and the strict comparison against the new zero threshold removed the genuinely nearer candidate. Reversing insertion order changed which physical vector survived. Recentering the already translated inputs restored the correct distances.
findings.limits: The two-vector release and debugger results agree. The digits table uses the released wheels and the original UCI train/test split. The offsets are controlled perturbations of integer features. All genuine distance ties are accepted. In one of three two-candidate digit reductions, a debug compilation changes the winning ID. Both the standalone and sharded native stacks were captured. The sharded stacks identify OS worker threads. No coroutine origin was verified.
