cases.title: Flink dropped the LISTAGG separator during aggregation planning

findings.observation: All four groups in the reported query contained commas where the query requested #. The Chinook catalog returned the correct genres for every invoice. All 166 invoices with multiple genres used the wrong separator. The other 246 invoices had one genre each. Both independent batches produced the same affected invoice IDs.
findings.interpretation: At SplitAggregateRule.matches, the debugger recorded the planner accepting a DISTINCT LISTAGG call with two operands. The physical plan still contained # in the partial aggregate. Its final aggregate received only the partial string. Flink then constructed the one-argument aggregate, and its streaming task used the default comma. Replacing just the upstream planning method made the same call return false and restored # in every affected group. Disabling splitting independently produced the same result.
findings.limits: The local jobs used Flink 1.18.0. The rule comparison transplanted the corrected method from 1.19.0 into that release. SQL leaves member order unspecified, so verification compared the members and delimiters separately. The Java debugger captured physical planning and worker stacks. A per-coroutine creation site remains unverified.

cases.title: Flink assigned pre-epoch events to a future window

findings.observation: The reporter’s eight events produced seven five-second windows in Flink 1.14.3. Three timestamps landed one window late. The events at −7,000 and −2,000 ms both printed a group size of two. Flink 1.14.5 produced eight singleton windows. Shifting the original stream forward by 20 seconds gave eight correct windows on both releases.
findings.interpretation: WindowOperator.processElement passed record c to TumblingEventTimeWindows.assignWindows. The helper received −7,000 ms, offset zero and width 5,000 ms. The affected signed-remainder expression returned −5,000. JDI then read the actual returned window [−5,000, 0). In the fixed JVM the helper had a remainder of −2,000 and returned −10,000. The assigner returned [−10,000, −5,000). Both starts matched the print sink. The physical frames, return values and shipped bytecode tie the discrepancy to the window-start calculation.
findings.limits: The original program used eight synthetic timestamps and five-second windows. A separate job used 76 USGS earthquakes and seven-day windows aligned to the Unix epoch. Both jobs also ran without a debugger. The catalog output matched two earlier batches byte for byte on each release. The six captures measure physical JVM task-thread frames. Coroutine creation was unobserved.

cases.title: kfake returned offsets 0 and 2 for two Kafka timestamp lookups that both required offset 1

findings.observation: The reporter published four records in one partition and batch with timestamps 0, 10, 10 and 20 milliseconds after a common base. At +5 ms, the affected service returned offset 0, whose record was too early. At +10 ms, it returned offset 2, skipping the first record with that timestamp. A consumer sought to each returned offset and read those records. The fix and Apache Kafka 2.2.1 returned offset 1 and the +10 ms record for both queries.
findings.interpretation: The Kafka contract selects the earliest offset whose timestamp reaches the request. The parent scanned the whole batch and updated its answer whenever a record timestamp was less than or equal to the request. At +10 ms this selected offset 1 and then overwrote it with offset 2. The fixed scan stopped at offset 1. The Go runtime recorded the creation of the service event loop in NewCluster. The same goroutine handled the sampled requests, and the peer, correlation ID, query and result match the captured Kafka exchanges.
findings.limits: The literal reporter test ran on Linux/amd64 with the reported Go 1.26.1. The six paired runs used a topic-specific client, uncompressed records and the Kafka 2.2 protocol cap. The singleton-batch topic and seven extra lookup times are local controls. The +21 ms wire reply had offset and timestamp −1. The admin client then looked up the partition end and returned offset 4. The goroutine evidence covers the two traced kfake runs. Apache Kafka supplies the independent broker and on-disk readback.

cases.title: Why did a seven-byte fsspec read return the whole ten-byte file?

findings.observation: For the static file abcdefghij, the reporter called cat_file(start=3, end=None). Both fsspec clients sent Range: bytes=3-. The server returned HTTP 200 with Content-Length 10 and the full document. On the reporter commit and the November 19 main-branch snapshot, both clients returned abcdefghij. Slicing the original file at offset 3 gives defghij. On a server that honored the request with HTTP 206 and Content-Range bytes 3-9/10, both clients returned those seven bytes. The first table shows the outputs shared by the aiohttp and Requests implementations in separate calls.
findings.interpretation: The full 200 response supplied no Content-Range. In range_response_window the start was 3 and the open-ended window had no length to check. With end=100 the calculated window was 97, also large enough to pass through the ten-byte body. The landed #2247 change caught the shorter [3:8] case. In the reporter capture, segment 1 identifies the actual HTTPFileSystem._cat_file coroutine. The trace hook found it in sync’s local variable before its first await. Its CPython cr_origin points to the preceding allocation line, coro = func(*args, **kwargs). The event loop’s _runner awaited that object. The same retained frame appears beneath range_response_window in segment 10. Two retained runs on the reporter’s build measured 7.298 ms and 7.402 ms from observing the created coroutine on the caller thread to the response stack on the I/O thread. Both events used the same process monotonic clock. The helper, coroutine and public caller all returned the same bytes object. In the separate CSV workload the file held four rows totaling 26 units. The second read returned the whole document and duplicated A and B, yielding six rows totaling 34 units on both affected snapshots.
findings.limits: The original program uses the upstream test server. The control matrix uses a regular file served over loopback. The 2026.9.0 wheel needed the test fixture from its tag to run the posted script. The CSV uses one client reading two disjoint byte windows sequentially. Four observed runs matched 24 distinct request coroutines to their allocation in fsspec’s aiohttp-backed client at asyn.py:85 on the reporter commit and asyn.py:91 on November 19. Requests was measured separately. At the archived tracker snapshot, #2408 and PR #2446 were open. The proposal’s source head raised ValueError for the unconfirmed tail and returned defghij on 206. Its original script exited on the first client. Separate control calls exercised both clients.

cases.title: An async fsspec download treats a file-like destination as a path

findings.observation: The original BytesIO example failed twice after reading all four bytes, while with proposed change #2435, the stream stayed open and the caller could read back “data”.
findings.interpretation: Task and object identities linked the successful read to split_protocol calling startswith on the destination, while both HTTP range responses in the control contained the correct bytes.
findings.limits: The report used one task with inline data. Concurrent callers and the loopback HTTP server were local controls.

cases.title: A larger second Parquet footer is assigned to the first file

findings.observation: Opening the small file first failed twice when a 1,106,965-byte footer exceeded the 1,000,000-byte sample. Reversing the order read all 20,000 and 1,000 rows correctly.
findings.interpretation: File offsets and hashes showed that the 106,973 extra bytes belonged to the second file but were appended to the first buffer passed to PyArrow. The proposal appended them to the second.
findings.limits: The original in-memory filesystem and both real files were checked independently. The stack was synchronous.

cases.title: Reading one line from an HTTP stream tried to seek backwards

findings.observation: The reporter’s script read all lines successfully. After reopening the same HTTP resource, readline() raised ValueError. That call received 14,999 bytes from the background read and consumed 15 bytes for its first line.
findings.interpretation: The submitting thread and the event-loop task shared the same coroutine object. The bytes returned by _read matched the buffer passed to the rewind request. The fix retained the remaining 14,984 bytes so the next line could use them. Both HTTP backends then returned all 2,000 flight records in order.
findings.limits: The coroutine evidence covers the aiohttp background read. The rewind exception occurred on the synchronous caller. The Requests backend provided a separate output check. All requests used a local HTTP server.

cases.title: Streaming a chat reply collapsed separate paragraphs

findings.observation: In the reporter’s application, three replies streamed one character at a time each became a single paragraph. Sending an entire reply at once preserved its paragraph breaks. After the fix, the streamed replies contained two, three and three paragraphs.
findings.interpretation: The queue event ID and task identity link start_processing to _postprocess_message_messages. The old postprocessor stripped the newly appended newline from the caller’s message dictionary. The generator then continued from the shortened value. The fix cleans a response copy, preserving the generator’s input for its next yield.
findings.limits: The original app used the Gradio queue and a generator with no model. The release runs used the browser files shipped with each wheel. Runs at the two source commits used the 5.3.0 browser files.

cases.title: A synchronous GraphQL list resolver creates an unawaited coroutine for a Django QuerySet

findings.observation: A real SQLite-backed QuerySet returned green, blue and red in rank order through the async entry point. The synchronous call in 3.3.0a11 and the fix parent raised AttributeError when it read .result on a coroutine. Both the fixed commit and 3.3.0a12 returned the three rows.
findings.interpretation: The old synchronous list-completion code chose the async iterator on an object that supports both protocols. The creation stack, failed attribute access and subsequent warning referred to the same never-started coroutine. The fix chose synchronous iteration for the default sync entry point.
findings.limits: The report described the QuerySet behavior without a complete application. The case reproduces it using Django 5.1.7 on SQLite. The coroutine never started and counts only in the extended origin total.

cases.title: A unary gRPC call loses the cancellation reason that a streaming call preserves

findings.observation: All 18 unary calls across six releases lost the message “my reason”, while sleep and a streaming RPC preserved it in the same process. An AnyIO unary timeout surfaced as CancelledError.
findings.interpretation: The inner _invoke Task received the message, cancelled itself again without it and finished cancelled, leaving the awaiter with a new empty exception. Rethrowing the original preserved the message.
findings.limits: Task and exception identities were traced on Linux with CPython 3.11.13. The original cancellation had no pre-existing nonempty context.

cases.title: A synchronous gRPC handler loses its async interceptor’s request ID

findings.observation: At the reported gRPC Python revision, synchronous SayHello read and returned None for the request ID, while the async handler returned the expected ID.
findings.interpretation: The interceptor task retained the ID through run_in_executor, but the worker thread read the default; copying the context at submission preserved the ID across the same thread switch.
findings.limits: The missing greeting.proto was reconstructed. The context-copy patch was tested locally and its PR closed without merging.

cases.title: The first gRPC calls concentrate on the first ready backend

findings.observation: With grpcio 1.21.1, all ten initial calls went to whichever backend became ready first, whereas the next ten reached one backend each once all ten were ready.
findings.interpretation: Every call reached the round-robin picker, but it had just one eligible backend during the first burst and ten during the second. Picker logs matched server receipts.
findings.limits: The replay used ten local HTTP/2 servers and static IPv4 addresses. The post omitted its server implementation, DNS settings and startup timing.

cases.title: HTTPX included the query string in the ASGI raw path

findings.observation: For GET /path?query, the upstream echo application returned {"raw_path": "/path?query"} on both the HTTPX revision cited in the report and the parent of the fix. The fixed revision and the direct Uvicorn control returned {"raw_path": "/path"}. All 72 loopback exchanges returned HTTP 200. The 16 incorrect bodies came from query-bearing requests relayed through affected HTTPX code. Each build returned identical response bytes with and without instrumentation.
findings.interpretation: The client kept the query in URL.raw_path. The affected ASGI transport copied those bytes into the application scope, which already exposed the query separately as query_string. The fix splits the request target at its first literal question mark. The encoded question mark (%3F) therefore stays in the path. In the parent relay capture, segment 10 records Uvicorn creating a request Task, segment 14 observes that same Task in the upstream echo function with HTTPX on its stack, and segment 18 records its normal exit.
findings.limits: The reporter identified a difference between HTTPX and Uvicorn. The concrete request and echo function come from the upstream fix’s regression test. That test calls the application in process. The TCP relay, additional targets and Task identity evidence come from the local controls. The tables cover the single batch identified as the primary run.

cases.title: HTTPX interprets elapsed seconds as days

findings.observation: After a successful loopback HTTPS request with a 1.70-second server delay, HTTPX 0.15.1 reported 1 day, 17:09:47.016604.
findings.interpretation: Independent clocks located the error at timedelta construction, where the first positional argument means days. Passing seconds explicitly corrected the result and matched 0.15.2.
findings.limits: Timings came from uninstrumented runs. The original used a synchronous client. Task-creation evidence belongs to a separate async control.

cases.title: HTTPX dropped an empty query field when it merged request parameters

findings.observation: The reporter added hello=world to an HTTPS GET whose URL already contained the bare field foobar. HTTPX 0.23.0 and the immediate parent of the fix sent /get?hello=world. The fixed commit and HTTPX 0.23.1 sent /get?foobar=&hello=world. The loopback server returned HTTP 200 for all 64 HTTPX requests and the independent reference request. On two fresh SeaweedFS stores, losing the uploads selector changed the list itself. The affected release returned one completed object, parts/complete. The fixed release returned the two pending uploads, parts/pending-a and parts/pending-b.
findings.interpretation: The affected parser received the string foobar and returned an empty dictionary. The merge consequently received an empty base and retained only the added field. The fix sets keep_blank_values=True at the parser call. The parser then returned one empty-string value under foobar. The same QueryParams object entered the merge, and the resulting request target matched the h11 writer and the server request line. In two additional batches, the GET_AWAITABLE instruction in the reporter’s main function exposed the newly created AsyncClient.get coroutine on line 6. Its cr_origin pointed to that line. The same pinned coroutine frame was present on the physical parser and writer stacks while it was running.
findings.limits: The reporter program changes only its destination authority for loopback HTTPS. The additional query shapes and no-merge runs are local controls. The fixed release emits an equals sign and places foobar first. The reporter’s literal spelling was checked with a separate stdlib request. Each plain/profile pair yielded identical HTTP bytes. The 32 detailed parser/merge graphs contain 256 synchronous frame samples. The separate lifecycle check measured eight real get coroutines and eight plain GETs across four builds. Its three segments cover creation, parsing and writing. Closure was read after execution. The separate SeaweedFS 3.93 control used local HTTP and matched the returned upload IDs to successful initiation responses from each store.

cases.title: HTTPX overwrote an explicit JSON media type

findings.observation: The reporter passed json= with an explicit Content-Type. On a local GeoJSON POST, HTTPX 0.9.3, 0.9.4 and the fix parent sent application/json. The merged fix and 0.9.5 sent application/geo+json. All 30 GeoJSON requests returned HTTP 200 with the same 42-byte request body. In a separate Django JSON:API application, the affected explicit POST received HTTP 415 and inserted zero rows. The repaired POST received HTTP 201 and inserted one row, verified by a subsequent GET and by reopening SQLite.
findings.interpretation: HTTPX computed application/json as the encoder default. On the parent, the synchronous Request constructor assigned it over the caller’s header. The one-line fix used setdefault. The captured Client.request coroutine was observed before its first await inside httpx.api.request. Its same running frame was present before and after header selection, and again in h11.write_request. HTTPX created Client.send after the decision. Its argument was the same Request object, and its running frame was present at serialization. The server received the media type observed at the writer.
findings.limits: The original report omitted a payload and media type. GeoJSON supplies the local header example. The independent consumer uses the JSON:API media type and the packaged rest_framework_json_api.parsers.JSONParser from version 7.1.0. Its evidence records the WSGI input, parser selection, response documents, subsequent listing and committed rows. These HTTPX releases named the async client Client. Coroutine object and frame identities are scoped to each process.

cases.title: HTTPX drops the start of a JSON line spanning multiple chunks

findings.observation: On 0.13.3 and the pre-fix commit, the reporter’s CherryPy app sent two lines, but the async client delivered only the tail of the 642,810-character JSON line and parsing failed.
findings.interpretation: The same reading task reached a decoder branch that replaced its buffered prefix with the next chunk, while the fix appends the chunk instead.
findings.limits: The original CRLF body was served over loopback, and each run was checked against its actual TCP chunk boundaries.

cases.title: Filling two columns in sequence drops the first replacement

findings.observation: The posted Ibis query filled two columns. Version 1.0.0 compiled only the second replacement into its Impala SQL. On 891 Titanic passenger records, SQLite returned 688 missing decks when deck was filled first, or two missing towns when embarkation town was filled first. Version 1.1.0 filled every missing value in both orders.
findings.interpretation: The stack follows the second mutate call to projection, get_result and try_fusion. At entry, the prior projection contains an IfNull expression for column b. The parent commit returns a fused projection that reads b from the base table, discarding that expression. The fix declines fusion and the inner query fills b. Filling both columns in a single mutation also gives the correct value for every passenger on all four builds.
findings.limits: The original report demonstrates Impala SQL compilation and gives no exact revision. The passenger queries ran on local SQLite. A targeted CPython probe captured the optimizer’s input and return value alongside its stack. This is a synchronous query.

cases.title: Ibis omits the window clause for lag inside coalesce

findings.observation: DuckDB rejected the reporter’s five-row query because it looked for a scalar lag function. The fix commit and release returned the expected grouped values 0, 0, 2, 3, 1 in value order.
findings.interpretation: The old traversal skipped a NodeList containing Lag and emitted SQL without OVER. Exposing Lag directly to the traversal produced a partitioned, ordered window and the correct results.
findings.limits: The exact Ibis revision was unspecified. The fix parent reproduced the database error in a synchronous query.

cases.title: A relative month starts 14 hours and 30 minutes late in a Flux query

findings.observation: With both queries fixed to the report’s November clock, InfluxDB 2.7.3 returned October 13 at 02:49 UTC for a relative month and October 12 at 12:19 UTC for date.sub in Berlin. That moved one boundary reading outside the range and changed the fixture’s spread from 30 to 20. Across five dates and two time zones, nine of ten monthly spreads differed on a counter derived from recorded household electricity use.
findings.interpretation: The controller created a query worker at controller.go line 229. On that worker, values.Duration.Duration converted one month to 2,629,800 seconds. ToQueryTime kept the fixed duration. Time.Time then applied it to the request clock, including during physical read planning. The returned start matched to the nanosecond. In the calendar control, date.addDuration preserved Berlin calendar and timezone rules. A separate Python calculation reconstructed every query boundary and spread from the input readings.
findings.limits: The original report used ARM64 and private meter readings. The local runs used Linux/amd64, six constructed boundary readings, and a historical counter built from 1,569,894 observed minute readings in the UCI dataset by Georges Hebrail and Alice Berard. Missing readings contributed no energy to this counter. Additive source probes recorded operands in two separate query processes. The official binary and unmodified source build independently served the same results.

cases.title: JetStream Direct Get returned a message written after the requested cutoff

findings.observation: The report's JSON asks for the last message on subject6077 before a time that predates every stored record. All 6 replays on the fix parent returned sequence 10, “Message 10”, followed by 204 EOB. All 6 replays on the fix returned a single 404 No Results frame. The verifier checked 144 checksummed records across 12 file-store replicas against 48 acknowledged writes and 48 sequence reads.
findings.interpretation: The parent mapped the cutoff to sequence 1, subtracted one, then treated zero as an unspecified ceiling and substituted the current tail, sequence 10. The fix checked the lookup against the first stored sequence before subtracting. The reply inbox identifies the handling goroutine on parent member n2 (Go ID 131) and fixed member n1 (Go ID 288). Each retained runtime trace links that instance's creation and exit to its stack in getDirectMulti.
findings.limits: The literal JSON comes from the issue. The binaries are built from the exact fix parent and fix. The reporter named a development build, and the separate Java follow-up was not executed. The upstream Go regression runs separately on a single file-store server. Three client endpoints, checksummed replica files, nanosecond boundary queries and the second subject are local controls. The captured goroutines serve multiple requests. This discrepancy concerns selection from replicated data.

cases.title: Synchronous single-message Kafka writes wait for the batch timer

findings.observation: One hundred writes took 100.54 and 100.55 seconds on two local three-broker clusters, versus 180.44 and 164.37 ms with Sarama. Setting BatchSize to 1 cut kafka-go to 139.48 and 115.50 ms.
findings.interpretation: The caller waited on its result channel while the partition worker waited about 1,000.1 ms for its timer before writing. Lowering BatchTimeout alone to 20 ms reduced the runs to 2.31 and 2.36 seconds.
findings.limits: The reporter omitted exact versions and hardware. Loopback runs reproduced a roughly one-second write statistic, but the reported two-second interval was unspecified.

cases.title: Nested Kornia augmentations interpolate a binary mask

findings.observation: With seed 0, four pixels of the 5×5 mask became 0.01823359 and 16 pixels were outside the label set after inversion, while the merged fix and release 0.6.9 produced no invalid pixels.
findings.interpretation: The inner container retained the image key when processing the mask. Passing the actual key restored nearest-neighbor labels, independently checked from the transform matrix, and raised the CPU test count from 5/7 to 7/7.
findings.limits: The reporter did not give a seed. Local runs fixed seeds 0 and 17 and used a CPU PyTorch build.

cases.title: A failed batch item receives another item’s successful retry

findings.observation: The posted program copied the second item’s result to the third in three runs, and local sync and async classifiers marked a twice-failed HTTP 503 input successful with another input’s classification.
findings.interpretation: The retry saved the success for index 1 correctly, then filled index 2 by popping that same value from the last round and delivered it through the original run ID’s success callback.
findings.limits: The original assertion was synchronous. Task origins came from abatch, and two proposed changes were tested separately on the reported version.

cases.title: The exit-mode checkpoint stream reports a stale parent

findings.observation: After resuming the posted graph, the last stream event reported no parent despite the checkpoint having a parent ID. With earlier history, the event could report the grandparent.
findings.interpretation: Skipping an intermediate save left prev_checkpoint_config stale when map_debug_checkpoint emitted it, although aput later wrote the correct parent to SQLite.
findings.limits: The original used synchronous InMemorySaver. Task evidence came from the AsyncSqliteSaver control, and the tested change from #9585 was never merged.

cases.title: LangGraph omits a Command tool message from the message stream

findings.observation: The messages stream omitted the tool reply although synchronous history, final state, and the next model request retained its result and tool_call_id.
findings.interpretation: The tool ran and updated state, but the node-end extractor handled ordinary message dictionaries and missed the extra list around a Command, and the PR regression test passed on both fixed builds.
findings.limits: The report did not pin a version. The 0.3.31 replay used the real ChatOpenAI client with deterministic in-process HTTP responses. Task attribution covers the supplemental astream callback.

cases.title: Command.PARENT can re-emit the user message after the AI reply

findings.observation: The example streamed the AI reply and then the original “hi” on 0.2.74 and the fix parent. Version 0.2.75 and the merge streamed only the reply, and all four builds preserved user-then-AI order in final state.
findings.interpretation: The old end callback published an input message whose ID was missing from seen. The fix registered it at node start, and all four upstream sync and async regressions switched from failing to passing.
findings.limits: The report omitted its version. Its example was synchronous, and the verified Task came from the upstream asynchronous regression.

cases.title: Why did awaiting a LangGraph task return None when its end event said “Task 2”?

findings.observation: The reporter's async task returns the literal string “Task 2”. The entrypoint awaits the task, prints what it received, and returns that value. Under ainvoke and astream it printed “Got: (Task 2)” on every build. Under astream_events the 0.3.21 and 0.4.6 wheels printed “Got: (None)”. The child end event still contained “Task 2”. The entrypoint and graph end events both contained None. The same discrepancy was present on both sides of the PR that closed the issue and on the 1.2.18 wheel. The parent of the later fix reproduced it. The merged fix, the 1.2.19 wheel and the November 19 1.2.23 wheel all delivered “Task 2” to the caller.
findings.interpretation: In the 0.3.21 capture, CPython recorded the allocation of the child task's arun_with_retry coroutine in submit at langgraph/pregel/executor.py:155 (segment 67). It observed the new object before its first await. The same retained frame was running at langgraph/pregel/retry.py:126 (segment 101). Its writes already contained (__return__, “Task 2”). The streaming branch had drained the child output and then returned None. The result-copy callback delivered that value to the waiting Future (segment 103), and the reporter's local task_value was None (segment 105). On the merged #9407 build the retry coroutine read the written value and returned “Task 2” (segment 84 of the comparison graph). The fix's regression task returned 42 and 0 under both event protocol versions, with and without an attempt timeout. The merge parent returned None for both values.
findings.limits: The reporter listed langchain-core 0.3.49 and omitted the LangGraph version. The reconstruction pairs that core release with the 0.3.21 wheel. The graph runs locally with a Python function and uses no model service. The #4805 async test checked stream outputs from a workflow that returned the literal “done”. Its stream assertion failed on the parent, and the merged version passed its event snapshot. That workflow discarded the values returned by its child awaits. The separate token-batch workload compares the child event with the object delivered to its caller. On affected builds the ordinary counts reached the child end event. The caller received None and raised TypeError when it indexed that value. On the fixed builds it received the dictionary and computed 3.0 or 5.0 tokens per sequence. The original literal-string program completed normally.

cases.title: Structured streaming drops tool calls after a model falls back to invoke

findings.observation: The original invoke returned Ada, age 36, while stream and astream yielded nothing. The author’s patch made each stream emit one Person.
findings.interpretation: Changing the message conversion sent AIMessageChunk through the parser’s standard tool-call branch, and all four regression tests passed.
findings.limits: The example used a deterministic local model. The issue was open and the fix came from the author’s branch.

cases.title: LitServe returned a float array to clients that requested base64 embeddings

findings.observation: The reporter requested an embedding for “hello”. LitServe 0.2.18 returned HTTP 200 and [5.0, -0.5, 0.25]. Release 0.2.19 returned “AACgQAAAAL8AAIA+”, the three little-endian float32 values encoded as a string. Each release served 31 requests per batch. All 14 base64 requests received the wrong JSON type on 0.2.18 and the correct type on 0.2.19. All 17 other requests passed on both. OpenAI Python 1.109.1 exposed the list to callers explicitly requesting base64 on the old release. Its default path requested base64 and delivered numeric lists on both. The reporter’s unchanged suite produced six failures and eight passes on 0.2.18, then 14 passes on 0.2.19.
findings.interpretation: Two simultaneous clients sent “hi” and “hello” over distinct loopback connections. A single CPU prediction handled both. Each received the correct numerical vector. On the fixed release only the base64 client received a string. CPython observed FastAPI creating the native endpoint coroutine before its first await. The identical coroutine and physical frame returned the affected response. On the fixed request the same frame called b64encode with the exact packed bytes. The model worker ran synchronously in another process and supplied ordinary floats on both releases. The two transport controls used multiprocessing and ZeroMQ. A second complete batch reproduced every response body.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied a deterministic three-coordinate CPU fixture. An additional workload used six original pretrained GloVe vocabulary rows to embed three two-word phrases. Independent rational averaging verified every one of 1,050 returned float32 components per release per batch. The complete fix parent and fix also served the reporter workload and matched the corresponding release byte for byte. The measured coroutine origin belongs to the HTTP endpoint. Synchronous worker prediction and response packing have their own physical samples.

cases.title: Mixed embedding cache hits and misses attach vectors to the wrong nodes

findings.observation: The five expected first coordinates [1,10,3,20,30] came back as [10,20,30,1,3], and all five retrieval queries against a reloaded CPU index chose the wrong document before the fix and the right one afterward.
findings.interpretation: The cache held the correct vectors, but batching grouped them by hit status while binding used input order. 78 of 99 configurations mismatched before the fix and none did in either fixed control.
findings.limits: The reporter used fixed mock embeddings. Retrieval impact was measured separately with a real, persisted TF-IDF index.

cases.title: The chat client could not read the token scores that Qwen generated

findings.observation: Two localhost requests generated “Two plus two equals” and “Bananas”, four tokens and two tokens. Release 0.3.2 sent every score in the legacy text-completion arrays. OpenAI Python 1.54.3 exposed zero records in choices[0].logprobs.content, both for buffered chat and across the complete stream. Release 0.3.6 exposed all six records. All six selected token scores and all 18 top-three entries matched the same release’s text-completion control exactly. Turning off probabilities preserved both replies. Using all 151,936 native pre-softmax scores per position independently recovered the selected tokens and every reported top-three alternative within 4.33 × 10⁻⁷. A seventh native row per release identified the fruit reply’s stop token. Fresh processes reproduced the SHA256 of each complete vector.
findings.interpretation: On 0.3.2 the model worker yielded the original scores, and the chat formatter returned the same dictionary by identity. On 0.3.6 the sampled conversion helper built a new chat record for each token. CPython recorded the SSE publisher allocation through EventSourceResponse.__call__, AnyIO start_soon and call_for_coroutine before its first await. The same coroutine frame was the physical caller when the first scored chunk was sent. The buffered route also matched its creation and return frames. The decoding and mapping samples ran synchronously on a separate worker thread. A second fresh process per arm reproduced all scores.
findings.limits: The reporter specified the endpoint and expected structure but supplied no checkpoint, prompt or exact version. The pilot fixture uses the public Qwen2-0.5B-Instruct Q4_0 model and a four-token cap. The fix first shipped in 0.3.3. A separate route error in 0.3.3 and a streaming cleanup error in 0.3.5 led us to use 0.3.6 for the complete HTTP comparison. The exact parent and fix ran through their own public Llama API and produced identical underlying scores. The released native libraries differ, so numerical controls are evaluated within each release.

cases.title: MLServer returned a class label when clients requested probabilities

findings.observation: With adaptive batching enabled, the original HTTP program received status 200 and one INT64 class label (8) from MLServer 1.0.1. Turning batching off returned all ten probabilities for the same digit. In a separate measurement, ten HTTP requests with distinct IDs reached the model as one 10 × 64 input. Version 1.0.1 returned ten labels. The merged fix returned a 10 × 10 probability matrix. We matched each split response to its HTTP request ID and checked every value by independently walking the 100 fitted trees.
findings.interpretation: The HTTP handler and queue both received predict_proba. The task created in AdaptiveBatcher._start_batcher_if_needed reached BatchedRequests._merge_requests, which returned a request with no output selection. The batcher created a second task to run the model. Its stack reached ForestClassifier.predict on the affected build and ForestClassifier.predict_proba after the fix. Both creation sites were matched to the executing coroutine and frame.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied the client code and described a random forest. We trained a seeded forest using the tutorial’s handwritten digits and train/test split. This accounts for the different example label. The traced service ran inference in-process. Stock runs with the default worker settings reproduced both release outcomes. The fix restored probability output while the batched response still omitted model_version. The 1.1.0 stable release returned v0.1.0 in that field.

cases.title: An MQTT v5 connection refusal surfaces as a timeout

findings.observation: In 0.9.0, a broker rejecting a retained will returned reason code 154, but the caller timed out after one second. Both retain-compatible controls connected and received a QoS 1 message.
findings.interpretation: ReasonCodes compared correctly with zero. The failure occurred when constructing the exception, and PR #59 let the original exception reach the caller by bypassing an integer-key lookup.
findings.limits: The broker settings, reason code and one-second limit were local choices. The callback ran in an event-loop Handle.

cases.title: The PyArrow backend returns the lower value as a two-element median

findings.observation: For [5.0, 1.0], Narwhals 2.17.0 returned 1.0 with PyArrow while pandas and Polars returned 3.0. The fix and 2.25.0 returned 3.0 for the whole column.
findings.interpretation: The old path selected approximate_median and finalized a t-digest, whereas the fix used a linear quantile, while grouped medians still returned 1 and 10 where the exact values were 3 and 15.
findings.limits: The replay matched the reported interpreter and backend versions on Linux x86-64. The original platform was macOS ARM.

cases.title: A grouped conditional sum includes every row on pandas and PyArrow

findings.observation: In the five-row example, Narwhals 2.11.0 returned [4, 4, 4, 6, 6] on pandas and PyArrow. Polars returned [0, 0, 0, 4, 4]. On the 344 Palmer penguin records, the two affected backends included every measured bird in each island’s total. For Dream Island they returned 460,400 g. The one bird there without a recorded sex weighed 2,975 g.
findings.interpretation: The stack reaches the grouping operation inside the window expression. On the affected build the numeric column still contains [2, 1, 1, 2, 4]. On the fix, the same boundary receives four nulls followed by 4. The conditional expression has removed the other four values before summation. Evaluating the condition in a separate column first also restores all three island totals on the old release.
findings.limits: The original report does not specify dependency versions. The replay held pandas 2.3.3, PyArrow 22.0.0 and Polars 1.35.2 constant. SQLite window queries and an independent Python sum checked each returned row. The captured stacks are synchronous.

cases.title: Filtered connection pages report the total for all NATS clients

findings.observation: An operator queried a three-server JetStream cluster with known client connections. On the first server, three of four clients matched Bob. The first page returned one Bob row and reported four matches. A query with zero matches also reported four. The fixed server returned totals of three and zero. All 36 message readbacks across the four runs succeeded.
findings.interpretation: The Go runtime trace follows the listener spawning the connection goroutine through the filtered count and the HTTP reply. For Bob’s first page, the count sample saw four open clients, three matches and a response total of four. The fix assigns the match count before paging the result. The client port and response pointer identify the request that received the sampled total.
findings.limits: The reproducer uses new HTTP connections on healthy local clusters. Both revisions ran with stock binaries and with observations on one server. The scope is the monitoring response’s total field.

cases.title: An ordered consumer reports zero pending before delivering an unseen key

findings.observation: All 200 subjects remained in file storage, yet 49 of 300 reads saw pending=0 before receiving a previously unseen key.
findings.interpretation: Matching the consumer’s wire ACK to loopAndGatherMsgs showed a cached count of −1 while delivering sequence 2976 of 2978. The new key followed at revision 2977.
findings.limits: The replay used a single 2.15.1 server with 50 keys being updated. Upstream was still discussing the precision guarantee, and no server fix was verified.

cases.title: JetStream direct reads lose the stored message timestamp

findings.observation: A broker HMSG contained its stored UTC timestamp. The 2.14.0 client returned None for that same direct read. Its standard read returned the timestamp.
findings.interpretation: The direct formatter received the real headers and returned the same RawStreamMsg that get_msg delivered. The exact source fix reads Nats-Time-Stamp and converts it to a timezone-aware datetime. All four clients preserved the payload, sequence and subject.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied a schematic call and omitted a version. The unchanged upstream KV test exercises the assertion. The coroutine identity was measured on the separate sensor stream; its broker timestamp is specific to that recorded trial.

cases.title: A slow callback serializes requests on one NATS subscription

findings.observation: In both runs, only one of ten concurrent requests received a reply within 500 ms when the subscription callback took 300 ms per message.
findings.interpretation: Deferring WaitGroup.Done removed the test’s separate one-second timeout but left nine request timeouts, while a second subscription on the same subject and connection received all ten messages in order despite the slow callback.
findings.limits: The loopback test used a contemporary release because none was specified. Scheduling determined which request succeeded.

cases.title: Three NATS consumers share one outstanding delivery limit

findings.observation: With 20 jobs and 50-second callbacks, three processes peaked at one unacknowledged message and finished in about 1,001 seconds. Raising max_ack_pending to 3 gave a peak of three and about 601 seconds.
findings.interpretation: All three subscriptions shared one durable consumer: async sleep alone left them taking turns at limit 1, while limit 3 allowed overlapping callbacks even with blocking sleep.
findings.limits: The broker supplied the pending counts. The report omitted versions, and a separate short-callback run measured overlap.

cases.title: JetStream key enumeration can finish before all keys arrive

findings.observation: All 200 keys remained present, yet 166 of 300 keys() calls on nats-py 2.16.0 missed keys and 65 of those reported an empty bucket while four connections updated 50 keys.
findings.interpretation: A zero pending count could enqueue the end marker before client dispatch finished, and one traced watcher had delivered 198 distinct keys at the marker and eventually received all 200.
findings.limits: Counts depend on scheduling. The concurrent program used no artificial dispatch delay, and the initialization change was a local diagnostic control.

cases.title: Why did JetStream still report 197 pending messages after the consumer drained?

findings.observation: NATS Server 2.6.1 reported 237 pending messages for an ephemeral consumer configured to deliver the latest message per subject. Reading all 250 stream sequences independently found 248 retained records and exactly 40 subjects. The consumer received and acknowledged precisely those 40 latest records. Its final ACK still reported 197 pending. A separate pull consumer returned 404 No Messages with the same count.
findings.interpretation: The consumer initialization stack reaches setInitialPendingAndStart. With a filter identical to the stream subject, the affected branch used 248 retained messages minus the 11 sequences before the first selected record. The native trace then shows that same request goroutine launching the delivery worker in setLeader. All 41 reply subjects encoded in deliverMsg match the receiving client byte for byte. The fix counts the 40 selected sequences and reaches zero after the last historical delivery.
findings.limits: The deterministic key history reconstructs the public counts. The original application data was unavailable. Stock releases establish the behavior with file and memory storage. The function stacks and intermediate values come from observed builds of the upstream fix and its direct parent. The upstream four-key regression also reproduced the opposite error on a different history: two pending instead of four.

cases.title: The Python NATS client keeps only the last duplicate header

findings.observation: The subscription callback received hdr2=val3, and reversing the two hdr2 entries yielded val2. Single-value headers and three distinct keys were preserved.
findings.interpretation: A 2.2.0 line trace showed the decoder assigning val3 to a dictionary key that already held val2, matching both observed header orders.
findings.limits: The report omitted versions. The replay used contemporary local releases. Upstream declined a nats.aio change, and nats-core was a separate control.

cases.title: Why did the JetStream subscriber receive all ten messages while its named delivery subject received none?

findings.observation: The reporter requested stream-test.consume3 when creating a durable push consumer. With nats-py 2.9.0, the broker stored a generated inbox as the delivery subject. The returned JetStream subscription received all ten binary records. An independent Core NATS subscription on the requested subject received zero. The landed fix and the first fixed release delivered all ten records to both subscribers. Explicit consumer creation through the manager and automatic inbox allocation when no subject was supplied both worked across all four builds.
findings.interpretation: The caller’s creation stack points to the original line awaiting js.subscribe. The same live JetStreamContext.subscribe frame allocated an inbox and assigned it to config.deliver_subject while creating the consumer. The next sample shows the new value on the caller’s config object. The outgoing request, broker reply and underlying subscription agree on that inbox. The fix checks whether the caller supplied a subject before allocating one. A separate experiment restarted the broker and rebound the stored durable with either client version. Each new client used the subject the first client had saved.
findings.limits: The report supplies a coroutine and consumer settings. The harness supplies the stream, missing imports, callback and payloads, connects to an ephemeral loopback port, and cancels the final sleep after delivery. All tests use the reported server release, 2.10.21. The three-message trace is an independent execution of the original coroutine. The restart experiment publishes one additional record per stage.

cases.title: A NATS subscription stops before its second message callback completes

findings.observation: The upstream test published first and second with an unsubscribe limit of two. Version 2.16.0 and the fix parent recorded only first, while the fix commit and 2.17.0 recorded both.
findings.interpretation: The trace located cancellation in the subscription’s own Task and matched the queued messages to their callbacks. Changing the queue check from empty to empty() restored the second callback.
findings.limits: The report identified a source error. The runnable test came from the closing PR and used one local NATS Core broker.

cases.title: A non-ASCII value makes nats.py drop every message header

findings.observation: The broker persisted the posted Go CLI request with Test: ø, but both Core and JetStream pull consumers on 2.14.0 received the body with empty headers, losing the ASCII Batch field too.
findings.interpretation: The read task failed during client decoding. Object identities linked that message to the error callback and pull result, and the fixed decoders matched PR #928.
findings.limits: The replay used the default parser and NATS 2.10.26. Task attribution covers the pull connection’s reader. Production messages and dead-letter handling were unavailable.

cases.title: A stream copy reports the source name in its success message

findings.observation: Running nats str cp old new printed “Stream old was created” with NATS CLI 0.3.0. The server had created new. Its two mirrored messages could be read through all three endpoints, and the original stream retained its creation time. A regular stream copied from Input to Output showed the same naming error.
findings.interpretation: The Go stack stopped at cpAction with the server result naming new. The subsequent Printf call received old as its formatting argument. On the fixed commit it received new, which matched the cluster state. Reading the argument at both call sites locates the discrepancy in the CLI output.
findings.limits: The original issue omits the source stream configuration. The exact command was run on a mirror, with a separate ordinary-stream control using distinct subjects. The detail heading below the corrected success message continued to show the old name. These stacks come from the synchronous CLI path.

cases.title: JetStream stream info labels local timestamps as UTC

findings.observation: The first and last timestamps of a three-replica stream displayed local clock times in UTC−6 and UTC+05:30, yet both lines retained the UTC label.
findings.interpretation: Sequence reads, node monitoring and CLI JSON agreed on the timestamps, while the formatting stack and a two-line patch isolated the literal label in the client.
findings.limits: Two messages covered the first and last sequence. The CLI debug stack was checked against uninstrumented output and carried no goroutine creation record.

cases.title: A dynamic route returns 404 for its own space-encoded URL

findings.observation: Requests to the URL generated for /hello world/{name} returned 404, as did requests under a static directory prefix containing a space.
findings.interpretation: Ordinary paths and an alternative route to the same file worked, and the recorded lookup keys narrowed the discrepancy to how registration and request resolution encode the path.
findings.limits: One named route and one directory were tested with ordinary spaces. The upstream PR was still open.

cases.title: trust_env adds executor lookups before aiohttp sends request headers

findings.observation: The report cited about 23 ms at 256 concurrent requests, and the loopback replay confirmed later request headers and a later first response chunk with trust_env enabled.
findings.interpretation: Supplying local credentials eliminated one executor submission, leaving only the proxy lookup, while disabling trust_env eliminated both submissions before headers were sent.
findings.limits: The replay used no vLLM server and did not time pool queuing, file reads, or event-loop resumption separately.

cases.title: A HEAD response without Content-Length prevents connection reuse

findings.observation: In a GET–HEAD–GET sequence against one HTTP/1.1 server, the second GET opened a new TCP connection after a bodyless HEAD response omitted Content-Length.
findings.interpretation: The Python parser discarded the connection after HEAD. Applying the open PR’s parser change made all four test cases reuse one connection.
findings.limits: The pool decision was observed directly. The order of flag updates in the native llhttp parser came from source inspection.

cases.title: httpcore can start a second HTTP/2 stream before the peer permits it

findings.observation: With one POST still open and a peer limit of one stream, httpcore 0.16.3 raised LocalProtocolError on the second request in all three uninstrumented runs. The server saw only stream 1.
findings.interpretation: The old gate used local settings while h2 enforced the peer’s limit. With the fix, the second POST arrived before the first finished when the limit rose to 1,000, and after it finished when the limit stayed at one.
findings.limits: Two loopback POSTs reproduced the protocol error. The reporter’s APNs application, credentials and 100-request workload were unavailable.

cases.title: Reading ClientResponse.content skips the chunk trace callback

findings.observation: In two uninstrumented runs, the client read the entire 4,519-byte PNG over HTTPS and printed only “main received 4519 bytes.”
findings.interpretation: The reader task’s stack and the returned data hash confirmed the read, while two positive controls showed where notification occurred on other read paths.
findings.limits: The original icon was served locally. The fix comparison used Python 3.12.4, separately from the reported 3.8.6 environment.

cases.title: Two exported AdaBoost trees lost a small class probability

findings.observation: The released converter reproduced the report’s 28 out-of-tolerance values among 2,000 probabilities. Fourteen input rows were affected, including two whose predicted labels changed. In the held-out digits 0 and 1 test, 202 of 360 images had a probability discrepancy and all labels agreed. The other two digit pairs and the ten-class run met the original tolerance.
findings.interpretation: Every input took the same tree branches as in scikit-learn. For binary leaves the converter kept only the second class weight. In trees 25 and 34 the retained values rounded to exactly 1 in float32, and the runtime returned 0 for the first class. The original probabilities were about 1.63e-8 and 9.79e-9. Clipping replaced zero with 2.22e-16 before the boost graph took its logarithm. The converter stacks expose the values before and after serialization. Replacing just these two trees’ weight attributes in the exported model removed all 28 discrepancies.
findings.limits: The report specified Python, scikit-learn and converter versions. The local CPU runtime was ONNX Runtime 1.18.1, available before the report. The two-weight encoding is a local control. The converter ran synchronously. The captured Python stacks establish the export path, and the ONNX Runtime profile records the later CPU kernels. Tree indices start at zero.

cases.title: ONNX Runtime averaged five boundary windows over too many cells

findings.observation: The reporter exported a 4×4 tensor containing 1 through 16. PyTorch eager and the opset-18 export both requested a 3×3 average with one cell of padding. On ORT 1.23.2, 1.27.0 and 1.28.0, five of the nine results were too small. The last row was [3, 5, 1.7777777910232544]. Release 1.29.0 returned [4.5, 7.5, 4] and matched the exact reference rounded to float32 at every position. All four releases passed the floor-mode, padding-exclusion and opset-19 controls.
findings.interpretation: The bottom-right window includes 16 and three padding zeros. In each affected shipping binary GDB read 16 and 9 from the registers at the divide instruction and caught the resulting write to that output cell. In 1.29.0 the divisor was 4 and a hardware watchpoint recorded writes of 0, 16 and 4. The source fix directs this configuration to a loop that stops counting at the edge of the explicit padding. Real-data measurements ran the same exported ceil and floor models on 7,188 unscaled quadrants from all 1,797 UCI test images. Each affected release returned exactly 21,293 incorrect ceil outputs on 6,957 tiles across all images. Dividing by nine accounted for every discrepancy. All 64,692 ceil values were correct on 1.29.0 and all 28,752 floor values were correct on every release. Both independent batches produced identical float32 bytes. E. Alpaydin and C. Kaynak, Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits (1998), UCI Machine Learning Repository, CC BY 4.0.
findings.limits: These measurements cover pooling layer values on the CPU. The digit labels identify groups of images. The report used a CUDA-capable PyTorch debug build and Python 3.10. This CPU replay uses PyTorch 2.11.0+cpu and Python 3.11. The parent and fix commits were inspected as source. All recorded arithmetic and full native stacks come from the released x86-64 wheels. The debugger used a bound output buffer to observe the store. Ordinary session.run calls separately verified every returned value. The physical graph contains synchronous samples and has zero coroutine origins.

cases.title: Exporting binary LDA to ONNX exaggerated class probabilities

findings.observation: The reporter trained a two-class linear discriminant model on 1,000 rows. For the first observation scikit-learn assigned the second class probability 0.52054489. The released converter produced an ONNX model that returned 0.5410205 on the same observation. Every row exceeded an absolute probability error of 0.00001. All 1,000 predicted labels agreed.
findings.interpretation: The converter wrote two opposite scores into the binary classifier. Applying softmax to that pair doubles the log odds. The proposed change applies the logistic transform for two classes. Its largest absolute error on the reported batch was below 0.00000006. Independent posteriors computed from class means, pooled within-class covariance and observed priors agreed with scikit-learn.
findings.limits: PR 1285 was open and unmerged when checked. Both published versions tested reproduced the discrepancy. The original program uses seeded training data. The Wine controls train on alcohol and malic-acid measurements and score held-out rows. Stack captures observe Python conversion and runtime returns. The separate ONNX Runtime profiles identify CPU operators. No coroutine creation identity was observed.

cases.title: ColumnTransformer loses a permutation when it selects every column

findings.observation: Both reported dependency sets and their ONNX reference evaluators reproduced the preprocessing error. A separate one-level decision tree changed class on two of four rows.
findings.interpretation: The converter skipped selection when the column count matched the input width. The fix also checked positions and emitted an ArrayFeatureExtractor with indices [1,0].
findings.limits: The replay used one known-width float tensor, integer indices and CPU execution. The classification example was a local control.

cases.title: A converted forest returned class probabilities that summed to 2.56

findings.observation: For input [1, 1], the original forest returned two distributions that each summed to one. After export, ONNX Runtime returned probability sums of 2.50 and 2.56. The top labels for this input still agreed. Across all nine possible inputs, three had a different predicted label. On 360 held-out digit images, 39 images had at least one label different from the reference forest.
findings.interpretation: The conversion stack identifies the multi-output forest’s leaf-vote calculation. For the first tree, both outputs had leaf counts [3, 3, 0]. The exported graph turned each nonzero count into one, giving [1, 1, 0]. The fix divided by the total count to produce [0.5, 0.5, 0]. Executing the saved models and independently recomputing the tree votes confirmed this difference.
findings.limits: The reporter’s model uses 100 trees and two categorical outputs. The additional digit workload derives parity and a threshold label from each digit. Label disagreement is measured against the reference forest’s prediction. CPU inference used ONNX Runtime 1.9.0, and the comparison allowed an absolute probability difference of 0.000001. Both conversion and inference were synchronous.

cases.title: How did a float32 threshold change six tree decisions?

findings.observation: The same fitted regressor predicted 3.452764 kW for a household meter record. Its ONNX export predicted 2.885078 kW. In total, 13 of 4,032 held-out records differed from scikit-learn by more than 0.001 kW. The tensor entering the ensemble matched the original preprocessing output on every row.
findings.interpretation: At tree 4, node 40, the converter received a threshold of 1166882752. The ONNX node stored 1166882816, exactly equal to this record’s float32 input. That moved the record to the lower leaf. Six trees changed leaves. Changing one split at a time reproduced each tree’s predicted contribution. Editing all six together restored the output to 3.452763796 kW.
findings.limits: The report identified the pipeline stages but supplied no training set or model. We fitted that architecture on UCI household and bike records plus a four-input boundary case. The household model uses calendar seconds as a float32 feature. Error here means a difference from the original model. The upstream 50-row regression test passed on both revisions. The measured paths run synchronously.

cases.title: Why did converting a one-hot encoder change five of six random-forest predictions?

findings.observation: The reporter trained a random forest on six rows, using two categorical columns and two numbers. With min_frequency=2, scikit-learn put CAT2 values a, b and c into one rare-category indicator and gave d its own column. The 1.15.0 and 1.16.0 converters and the parent of PR #1029 produced separate columns for all four CAT2 values. ONNX Runtime on CPU therefore passed eight columns to a forest trained on six. The original unseeded program printed different labels after conversion on each of those three builds in both recorded trials. With seed 17 they all changed five of the six labels. The merged source and 1.17.0 each produced six columns, matched all six labels and kept the largest absolute class-probability difference below 0.000001. In a separate control, retraining with the default frequency setting gave both pipelines eight columns and identical labels on every build.
findings.interpretation: On 1.15.0 the converter received the fitted encoder (segment 6) and passed [-1, 6] to the categorical Reshape (segment 17). Appending the two numeric passthrough columns put them at positions 6 and 7. The forest reads positions 0 through 5, so its splits on positions 4 and 5 received indicators for CAT2=c and CAT2=d. On the merged source each encoder split its frequent and rare indicators and summed the rare group. For CAT2 the split sizes were [1, 3]. The categorical Reshape then used [-1, 4] (comparison segment 47). The intermediate shape calculator reported six categorical columns on both builds. The emitted Reshape and the CPU tensor read at the forest input establish the widths that inference actually used. Extracting TreeEnsembleClassifier from each of the five saved trial-one pipelines yielded identical node bytes. Feeding the correctly grouped tensor directly into that forest recovered all six sklearn labels. A separate traversal of the 100 serialized trees checked both possible input layouts. In two held-out rows with categories (a, d), changing the numeric pair from (0.36, 0.85) to (0.54, 0.57) left the affected pipeline’s class-1 probability at 0.32. The same forest given the grouped features returned 0.37 and 0.88.
findings.limits: The issue is open and the reporter omitted a converter version. 1.15.0 was the latest wheel at the time of the report. PR #1029 came from branch i1026 and its description refers to earlier PR #1028. The adjacent source runs locate the grouping change at #1029, and 1.17.0 was its first release. The parent and merged comparisons used full Git packages, both labeled 1.17.0 internally. All five ran with scikit-learn 1.3.1 and ONNX Runtime 1.17.3 on CPU. The reporter’s classifier used random training, so the first table gives the wrong-label count separately for each original run. The reproducible label and probability comparisons use a separate seed-17 fit. The ten-row forest-input experiment reuses those fitted trees on the six posted rows and four held-out rows. Its second table shows class-1 probabilities rounded to two decimals. CPython sampled synchronous converter calls. The ONNX tensors and predictions came from actual CPU executions. This case contributes zero coroutine origins.

cases.title: An ONNX ordinal encoder assigned distinct codes to categories trained to share one

findings.observation: With a minimum frequency of five, the reporter’s 100-row program trained an encoder in which all 47 known categories shared code 0 on the saved draw. For the first input, 22, scikit-learn returned 0 and the ONNX model from skl2onnx 1.19.1 returned 12. Across the 100 rows, 87 codes were wrong. The seven literal inputs in a later issue comment reproduced all of its printed values, including six incorrect ONNX codes. Release 1.20.0 produced the expected codes for both programs.
findings.interpretation: The parent converter passed sorted category indices 0 through 46 to the ONNX LabelEncoder. Its fitted estimator already held 47 zeros as the frequency-group mapping. The fix passed that mapping to the node. The converter stack, serialized node attributes and CPU inference results agree. In the Auto MPG control, two rare cylinder counts shared code 3. Grouping also renumbered ordinary four-, six- and eight-cylinder categories, which explains why every held-out vehicle received an incorrect code on 1.19.1.
findings.limits: The original program supplied neither random seeds nor installed versions. Its published sample had 86 discrepancies. The local runs execute the unchanged program with seed 1215 and save the exact 70-row training split. Both releases and both source revisions use the same CPU backend. The 80-row Auto MPG holdout is independent of fitting. The per-cylinder table also scores the complete 398-row public file to cover rare cylinder counts present only in training. The Python stacks cover synchronous conversion and the inference API. Native operator profiles come from separate executions of the saved models.

cases.title: Sigmoid calibration uses probabilities instead of raw pipeline scores

findings.observation: The exported model classified all 500 test samples as class 1, disagreeing with scikit-learn on 271 labels with a maximum probability error of 0.460038, while an unwrapped tree worked.
findings.interpretation: Intermediate tensors showed logistic-transformed probabilities entering calibration. Passing the raw-score option to the child estimator restored correct probabilities with the same trees and coefficients.
findings.limits: The replay covered binary gradient boosting, identity preprocessing, sigmoid calibration and the CPU execution provider.

cases.title: OpenRaft publishes the snapshot index before installation finishes

findings.observation: While the learner held the installation write lock, all four old-version runs advertised index 9 with no current snapshot. All four fixed runs showed neither value yet.
findings.interpretation: The old metric used the engine’s prepared index, whereas the fix waited for I/O completion. The learner ultimately stored and advertised index 9 and applied log entry 11 in every group.
findings.limits: The replay used the healthy t51 integration fixture. The snapshot slot was checked in memory, and no cross-task message edge was inferred.

cases.title: OpenRaft’s storage suite rejected a valid node display format

findings.observation: A store that displayed node zero as Node[0] failed the public OpenRaft conformance suite on commit 548a449. The tenth check read the initial state of an empty store. It expected the string “0” for LogIO, Apply and Snapshot, while the store returned “Node[0]” for each. Substituting exactly those three labels made the full printed states identical. Formatting the same node type as a plain integer let the parent complete the entire suite. Commit 5863174 passed both formats. Each condition ran twice, with matching stock and debugger outcomes.
findings.interpretation: The storage helper formats the configured node type. The parent suite built its expectation by formatting a raw u64, and the derived equality operation included the three progress-label strings. PR 1660 converts the constant to the configured node type before formatting it. At the actual assertion, GDB inspected both operands and followed the physical stack through the individual check, run_test and test_store to the active Suite::test_all poll. At creation, the fixture called the original Rust future constructor. Both complete 2,360-byte moves, the first poll and the self pointer recovered from the third poll frame establish which future was executing.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied a formatter example. The runnable store and full test_all regression come from the merged PR. The parent receives that fixture and its workspace registration. A separate public-API control saved and reread a vote, a blank entry and a committed log ID on every build. These results cover the in-process memstore and conformance suite. Deployment, restart durability and Raft cluster behavior were outside the experiment. The origin edge belongs only to the original test_all future. The full comparison stack and its suite-frame view share one debugger stop. Both commits use the same reproduction lock and stable Rust 1.100.0.
