cases.title: A five-record ormar page returned only two parents

findings.observation: The posted query asks for five parent models with their keywords. In 0.7.5 the five database rows belong to parents 1, 1, 2, 2 and 2. ormar returned two parents. The fixed query fetched eight joined rows and returned five parents with their keywords. The original pytest suite passed all 21 cases on 0.8.0. In a second dataset of seven Chinook playlists, the old second page still contained TV Shows from the first page. The fixed second page contained three classical playlists.
findings.interpretation: At the await expression in the posted test, CPython exposed the unstarted QuerySet.all coroutine and its creation frame. The same coroutine was running when LimitQuery.apply added a limit to an expression that already contained both joins. SQLite executed that statement, and the recorded input to merge_instances_list contained only two distinct parent IDs. The fixing commit called LimitQuery.apply inside a parent-only subquery and then joined its rows. The new opt-in raw-row limit reproduced the former first-page behavior.
findings.limits: The reporter did not specify a version or provide the database bootstrap module. We supplied a private SQLite database and tested the release available on the reporting date as well as 0.7.5. On 0.7.3 the single-loop harness also encountered relation bookkeeping and child hydration differences. The primary capture uses 0.7.5. The playlist dataset retains all memberships in the seven selected playlists, with the title field widened to fit the original track names.

cases.title: Grouped OHLC fails on Arrow-backed numeric data

findings.observation: Grouping the reporter’s three floats into two groups raised “Mask must be 1D array” with Arrow, while pandas nullable floats and NumPy floats produced the correct four OHLC columns.
findings.interpretation: Aggregation had already produced the correct values and a two-dimensional mask when __arrow_array__ passed them to a one-dimensional conversion. The proposal preserved the result for table construction.
findings.limits: The replay used Linux x86-64 instead of macOS ARM. Closed PR #71975 was built locally and was not verified as a released fix.

cases.title: A missing categorical key contributes to the wrong group

findings.observation: The reporter’s February row appeared in January group 2, raising its sum from 5 to 13. In another case an empty category took the missing-key row’s value, first 31 and then 131.
findings.interpretation: The combined ID for missing key −1 collided with a valid group. Restoring −1 after reordering returned the sum to 5 and made all four upstream parameter cases pass.
findings.limits: The isolated patch ran on 3.0.0 with 3.0.1 as a release control. The Cython wrapper was observed, not the C summation internals.

cases.title: Paxos treats identical voting members as different

findings.observation: The conditional insert succeeded, but all 192 remote responses in Cassandra 4.1.7 returned three extra gossip entries, while all 96 in-process responses returned none.
findings.interpretation: The remote HashSet and local AsList contained the same three addresses; replacing only Electorate or upgrading to 4.1.8 made all 192 remote comparisons equal and removed the extra entries.
findings.limits: Fixed membership and serial requests on loopback. TCP counts include background traffic, and messages were not linked across nodes by ID.

cases.title: Conditional updates treat null lists differently in Cassandra

findings.observation: In 4.1.5, a null non-frozen list passed l < [1,2] and became [9], while a frozen null list failed the condition. An update guarded by l >= [] also applied where 4.1.6 rejected it and preserved [3].
findings.interpretation: In 4.1.6, valueAppliesTo returns false for an empty storage iterator. Replacing just the collection-condition class on a 4.1.5 node reproduced that decision.
findings.limits: Three healthy loopback nodes exercised Paxos v2. The reported DELETE condition behaved differently locally, and no cross-node stack edges were inferred.

cases.title: Why did a PostgreSQL cursor with 42 rows evaluate as false?

findings.observation: Peewee 3.17.2 returned False when the reporter tested a freshly executed cursor. Iterating that same cursor returned all 42 IDs. When the reporter called list(cursor) first, the truth test returned True. A separate empty result also evaluated as True after iteration. The immediate fix and release 3.17.3 returned True for the 42-row result and False for the empty result at both points.
findings.interpretation: The physical trace links the wrapper returned by SelectBase._execute to the receiver of the actual truth test. In 3.17.2 the __bool__ method read populated. It was false before the first fetch and true once iteration reached the end, including for the empty cursor. The fixing commit removed that method. Python then called the existing __len__, which filled the cache and returned the row count. Direct psql reads on separate connections confirmed every row ID before and after each trial.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied two code blocks and observations in comments. The harness supplied the model, 42 committed rows and the public bool(cursor) call. Every locking SELECT ran on a real, private PostgreSQL 10.23 server. The two trials used the release that is also the fix parent, the fixing source commit and the next release. The six captures observed synchronous calls and returns. All three builds yielded the full rows during iteration. Matched coroutine origins total zero.

cases.title: Why did a two-column group count return four fields?

findings.observation: The reporter passed six rows to petl.aggregate with key=['foo'] and aggregation=len. The first group key was the string 'aaa'. petl 1.7.4 printed it as three cells, followed by the correct count 2. The table header still named only two columns, foo and value. Iterating the returned table exposed the same four fields seen in the printout. The other groups split 'bbb' and 'ccc' in the same way. In 1.7.6 each row held a complete key and its count. A SQLite GROUP BY on the original six rows independently returned ('aaa', 2), ('bbb', 3) and ('ccc', 1).
findings.interpretation:
While print(table2) rendered the reporter’s table, CPython recorded the actual generator yield in petl.transform.reductions.itersimpleaggregate. Segment 1 holds the two-column header. In segment 2, the local group value k is 'aaa' and the key selector is ['foo']. On 1.7.4, line 277 yields tuple(k) + (aggregation(grp),), expanding the string into three characters. The landed code unwraps a one-element list or tuple before deciding how to emit the group. On 1.7.6, segment 2 at line 290 returns ('aaa', 2). Changing only the selector to the scalar 'foo' gave the expected result on all five builds. A one-element tuple reproduced the list behavior.

A second input used unequal-length product names and summed quantities. The affected rows for apple, apricot and pear had six, eight and five fields under a two-field header. The numeric sums matched SQLite across builds. Grouping by both product and region also matched SQLite on every build.
findings.limits: The reported release was petl 1.7.4 on Python 3.8.5. This replay used CPython 3.10.12 and the full posted code block, including its print statement. It exercised the simple aggregate implementation. The two source packages were built with upstream setup.py. The earlier 1.7.5 tag and its PyPI distribution still have the affected implementation. PyPI uploaded that distribution on February 5, 2022, three days after uploading 1.7.6. The stack observations follow synchronous generator yields. The coroutine-origin count is zero.

cases.title: Piccolo rounds large SQLite integers when reading them

findings.observation: After writing 625757527765811240, Piccolo 1.22.0 read 625757527765811200 from all three fields, while native aiosqlite returned the original integer each time.
findings.interpretation: The old int(float(value)) conversion collapsed two adjacent stored integers into one result, losing 40 and 41 respectively. Int(Decimal(value)) preserved both in either submission order.
findings.limits: The replay ran on Linux. The original reads were sequential. Task origins were verified only for the separately scheduled control reads.

cases.title: Piccolo generates invalid SQL for JSONB null checks

findings.observation: Both == None and is_null() generated IS NULL$1 on 0.66.0 and the fix parent, and PostgreSQL returned 42601. The fix commit and 0.68.0 returned only the expected row, id=1.
findings.interpretation: The old query builder serialized an UNDEFINED object, and the resulting SQL and argument matched what the driver received. The fix omitted the argument and returned the same row as psql.
findings.limits: The report supplied the two expressions. The local schema and four rows were reconstructed, and Task attribution covers query execution only.

cases.title: Piccolo inserts an empty string for a null get_or_create condition

findings.observation: On 0.101.0, creating A stored an empty string and creating B hit the optional_id uniqueness constraint, while 0.102.0 stored both rows.
findings.interpretation: The old mapper extracted values only from Equal conditions, leaving Varchar to supply an empty default, while the fix maps IsNull to None, and a default=None control also inserted successfully.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied the app without version pins. Both calls shared one Uvicorn lifespan task. Separate tracing and database logs verified the bindings.

cases.title: Prefetching a related row decodes a JSON array twice

findings.observation: With [1, 2, 3] in the parent row, the first two queries succeeded, but prefetching the child with load_json raised TypeError in both the reporter’s example and the maintainer’s script.
findings.interpretation: The nested mapper passed the already-decoded list to the decoder again; restricting the second decode to strings and byte-like values preserved the original list.
findings.limits: Database and driver versions were unspecified. Both upstream examples ran sequentially, and task creation was verified only in a separate two-query control.

cases.title: Why did SQLite return a float from a decimal array?

findings.observation:
The reporter saved a list containing Decimal('0.1') and awaited the first row. On SQLite, Piccolo 1.38.0 returned a Python float. Its display is 0.1 and its exact binary value is slightly above one tenth. The scalar Numeric column returned Decimal('0.1') in the same environment. PostgreSQL returned Decimal('0.10') from its numeric array on every build. With a table created and read by Piccolo 1.39.0, SQLite returned Decimal('0.1'). The first table shows one element of each returned row.

The type affects ordinary arithmetic. A second SQLite row held the two input prices 0.10 and 0.20. The JSON bytes on disk were [0.1, 0.2] in both schemas. Adding the two returned floats yielded 0.30000000000000004. Adding the two returned Decimals yielded Decimal('0.3'), equal to thirty cents.
findings.interpretation:
The earlier code declared the SQLite column as ARRAY. Fetching the row invoked convert_array_out, whose JSON decoder produced a list of floats. The landed change gives a new numeric-array column the declaration ARRAY_NUMERIC(5, 2). Its converter also handles numeric JSON elements, passing their string forms to decimal conversion. In the crossed reads, each reader opened exactly the same saved database as the other reader. The fixed reader still returned floats from the old ARRAY column. The old reader also returned floats from the new declaration. The new declaration and the new reader together produced Decimal values. The prior equality check could pass on 50.0 because the float equals Decimal('50.0'). The landed test checks the element’s Python type.

The reported await at posted.py line 5 entered Proxy.__await__, which created First.run at piccolo/query/proxy.py line 40. In the 1.38.0 SQLite graph, segment 1 records that unstarted coroutine. Segment 21 samples the same object and frame at select.py line 102 as it returns the selected row. A separate aiosqlite worker executed fetchall and returned the converted list at segment 14. The fetch job’s Future, the bound cursor and the returned element’s identity connect that worker to the row delivered on the event-loop thread. On 1.39.0 the corresponding worker returned a list containing a Decimal at segment 16.
findings.limits: The issue supplies an awaited code block and identifies SQLite and PostgreSQL. It gives no exact library, driver or server versions. The 1.38.0 wheel was current at opening, and 1.39.0 shipped after PR #1445. The replay supplies imports, starts each database and creates the table before running the posted block. It tests CPython 3.11.15, SQLite 3.53.1 and PostgreSQL 10.23. Installing the corrected reader leaves pre-existing SQLite column declarations in place. The tested SQLite JSON representation also drops trailing zeroes in the paired prices. PostgreSQL retained the two-place decimal scale. A separate PostgreSQL numeric_send read confirmed the value and scale. The coroutine-origin count for this issue is one, for the select coroutine. The worker conversions and Future callbacks have their own physical stack records.

cases.title: Grouped min_by returns the first value when all sorting keys are null

findings.observation: For group a in the three-row example, Polars 1.39.0 returned 1 in memory and null in streaming mode. Both returned 3 for group b, and 1.40.1 returned null for a in both modes.
findings.interpretation: The Rust stack and row-replacement control localized the discrepancy to the grouped take after agg_arg_min: the old path took row indices, while the replacement preserved a null position.
findings.limits: GDB recorded function entries. The internal validity bit was inferred from separate position queries, outputs and source. The original streaming query used only min_by.

cases.title: A positive rolling window returned a negative mean

findings.observation: On Polars 1.30.0 the last three positive values in the posted array had an exact mean of 0.000058577603340381756, yet the centered rolling mean returned −0.000004144294508 in both runs. In 39 of 51 windows the mean fell outside the input range. Release 1.31.0 kept every posted mean within one Float32 step of its correctly rounded value. On a separate 587-event USGS catalog workload, the old release exceeded one step in 576 windows. At event usp000hw42 it returned 1,603,985.75 for an exact 1,484,142.3671875. The fixed release returned 1,484,142.375. Both releases correctly rounded the ordinary mean of [1, 1, 2] to 1.3333333730697632.
findings.interpretation: GDB followed the expression evaluator through rolling_mean and rolling_agg into the released Rust kernel. As the input 92439.234375 left the reporter’s window, 1.30.0 executed the scalar Float32 add vaddss and finished the update with a sum of 0.0000428866. Release 1.31.0 executed the Float64 add vaddsd and retained 0.0002310523. Native state and return registers matched every one of the 51 updates in each run. PR 22944 widened the sliding sum and compensation. Initialization still summed the first window in Float32, and the result still used Float32 division.
findings.limits: The 51 history variants keep the same final three values. All ten starts retaining the earlier peak gave a negative final mean in 1.30.0. Replacing just that peak with either neighbor gave the exact mean. In 1.31.0 all final means were positive, but starts 7 and 8 remained about 67% and 33% low. At start 7 GDB read an initial sum of 92439.234375 and zero compensation for an exact sum of 92439.23449328267. The wider updates inherited that loss. Each batch checked all 129 live sums, corrections and returned means across starts 7, 8 and 9. After the July initialization rework, all 51 results in 1.32.0 matched the wide-initialization model within one Float32 step of the reference. Release 2.1.0 gave the exact final mean in all 51. Each release control was measured twice. The USGS workload derives a relative energy index from catalog magnitudes. The captured stacks are synchronous.

cases.title: A nearest-date join selects the same date with exact matches disabled

findings.observation: With allow_exact_matches=False, every row of the five-date example matched itself on Polars 1.22.0. On 1.36.1 the matched row IDs were [2, 3, 4, 5, 4]. The older nearest join also paired each of 12 USGS earthquakes with itself. Both an exhaustive Python search and a SQLite ranking query agreed on the nearest distinct event for every row.
findings.interpretation: Inside the Rust nearest-neighbor kernel, the old scan evaluated an equal right-hand key while its allow-equality flag was false. Its distance of zero beat the preceding date. The fixed iterator skipped that key and compared the strictly earlier and later dates. At a midpoint in the reported five-date input it selected the later date.
findings.limits: Five builds ran the posted program and 54 control joins each. The controls include duplicate keys, empty tables, missing neighbors and both directional strategies. GDB captured operand values from the parent and fix source builds. The 1.22.0 release wheel supplied a function stack. The joins ran synchronously.

cases.title: A partial weighted rolling window gets the wrong mean

findings.observation: With weights [1, 2], Polars 1.30.0 gave 1/3 for the first window and 1.33.0 gave 1, while the other four rows agreed. Grouped Parquet input showed the same first-window error.
findings.interpretation: Unit-vector controls showed the old implementation took the first weight and divided by the full weight sum, narrowing the defect to alignment and normalization in incomplete windows.
findings.limits: Native stacks reached the rolling operator’s entry. Coefficient checks covered positive weights and inputs without nulls.

cases.title: Why did Polars return b as the minimum of [b, a, c]?

findings.observation: The reporter sorted xb, ya and zc and then removed the first character with str.slice(1). All four releases returned [b, a, c]. Polars 1.43.0 and the reported 1.43.1 release marked them as ascending. Series.min() and a one-group minimum both returned b, and DataFrame.sort() left the rows in place. Polars 1.43.2 and 2.1.0 cleared the flag, returned a, and sorted the rows as a, b, c. In the reporter’s tail example, the last two characters of ab, abc, b and ba are ab, bc, b and ba. The affected maximum was ba and the correct maximum was bc. Taking the first character preserved order in both directions on every build. In the separate SQL test, 16 of 192 queries disagreed with SQLite, all on the two affected releases. The materialized fruit suffixes gave minimum pear and maximum fig. SQLite returned apple and plum.
findings.interpretation: The 1.43.1 native substring function returned [b, a, c] with its ascending flag still set (segment 11). The string min_reduce read flag word 1 on the same Arrow array and view buffer (16). It took the ascending branch (18) and selected b at index zero (19). In the 1.43.2 comparison the scalar slice cleared the order bits (11). The reducer read word 0, entered its scan and returned a (25). In a separate experiment, importing the affected series through the public Arrow stream reused the same 48-byte string-view buffer. Both exports were held open during the address comparison. The imported series had neither sort flag and returned a. The list reconstruction and disk IPC round trip agreed. PR #28573 clears the order bits for a scalar nonzero-offset slice or a scalar tail and retains them for a zero-offset prefix.
findings.limits: The reporter used macOS arm64. The wheel runs used Linux x86-64, with the same CPython 3.14.6 and UInt32 index type. Separate Rust executables called public polars-core and polars-ops 0.54.4 methods at parent 72c95bfad0 and merge 36e414b4cb. On the reported examples the parent matched the 1.43.0 and 1.43.1 wheels, and the merge matched 1.43.2 and 2.1.0. For a second suffix sequence [c, b, a], the parent returned minimum c and maximum a. The merge returned a and c. GDB sampled str_slice calling substring, min_reduce reaching min_str, max_reduce reaching max_str, and Series::sort in both executables. SQL results and plans came from separate processes. On these two tables the optimized single-statement MIN/MAX plan applied str.slice directly to the source with no SORT node. The materialized MIN/MAX plan scanned the frame [id, k]. All single-statement, prefix and LIMIT 1 controls matched SQLite. The Series minimum diagnosis comes from synchronous native execution. These runs contribute zero coroutine origins.

cases.title: A valid sorted flag misaligns ordered window results

findings.observation: With every group key equal to 1, adding set_sorted put the cumulative sum 40 for t=1 on the first row, where t=4. A second dataset also showed misalignment.
findings.interpretation: Sorting within a group by t can change its row mapping even when the group key is sorted. The fix restricted direct expansion to slice groups, and 1.9.0 matched the reference on all 24 permutations.
findings.limits: The report omitted an exact version. Tests used CPU wheels and unique within-group sort keys. Native stacks and Rust source identified the mapping path.

cases.title: Why did a three-row DataFrame return a cached count of two?

findings.observation: The reporter called a Prefect task that returns len(frame) with two zero-column DataFrames and a copy of the second. Their row indexes were [1, 2], [3, 4, 5] and [3, 4, 5]. With persisted results and the INPUTS cache policy, the reported checkout, 3.9.3 and the fix parent all returned [2, 2, 2]. Only the first call executed the task body. The landed fix and 3.9.4 returned [2, 3, 3], executing both distinct inputs. Adding one column of ones gave [2, 3, 3] and two body executions on every build. A separate two-row task returned the index labels themselves. When the labels changed from [1, 2] to [3, 4], the three affected builds returned [1, 2] again. With two-level indexes they likewise returned the old labels [(a, 1), (b, 2)] for [(a, 3), (b, 4)]. Both corrected builds returned the changed labels, and all five passed the populated-frame label control. Nine upstream regression cases also passed on the landed revision.
findings.interpretation: Prefect's DataFrame transform retained column names and their Series. With zero columns both lists were empty, so different row indexes produced the same hash input. On the reported checkout the legacy hashing module encoded plain JSON and produced 50d1743b8e3cb8d91a3767afb7293aff. The 3.9.3 wheel and the PR parent hashed a zero byte followed by JSON with a tuple tag, producing be9919c1b8b78f044eb31bb2a55eee9d. The landed transform includes the actual Index for a zero-column frame. In the async replay of the three-row call, the engine coroutine created by run_task at task_engine.py:1986 (segment 15) was on the physical Inputs.compute_key stack when the shared key returned (segment 19). Prefect found the two-row result on disk. At task_engine.py:1722, call_task_fn executed “result = await transaction.read()”. CPython recorded the read coroutine before its first await (segment 25). Its identical frame returned the stored record with value 2 at transactions.py:475 (segment 29). The fixed trace retains [3, 4, 5] in the key input and reaches the row_count body, which returns 3 (segment 25 of the landed graph).
findings.limits: The posted program is synchronous. Each of the five builds ran it directly and in two instrumented trials on Linux x86-64 with pandas 2.3.3. The reporter used macOS arm64. The coroutine captures come from a separate public async task with the same inputs and cache policy. In the cross-process experiment, six fresh interpreters per source revision shared one local Prefect server. Each input order had private result storage and used JSON serialization. The third worker hit the cache in all four sequences. Every byte in its result directory was identical before and after the call.

cases.title: Beam’s processing-time trigger resets a pending timer

findings.observation: All ten inputs arrived, but the affected runner emitted panes of four and six elements, while the fix emitted five pairs.
findings.interpretation: Eight of ten timer writes overwrote pending timers before the fix, versus zero of five after it, while spacing elements three seconds apart produced ten singletons on both builds.
findings.limits: The local Python DirectRunner used TestStream’s virtual processing clock. Java and Dataflow were outside the test.

cases.title: worker_client fails inside an async Dask worker function

findings.observation: On 2021.10.0, the async worker failed on a missing thread-local start_time, while the synchronous control processed the file and the async worker on 2023.6.0 returned 2016.
findings.interpretation: The upstream async-worker regression failed at the same line only on the older build; the newer code could catch the same exception during its check and still finish the job.
findings.limits: The report specified “Latest” on macOS. The Linux comparison held Python 3.9.25 fixed and did not establish the first affected or fixed release.

cases.title: A Dask parent waits for a child that only its own busy worker may run

findings.observation: The reporter’s example remained pending in two local process groups. Across three snapshots one worker ran the parent with the child ready, while the other three workers were idle.
findings.interpretation: The parent waited in gather while occupying the only thread eligible for the child. Both controls that relaxed the constraint completed, and the worker states matched the reporter’s dump.
findings.limits: Ran the public example in six local processes. The AWS deployment and private transformation workload were unavailable.

cases.title: Dask leaves queued work undispatched after a task secedes

findings.observation: After a task on a single-threaded worker called secede, the affected scheduler left a root task queued even though the worker had capacity.
findings.interpretation: After the fix, the first handle_long_running call cut the queue from four tasks to three and all five tasks could secede before the second event. Disabling queuing on the old build also passed.
findings.limits: The 0.8-second window measured entry into the long-running state in the PR’s local scenario, not recovery time.

cases.title: Nested worker_client calls try to release the same worker thread twice

findings.observation: The inner worker_client raised KeyError before submitting file work. Disabling its secede call, removing the outer context, or using the fix produced all four file sums.
findings.interpretation: The inner call tried to secede a thread that had already left the pool, while the fixed worker_client caught the internal KeyError and the task succeeded.
findings.limits: The replay used a real local scheduler, nanny and worker with numeric files. The reporter’s ETL job was unavailable.

cases.title: An OR condition makes a DuckDB ASOF join skip a valid row

findings.observation: On the same five-row table, repeating an equality condition inside OR dropped (5,I) from the three matches on the reported commit, 1.3.2, and 1.4.0.
findings.interpretation: Native stacks and separately observed row values showed the search choosing one candidate by time and stopping when the residual predicate rejected it, despite a valid alternative.
findings.limits: The Linux x86-64 run used synchronous native stacks. Separate probes supplied row values. The report used macOS ARM64.

cases.title: Dask’s peer-to-peer shuffle can keep the wrong first row for a duplicate key

findings.observation: In two uninstrumented runs over 2,592,000 rows in 30 partitions, all tasks succeeded and all 26 names survived, but every selected row differed from pandas’ first row for that name.
findings.interpretation: All 30 local candidates per name were present, but a later partition could come first. The fix retained input partition numbers and sorted by them during output conversion, also verified by patching the original workers.
findings.limits: Fixed random seed and two local TCP workers. Three full-size instrumented runs had 0, 0 and 26 wrong rows, so the frequency is undetermined.

cases.title: Multiprocess histogram export interleaves OpenMetrics label groups

findings.observation: A local HTTP scrape reproduced the report’s 38 samples and HELP/TYPE lines byte for byte. The parser rejected the first histogram group that reappeared later in the output.
findings.interpretation: The collector inserted both views’ sums before their buckets and counts, and the exporter preserved that order. The fix accumulated each label group separately so its samples stayed together.
findings.limits: Used the reported observations and 17 buckets with a real WSGI scrape. The original Django and Gunicorn configuration was unavailable.

cases.title: Timestamp comparison lets nanoseconds override the seconds field

findings.observation: The old client evaluated Timestamp(2,5) > Timestamp(3,4) as true, so its OpenMetrics parser rejected two increasing gauge timestamps that the fixed version accepted.
findings.interpretation: The old comparison checked 5 > 4 even after 2 > 3 was false, while the fix compares nanoseconds only when the seconds are equal.
findings.limits: The report gave no exact version. The comparison used 0.20.0, the commits around the fix, and valid nonnegative timestamps.

cases.title: A notification received during a health check disappears

findings.observation: With psycopg 3.2.3 and PostgreSQL 14.13, the reporter’s synchronous listener received 1 and 3 but missed 2, even though all three sends committed.
findings.interpretation: The query consumed the notification before ReadyForQuery and _notify_handler returned with no application callback. The fix queued the decoded object for the generator, which returned that same object.
findings.limits: The replay used Linux, a Unix socket and CPython 3.12 instead of the reporter’s macOS environment. The creation graph used the pure-Python driver.

cases.title: The notification generator bypasses registered callbacks

findings.observation: In the upstream LISTEN/NOTIFY regression, the 3.2.3 generator received foo/1 but the registered callback set_n2 left its result as None; the fix passed the same test.
findings.interpretation: The sender PID and payload identified the same notification in the old task’s generator branch and in the fixed task, which also invoked notify_handler and selected set_n2.
findings.limits: Task identity was captured in the pure Python driver on Linux over a Unix socket. The related report used macOS.

cases.title: Psycopg mistakes a row mapped to None for the end of a cursor

findings.observation: On 3.2.7, two fetchone calls on the reporter’s NULL/0 input both returned None, iteration yielded nothing, and streaming yielded only 0.
findings.interpretation: A traced async task had received three rows when its row maker mapped −1 to None and iteration stopped at position 1. A callback control read ID 1 three times before the fix and IDs 1, 2, 3 afterward.
findings.limits: The report did not pin versions. The concurrent tasks and ID callback were local controls. A three-row streaming chunk was checked with bundled libpq 17.

cases.title: executemany reports −1 after two deletes that match no rows

findings.observation: Both posted programs issued two unmatched DELETEs with a nonempty parameter sequence, and only 3.0.6 failed the final rowcount assertion by returning −1.
findings.interpretation: libpq recorded two DELETE 0 replies, and the runtime trace showed nrows or -1 converting zero to −1. The fix preserved zero and positive mixed-batch counts.
findings.limits: The original cursor was synchronous. PostgreSQL 14.13 was used locally, and the verifier added a final commit for persistence checks.

cases.title: Why did a decimal equality scan miss a row in an Iceberg table?

findings.observation:
PyIceberg 0.11.1 put Decimal('-1.28') in bucket 12 when the reporter called the 16-bucket transform. Apache Iceberg Java 1.9.2 returned 13. So did PyIceberg 0.12.0. The immediate parent and landed commit of PR #3746 reproduced the same difference. The first table shows the exact input bytes and signed hash on each build. All four Python builds agreed with Java on ten neighboring and ordinary values. The earlier scalar implementation differed at three signed-byte boundaries.

A table scan made the discrepancy visible in returned rows. PyIceberg 0.12.0 wrote six decimal amounts to six Parquet files in one snapshot. Every reader returned all six rows in an unfiltered scan. With an equality filter for -1.28, 0.11.1 selected zero files even though row 1 was present in bucket 13. For -327.68 it also selected zero files, leaving out row 3 in bucket 3. The corrected readers selected one file for each filter and returned the corresponding row. The other four equality filters agreed on all readers. The second table gives row IDs read directly from Parquet, alongside the file plans and query results.
findings.interpretation:
At scale two, -1.28 has unscaled value -128. Its shortest signed big-endian representation is the single byte 80 (hex). The earlier width calculation used the magnitude’s bit length and allowed another sign bit. It serialized -128 as ff80. Both byte strings represent -128, but the bucket transform hashes the actual bytes. The corresponding native MurmurHash3 results were 1817059852 and 267099677, which select buckets 12 and 13. For negative integers the landed code adds one before measuring bit length. It also removes the extra ff from -327.68, changing bucket 8 to 3, and from -83886.08, changing bucket 11 to 13.

In each release graph, reporter segments 3 and 4 record bytes_required and the bytes returned by decimal_to_bytes. At segment 6 GDB read those same bytes at the same address on entry to murmurhash3_x86_32. Segment 7 records its output word. Segments 9 and 10 record the Python hash and final bucket. The plain interpreter printed the same bucket. In the separate table run, sampled plan_files calls showed the same byte widths and encodings as BucketTransform.project derived the partition predicate. The wrong predicate excluded the matching file before any row in it could be returned.
findings.limits:
The June 17 report gives no PyIceberg version. Its two fenced snippets are archived verbatim. The runnable copies remove fence indentation, join the split -1.28 literal and rejoin a wrapped comment in the length example. The Java control calls the released Apache Iceberg bucket transform and BucketUtil on BigDecimal values. The table experiment uses one 0.12.0 writer, one local SQLite catalog and the same catalog, manifests and six data files for all four readers. Its conclusions apply to reads of that snapshot.

The Arrow batch transform takes a separate native path. For -1.28, the 0.11.1 environment with pyiceberg-core 0.8.0 returned bucket 4 on that path. Both source builds used pyiceberg-core 0.10.1 and returned 13 on the batch path, while their Python scalar buckets differed. The measured PR change is in the Python scalar width calculation. The captures follow synchronous scalar calls and record zero coroutine origins.

cases.title: A zero-second timeout converted an earlier external task cancellation

findings.observation: The posted program caught TimeoutError and printed that it continued on CPython 3.11 and 3.12. The reporter's 1 ms timeout control propagated CancelledError.
findings.interpretation: The same Task received the application cancel and the timer cancel. At Timeout.__aexit__, the incoming exception was CancelledError. The cancellation count fell from two to one, and the frame still raised TimeoutError. The graph joins the running test instance back to its allocation in the reporter's module.
findings.limits: The 1 ms comparison changes one timeout literal in the reporter's script. The upstream issue remained open in the archived tracker. Times cover prepared local reproductions.

cases.title: AsyncIO wait_for swallowed an external task cancellation

findings.observation: The unchanged GitHub example printed past its cancellation on CPython 3.10 and 3.11. On 3.12 the caller received CancelledError from the following sleep.
findings.interpretation: The affected wait_for frame received CancelledError while its inner Future was already done. It executed return fut.result() and the cancelled coroutine proceeded. The captured create-to-sample edge links that instance to main's create_task call.
findings.limits: The comparison uses three installed Linux CPython builds. The graph time includes the rest of the reporter's run, including its deliberate sleep when cancellation is swallowed.

cases.title: Three spellings of one UUID produce three local vector points

findings.observation: The reporter’s first program wrote the same UUID in uppercase, compact and canonical form. Client 1.19.1 counted three points and still had two after deletion. Client 1.20.0 counted one and deleted it. A second original program passed the previous page’s cursor back as a UUID object. The affected client raised TypeError. The fixed client returned the next two points.
findings.interpretation: All three writes reached _add_point on the same local collection, with a different string key each time. The fix canonicalized the UUID, so the second and third writes reached _update_point. The cursor sample shows the comparison receiving the same identifier the previous page returned. With the fix, normalization runs before the comparison. Independent vector queries and SQLite reads show which revisions survived.
findings.limits: The original calls are synchronous. A separate upstream async regression failed on the affected builds and passed on both fixed builds. The Rust 1.17.1 server supplied an independent reference through its HTTP API. The issue author describes an agent-assisted discovery followed by a personal rerun.

cases.title: Raft reports configuration index zero after bootstrap

findings.observation: The single-node test read 0 instead of 1 twice on both v1.8.0 and the PR parent, and a three-voter cluster also reported 0 after election and normal writes.
findings.interpretation: Disk, callback, snapshot, and cache evidence distinguished the membership index from ordinary log indexes, while storing membership and its index together made both proposed-fix runs pass.
findings.limits: PR #723 was still a proposal. The Linux TCP/Bolt run supplements the macOS in-memory example. Only the local leader’s publication goroutine had creation evidence.

cases.title: Why did Raft write snapshot index zero after restoring ten committed rows?

findings.observation: A fresh process reopened the node’s Bolt database and restored ten application records from a snapshot at index 11, term 1. With no new application write, the original revision accepted a manual snapshot and created a second file at index 0, term 0. Both state files contain the same 384 bytes. The fixed revision returned “Nothing new to snapshot” and retained the original file. Two restarted followers in the same three-voter cluster showed the same difference while the leader stayed up.
findings.interpretation: NewRaft restores the index and term on the Raft object before it starts the state-machine goroutine. The Go trace records that goroutine’s creation in NewRaft and its first snapshot request in runFSM. In the recorded single-node restart, the applied index had reached 12, but runFSM on goroutine 9 still held local index 0 and term 0. Goroutine 10 in takeSnapshot read those values from the same request and passed them to the snapshot store. After a Barrier reached runFSM, the local index advanced and both revisions produced valid snapshots.
findings.limits: The experiment covers the 2015 revision immediately before PR #58 and its fix. The local TCP cluster used Bolt storage and kept all snapshot files. All ten application records survived the restart. Stock source establishes the file behavior. Go runtime traces and local values come from separate builds with logging at the relevant source lines.

cases.title: Raft logs a snapshot error when only no-op entries have advanced

findings.observation: After restart and two normal leadership transfers, all three nodes reached committed and applied index 24 on three no-ops, while their snapshots stayed at 21 with 19 application records.
findings.interpretation: Raising the threshold to four suppressed retries, substituting a barrier produced snapshot 24 with unchanged data, and the fix stopped logging the no-new-snapshot result as an error on both automatic and manual paths.
findings.limits: The production log entries, FSM, version and trigger were unknown. The local run verifies the logging behavior, not what triggered it in production.

cases.title: etcdctl prints RaftTerm twice in endpoint status

findings.observation: Against the same healthy member, three successful queries with client 3.7.1 each printed RaftTerm twice. Version 3.7.2 printed it once, and the term was always 2.
findings.interpretation: JSON and table output agreed on the value. Removing one field-printing line in the client eliminated the duplicate even against the original 3.7.1 server.
findings.limits: Tested one Linux/amd64 member rather than the reported Darwin/arm64 environment. Only synchronous printing was traced.

cases.title: Why did Ratis reject a listener addition before the leader received it?

findings.observation: A healthy group of three voters (s0, s1, s2) had a fourth server ready to join as listener l0. The Java client supplied all four IDs to AdminApi.setConfiguration. With the array overload, 3.2.2, 3.3.0 and the immediate parent threw NullPointerException. The servers counted zero configuration RPCs and the three voters retained their original configuration. The list overload succeeded on all five builds. The fixed array overload also sent one RPC, committed the joint and final configurations, and let l0 apply the subsequent write. Each table entry was checked on two fresh groups.
findings.interpretation: In a separate four-server run, a debugger followed the production client reasserting its installed membership. On 3.2.2 the builder wrote a list backed by the voter array into the listener field, then overwrote it with a list backed by the listener array. The voter field was null when Preconditions.assertUnique threw. The debugger saw exception object 4491 both at the throw and in the caller’s catch. On 3.3.1 the builder wrote each array to its own field. AdminImpl constructed request object 4702, the gRPC serializer received that same object, and the successful reply matched call ID 17.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied the API code and exception stack. The fix supplied the two JUnit tests and peer IDs. Those tests capture configuration arguments at the client API boundary. The live listener additions also checked server RPC counters, group membership and replicated log entries through writes before and after the call. Ratis 3.2.2 omits an optional configuration field in GroupInfo replies. Its member IDs, division configuration and committed log entries establish the result. The cross-version control below changes one voter’s priority on a single-voter leader. The graphs follow synchronous work on the Java main thread and contain zero creation edges.

cases.title: The Ratis counter writes snapshots without updating its cached index

findings.observation: After three increments, GET returned 3, but 2.4.1 wrote snapshots at indexes 2 and 6 with an empty cache. A separate state machine restored at 2 still reported 2 after writing index 5.
findings.interpretation: Disk readback and object identity traced the stale value to the example’s metadata cache, and removing only the cache update from 2.5.0 reproduced it.
findings.limits: Snapshots were requested explicitly on a single member and a separate restored CounterStateMachine.

cases.title: Why did a Ratis follower’s reported index stop advancing while it kept applying writes?

findings.observation: The Apache Ozone reporter saw the gap between the applied index and a follower’s reported next index grow. In the local Ratis cluster the client wrote initial, then the leader restarted one follower’s log appender. The client wrote apricot, pear and plum. All three peers held identical copies of each client log entry and had committed and applied through its index. On stock 3.3.1 and on the PR parent overlay, the restarted follower’s next and match gauges stayed at 3 and 2 across the three writes. Its live indices reached 9 and 8 after plum. The landed overlay reported 9 and 8. The other follower on the same leader and the trials that kept both appenders running reported current indices on all three builds. In the separate registry experiment the old and replacement objects had next/match values of 200/100 and 300/250. The first table also shows the RPC age immediately after re-registration, when the two timestamps were about 120 and 30 seconds old. Per-supplier call counters identified which timestamp each gauge read.
findings.interpretation: On stock 3.3.1, Dropwizard’s getOrAdd returned the existing match gauge (segment 37). Reading it after plum executed getMatchIndex on the original FollowerInfo, JDI object 4466, and returned 2 (segments 81 and 82). The replacement appender used object 4959. The next-index and last-RPC getters also ran on the original object. PR #1587 changed addFollowerGauges to remove each metric by name and then register its replacement in the add path. In the landed capture the match name was removed in segment 64, getOrAdd returned a new gauge in 65, and its getter on the replacement object returned 8 in 110. The timestamp getter supplies the elapsed-milliseconds gauge. An aging timestamp can yield a rising reading even after its original appender stops. After orderly shutdown the 36 peer log segments from the 12 uninstrumented clusters contained exact copies of all 144 client-entry receipts. The independent decoder checked each frame’s CRC32C. A second pass using Ratis’s own SegmentedRaftLogInputStream matched the same bytes to their live receipts. For example, the release target’s 32-byte plum entry at index 7 starts at byte offset 249 in cluster/3.3.1/restart/trial-1/segments/s1/7146cff5-21e7-48a6-ba9b-62f859cb3a95/current/log_inprogress_0.
findings.limits: The release run used the stock 3.3.1 Maven libraries. The two source comparisons used those same libraries with only LogAppenderMetrics compiled from the exact parent or merged commit. At the snapshot date 3.4.0 was the issue’s target and the latest published Maven release was 3.3.1. The landed JUnit regression supplied the executable two-object fixture. On the release and parent its first assertion stopped the test at next index 200, expected 300. The separate registry probe read all three gauges on every build. The cluster workload used three local gRPC peers in one JVM with separate log directories and an explicit restart of one appender. The reporter used Apache Ozone. JDI sampled executing Java methods, receiver identities and returns. These captures contribute zero coroutine origins.

cases.title: Why did Ratis report a sync batch size of zero after writing three receipts?

findings.observation: A writer appended three receipts to a fresh local Raft log and waited for each append to finish before reading the registered syncBatchSize gauge. The parent of the fix returned 0 after each write, even as the completed sync counter advanced to 1, 2 and 3. The source fix and the 0.5.0 Maven release returned 1 each time. On every build the segment received three data syncs plus one earlier sync for the file header. The 48-, 49- and 50-byte record frames and the 8-byte header accounted for all 155 bytes. A second JVM reopened the log and recovered the three original receipts.
findings.interpretation: On the parent, the Java Debug Interface (JDI) captured the worker completing the data force (segment 8) and clearing pendingFlushNum (10). The registered gauge then read that field on the same worker (14) and returned 0. On the fix, flushWrites saved the difference between the last written and previously flushed log indices in flushBatchSize (7). The gauge read that saved count after the pending count had been cleared (15). In the separate six-record workload, segment write bytes and the following successful syncs identify each physical batch. With the default threshold the batches contained 3, 2 and 1 entries. Setting forceSyncNum to 1 gave six single-entry syncs for the same submissions. Both corrected builds reported the size of the last actual sync at each of the three sampling points.
findings.limits: The JIRA ticket supplied a description and patch. The local harness follows the existing upstream testAppendEntry pattern and adds metric reads. The measurements cover the file-backed SegmentedRaftLog, registered metrics, data syncs and readback after an orderly close. Replication and quorum commit are outside this workload. The grouped experiment uses state-machine write futures to control when a submitted group can complete. A second JVM recovered all six entries and their side data. JDI sampled the worker and gauge caller threads. The captures contain no verified coroutine origin.

cases.title: The client-write timer starts after request processing has begun

findings.observation: One warm-up and 16 measured counter increments over loopback gRPC produced a final value of 17 and 17 JMX write samples.
findings.interpretation: Debugger object identity linked the timer’s start and stop to the same context. Uninstrumented client timings and JMX showed that the old start point omitted request-processing time.
findings.limits: The replay used one healthy leader and the merged timing change. Durations came from uninstrumented runs. The debugger identified platform threads.

cases.title: Ray Data returns all 100 rows while its progress bar stops at 10%

findings.observation: The original Ray 2.3.0 driver created 100 one-row blocks and mapped them in batches of ten. It printed all integers from 100 through 199. The final terminal line still read 10/100. The same result appeared with and without the stack observer.
findings.interpretation: The bulk executor initialized the bar from the estimated output count of 100. It advanced the bar once per output bundle and emitted ten bundles. Samples at initialization, the last increment and the underlying display’s close operation identify the same bar. With the upstream change, the final display used the completed bundle count. The seven-row control showed 15/15, and one row per batch showed 100/100 on both builds.
findings.limits: Ray 2.6.0 rejects the original Python list blocks. The cross-version control carries the same indices in Arrow tables and compares every returned value. The isolated commit comparison loads the two Python modules changed by the fix on the 2.6.0 runtime. The measured stack belongs to the synchronous driver.

cases.title: Why did Ray return one patch when the application requested one image?

findings.observation: The original image pipeline generates 10–19 patches per image. On Ray 2.53.0, take(1) returned one 128-component vector. On Ray 2.54.0, it returned 18 vectors. In a separate observed run on 2.53.0, workers extracted and encoded 16 patches for UUID_0. Only 1 reached the grouping function. The table follows the same image through each worker stage within the observed run. The stock run uses the original unseeded random generator independently.
findings.interpretation: GroupedData.map_groups marked the grouping function as preserving row count. The stack in LimitPushdownRule._push_limit_down records that flag on the batch operator and the rule moves Limit ahead of grouping. One input patch then becomes one incomplete output image. The fix keeps Limit after grouping. On five known values, reversing only the flag recovered their full sum of 115 on the affected release and reproduced the partial group on the fixed release. Even the row-preserving centering function returned a different feature value when its worker saw one input.
findings.limits: The measurements use the reporter’s Ray 2.53.0 release and the first fixed release, 2.54.0, with Linux CPU workers. Full and limited reads of the posted script can select different images or regenerate features. A separate six-image workload verifies every returned pixel and feature component against a scalar calculation for 54 patches. The captured optimizer calls are synchronous.

cases.title: Ray Data’s ordered async map can return zero rows from ten inputs

findings.observation: With the reporter’s two blocks and ten integers, Ray 2.43.0 counted ten source rows but zero MapBatches output rows. Version 2.45.0 returned all inputs and powers in order.
findings.interpretation: Each block queued its end marker before its batch Task queued the rows, so the consumer saw only two markers. Waiting for the tasks before sending the markers, or disabling order preservation, restored all ten rows.
findings.limits: One local CPU cluster, one map actor and one row per batch. The reporter’s development commit was unspecified.

cases.title: Ray Serve swapped two features in a batched prediction

findings.observation: The second caller sent a=2 and b=20. The completed deployment handle returned a=20 and b=2 on the reported nightly. In a two-feature Iris classifier, mixed keyword order reversed 30 of 60 held-out feature pairs and changed 16 predicted species. Accuracy fell from 56 to 44 correct. Two independent runs agreed, with profiling on and off.
findings.interpretation: The create stack reaches _BatchQueue._process_sub_batches as it starts an asyncio task. The execution stack reaches _batch_args_kwargs inside the same live _process_batch_inner coroutine. The recorded inputs were [a, 1, b, 10] and [b, 20, a, 2]. The merge took the keys from the first request and grouped values by position, yielding a=[1, 20] and b=[10, 2]. The observer matched the task, coroutine and executing parent frame for all 95 batches per traced actor. With the proposed change, both requests reached the merge in declaration order.
findings.limits: The reporter used Windows. These runs used Linux x86-64, the same nightly commit and CPython 3.13.4. The comparison substituted the batching module from proposed PR #67405. The classifier exercises two named features from the UCI Iris dataset. Its correctly bound baseline classified 56 of 60 flowers correctly.

cases.title: Why did a Redis Cluster scan return one of nineteen keys?

findings.observation: Redis-py 4.1.2 returned one key from a six-node cluster with 1, 13 and 5 keys on its three primaries. The servers recorded one SCAN on the first primary. Version 4.2.0 contacted all three primaries and returned all nineteen. On the fourteen binary keys published in the follow-up, Redis returned 10 keys and cursor 5 on its first page. The affected client reported cursor zero. The fixed iterator read all fourteen.
findings.interpretation: The affected call stack enters _determine_nodes, which selects the default node. A second issue appears even with explicit primary targets. In parse_scan_result the input contains real per-node cursors, but the return statement substitutes zero and scan_iter stops. With COUNT 1 the three primaries supplied 3 keys in their first pages. The intermediate upstream commit preserved the cursor map, then the generic iterator submitted the entire map as a scalar and raised DataError. Continuing separately on each node produced all nineteen keys. The merged fix performs that loop inside the cluster iterator.
findings.limits: The nineteen-key test preserves the published distribution and the one key the author disclosed. The independent fourteen-key test uses every published key byte. The server chooses its own per-process hash seed, so opaque cursor values and page boundaries can change between runs. Released wheels and the adjacent upstream source revisions were checked against a real Redis 6.2.6 cluster. The client path is a synchronous generator.

cases.title: The default Redis protocol returns sorted-set scores as bytes when text was requested

findings.observation: The reporter’s four synchronous sorted-set calls reproduced on a local Redis server. With decoding enabled, the default protocol returned scores as bytes. Explicit RESP2 returned text. An asyncio rank query for the east board then returned a score of b'2.5' on the reported revision and '2.5' on the fix. The 8.2.0b1 prerelease also returned text.
findings.interpretation: The rank callback received the same list [1, 2.5] in both builds. The affected converter produced bytes even with decoding enabled. In the two-board run, the creation stack in read_directory and the sample inside _score_to_resp2_bytes identify the same east-board task. Redis CLI and a separate protocol reader confirmed the stored scores and ranks.
findings.limits: The original reproducer is synchronous. Its connection endpoint was redirected to a private local Redis 8.10.2 Unix socket. The coroutine origin belongs to a separate two-board asyncio query that reproduced the same conversion error. The tested published client package is a prerelease.

cases.title: LMOVE and BLMOVE return True instead of the moved value

findings.observation: Both commands returned True for abc, and moving three across lists also returned True even though Redis moved the requested element.
findings.interpretation: Both wire replies contained abc as a bulk string, and the client applied builtins.bool in the same response parser. Empty-string, empty-reply and SMOVE controls distinguished the conversion.
findings.limits: Local Redis Community 6.2.3 and CPython 3.10.12 replaced Enterprise 6.2.3 and Python 3.8.10. The stack was synchronous.

cases.title: Redis pipeline command packing blocks the asyncio loop

findings.observation: In two 200,000-command transactions, no heartbeat ran during 589 ms and 624 ms of packing, although all replies and all 17 final counter values were correct.
findings.interpretation: Packing ran in the caller’s Task and the pause followed the larger batch. The fix moved packing to a thread, while later changes yielded 199 times in each of two reply-processing loops.
findings.limits: Tests used local Redis 6.0.16, RESP2 and the Python parser. The reporter supplied the batch size and source but no complete workload.

cases.title: Why did asking Redis for a rank and its score raise TypeError?

findings.observation: The reporter’s synchronous program adds one with score 1 and two with score 2, then asks Redis for the zero-based rank and score of two. Redis replied with an integer 1 and a one-byte score, 2. The 4.6.0 client raised TypeError. The 5.0.0 client printed [1, b'2']. Running the same script again reproduced the reporter’s two leading zeros because both members already existed. On an empty set the two ZADD calls each printed 1. The rank outcome was the same in both states. Rank alone returned integer 1, and a scored query for an absent member returned None. Both a released Redis 7.2.0 server and the dated unstable server produced the same replies. The first table shows results shared by the synchronous client and its asyncio companion.
findings.interpretation:
The synchronous process sent the posted lower-case ZRANK command and read a 15-byte RESP2 array. An independent socket read the same bytes. redis-py 4.6.0 decoded them into [1, b'2'], dispatched the list to int_or_none and called int(response). That scalar conversion raised the reported exception. A normal redis.asyncio.Redis client reproduced the error on the same public command. Its parser, connection and callback all received the same list object. In the 4.6.0 graph, segment 2 records the library creating parse_response at redis/asyncio/client.py line 492. Segment 11 observes the same running coroutine frame at line 551 as it received the callback’s TypeError. The separate stream-reader callback recorded the server bytes while the coroutine was suspended.

On the 5.0 development branch, parent e13b239c still dispatched to int_or_none. Change 2a935eb9 removed the ZRANK callback registration, so parse_response returned the decoded list directly. Both source snapshots lacked the withscore keyword on the convenience method. By release 5.0.0 the keyword was available and ZRANK had a registered zset_score_pairs callback. On the reporter’s call this callback returned the original list object. The return path and the independent wire read agree on its two field types.
findings.limits: The original program used redis.Redis synchronously on macOS with Python 3.9 and an unspecified Redis unstable commit. Replay ran the posted source on Linux with CPython 3.9.15 and the latest unstable commit at the report timestamp. It also ran against Redis 7.2.0. The coroutine certificate belongs to the separate asyncio companion. The synchronous reporter contributes zero coroutine origins, and the shared issue contributes one. Across the eight observed processes, 4 parser coroutines failed on the reported command, 2 failed on the scored wrapper and 22 completed successfully. Release 5.0.0 was already on PyPI when the issue opened on August 25, 2023. The maintainer identified it in a later comment. The two branch commits document an earlier behavioral transition. Separate issue #4428 concerns score bytes versus text under a later client’s protocol and decode_responses settings. This experiment used RESP2 and the default byte decoding.

cases.title: A pipelined vector search returned raw replies instead of document objects

findings.observation: The same search returned neighbors a and b on every path. In redis-py 4.5.1 and the parent of the fix, direct search returned a Result with two documents. Both pipelines returned a raw array. All 99 ordinary pipelined reads in the reporter’s program returned their expected values.
findings.interpretation: The captured FT.SEARCH replies contained identical IDs and distances on all three paths within each run. The parent transaction stacks showed that neither pipeline had a response callback for FT.SEARCH. The fixing commit registered the callback on the search module’s pipeline and that instance entered the document parser. The generic pipeline still returned an array. On 8.1.0 the search module pipeline produced Result objects with unified responses enabled for either tested protocol.
findings.limits: The reporter gave no client or server version. We chose 4.5.1 from the month before the report and ran all clients against Redis Stack 7.2.0-v18. The original script used a synchronous client and an HNSW index. A separate FLAT index checked 120 searches over 150 Iris records against independently calculated distances.

cases.title: The Redis client dropped the cursor for the next stream page

findings.observation: The Redis server returned ["21-0", [], []] on the first page of a 412-entry pending list. redis-py 4.3.3 returned [] to the application, leaving it without the next position. All 108 eligible invoices remained with the original consumer. On 4.3.4 the application reached the terminal cursor after 56 calls. Independent ownership checks found all 108 invoices with the replacement consumer.
findings.interpretation: The recorded RESP2 bytes contain the cursor before the result reaches the callback. In the asyncio client, StreamCommands.xautoclaim created the Redis.execute_command coroutine whose execution stack reaches Redis.parse_response and parse_xautoclaim. The old callback returned element 1 alone. The fixed callback formats the entries in that element and returns all three elements. Replacing only this callback on 4.3.3 recovered the 108 invoices and the three IDs removed from the stream.
findings.limits: The reporter described the iterative operation. This workload supplies the stream entries, idle times and consumer groups, using the reported Redis and redis-py versions on Linux. The measurements cover normal full-entry calls. A separate JUSTID control returned only the message IDs on both releases.

cases.title: Why did River return 0.44723478 for a predictive standard deviation of 0.20001895?

findings.observation: River 0.25.0 and the immediate parent returned a predictive standard deviation of 0.44723478. Computing the posterior independently from the 5,000 actual training rows gave 0.20001895. The landed source and 0.26.0 returned that value. The point prediction was 1.69998705 across all four builds.
findings.interpretation: Segment 1 records the variance computed by the regressor and the value it passed to the Gaussian constructor. On the parent, it passed the square root of that variance. Segments 2 and 3 identify the variance state attached to the returned Gaussian. Segment 4 records the caller reading sigma on that same object and taking a second square root. On the landed source the constructor received the variance itself. A zero-valued feature produced the expected sigmas 1, 0.5, 0.2 and 0.1 at noise precisions 1, 4, 25 and 100 on both corrected builds. Only the first precision concealed the defect on the affected builds.
findings.limits: The report used Windows and CPython 3.13.14. These measurements used Linux and CPython 3.12.8. The posted program completed on both source commits and 0.26.0. On 0.25.0 it trained the same model but stopped at the private field _idx. The release result comes from its public prediction on that trained instance and the original query. The landed regression uses an untrained empty query, which 0.25.0 rejected before reaching the assertion. Each profiled call ran synchronously and the graph has zero coroutine origins.

cases.title: Why did River return three clusters when none met the minimum weight?

findings.observation: The reporter fed DBSTREAM one observation at each of (0, 0), (50, 50) and (100, 100), then printed the centers and weights in its clusters property. River kept three micro-clusters, each of weight 1. With minimum_weight set to 5, zero qualified for the result. River 0.23.0 printed all three. The exact parent reproduced those three lines. The merged source, 0.24.1 and 0.24.2 printed no lines and returned an empty mapping. With isolated weights [5, 4, 6], the fix returned the first and third centers. With weights [5, 5], every build returned both.
findings.interpretation:
In the 0.23.0 trace the reported property called _recluster, then _generate_labels. The weighted adjacency map was empty. The labeler assigned 0, 1 and 2 to the three weight-one micro-clusters (segments 10, 12, 14). The label map returned in segment 15 was the same object passed to assembly. The public property returned its three-entry result. In 0.24.2 the weight check skipped all three (segments 11, 14, 17). The three labels remained None and assembly returned an empty dictionary. Both traces reached these decisions before periodic cleanup. The landed change checks each micro-cluster’s weight before assigning a label and handles the empty set of assigned labels.

A separate stream formed two neighboring micro-clusters of weight 14. Both contributed to a single weight-28 center at x ≈ 0.75 through an edge of density 4/7. After one observation at x = 50, predict_one selected the new singleton on 0.23.0 and the parent. The fixed builds still selected the weight-28 center. Four more observations brought the distant point to weight 5, and each of the four builds in this control selected it.
findings.limits: The exact source builds both reported version 0.23.0. Their commits and loaded DBSTREAM file hashes identify immediate parent 7b1da16c8b and landed fix f72a0da16a. The 0.24.0 release tag contains the corrected module. Its yanked Linux CPython 3.12 wheel omitted it, so the reporter’s import failed. The 0.24.1 wheel ran the corrected code. PyPI yanked that release for missing source-distribution files. Version 0.24.2 was the first non-yanked successor tested. Cluster counts come from the public mapping. With no output centers, predict_one can still return its default label 0. The physical samples cover synchronous CPython calls and contribute zero coroutine origins.

cases.title: The execute endpoint ignores associative response formatting

findings.observation: On 9.1.3, UPDATE RETURNING produced positional arrays despite the associative flag, including when a follower forwarded the write.
findings.interpretation: The request flag was true but the encoder flag was false in the same HTTP goroutine; copying the flag during execute response initialization restored the expected output.
findings.limits: The report used macOS and the local comparison used three Linux nodes. Uninstrumented response bytes confirmed the formatting difference.

cases.title: Successive automatic backups reuse the first timestamp in their object name

findings.observation: With timestamped backups enabled, a three-voter rqlite 8.26.6 cluster uploaded two database snapshots exactly 300 seconds apart under the same object name. The object store assigned distinct versions. Downloading and opening them with SQLite showed one committed row in the first snapshot and two in the second. Version 8.26.7 wrote two distinct timestamped names over the same interval.
findings.interpretation: The Go runtime traced the periodic worker to Uploader.Start. Its stack enters S3Client.Upload and TimestampedPath. On the fix parent, the worker supplied exactly the same timestamp on three successive calls even as the database index and object write time advanced. The old client bound the UTC method to the first time value. The fix reads the clock on each invocation.
findings.limits: The test used a local three-voter cluster and a versioned S3-compatible VersityGW service. Both release builds ran at the reported five-minute interval. The recording builds used a four-second interval so three timestamp arguments could be compared on the same goroutine.

cases.title: A read-only rqlite query printed the previous write count

findings.observation: The maintainer’s common table expression should return one row containing x = 1. The v8.43.3 shell printed 3, 0 or 2 affected rows, depending on the preceding write. Across three voters we found all three reads in the replicated log. The v8.43.4 shell returned the expected row each time and the reads added no entries. Switching only the client changed the outcome on either server release.
findings.interpretation: Four Go stack samples follow the shell from its WITH dispatch into executeWithClient, through the actual endpoint and into the affected-row display. The older CLI sent the read to /db/execute. Its response contained the same change count that SQLite retained after the preceding write. The repaired requestWithClient selected the table display using the columns and values returned by /db/request. A recursive read of eight Chinook employees showed the same routing difference. A recursive INSERT committed all eight employees on both releases.
findings.limits: The 2017 report omitted the version. The stock v3.9.2 CLI has the same source tree as the shell on the reporting date. On its matching daemon it printed one affected row for both a one-row result and an empty result. The later maintainer report and fix supply the SQL for the three-node comparison. The main comparison uses adjacent 2025 releases, with official client binaries, a local three-voter cluster and a separate line-preserving stack observation build. The stack samples track synchronous work on the CLI main goroutine.

cases.title: An aggregate returned its numeric value with an empty column type

findings.observation: The two inserts from the report summed to 133.46 on all four rqlite versions. Version 7.5.0 and the fix parent sent an empty type name. The fixed revision and 7.21.3 sent real. Independent reads on each of three voting nodes also returned 412 invoices totaling 2,328.60. All 18 replica backups contained the same invoice rows.
findings.interpretation: The Go runtime trace follows the connection goroutine created by net/http through the rqlite HTTP handler into the SQLite driver. The driver returned an empty declared type for SUM. In that same goroutine rqlite scanned a float64 value of 133.46. The parent returned the empty metadata. The fixed query code filled it from the scanned value. A separate native SQLite check on each backup returned a null declared type and real storage for the aggregate.
findings.limits: The original curl example used port zero. The local command used the port actually assigned to the server. The three-voter runs added a public Chinook invoice catalog and explicit replica-local reads. An expression with no rows or a null aggregate could still return an empty type after the fix.

cases.title: An rqlite dump of one table includes objects from unselected tables

findings.observation: Exporting only t1 on v10.3.2 reproduced the reported SQL byte for byte. Restoring it into empty SQLite failed on two indexes and a trigger belonging to unselected tables.
findings.interpretation: DB.Dump received the correct selection, but the three extra objects matched the failing SQL lines. The fix filtered by tbl_name and retained t1’s own index and trigger.
findings.limits: Adjacent releases on a single Raft leader. The fixed dump still included two views that could be created but could not be read without t2.

cases.title: A Raft leader reports its own read as stale

findings.observation: The original JavaScript calls created a table on a single elected leader. A local read allowing up to 100 hours of staleness returned HTTP 200 with a stale-read error. After two voters joined and the cluster committed a fourth row, both followers returned all four rows under the same bound. The old leader still rejected the read.
findings.interpretation: The Go runtime recorded Store.Query taking its stale-read return path on the leader. The saved last-contact time was January 1 of year 1. The elapsed duration saturated at the largest signed 64-bit value and exceeded the 100-hour limit. The trace links this exact request to the HTTP connection goroutine started by net/http.(*Server).Serve. The fix applies the contact check only on followers.
findings.limits: The replay used the reporter’s source commit and Go 1.18.2 on Linux amd64. The original ran on Windows. Seven runs compared ordinary and traced servers, including the parent, fix and two releases. The database backup contained the same four rows that the cluster returned. Both followers still enforced a one-nanosecond limit after the fix.

cases.title: DNS-SRV discovery gives a configured rqlite non-voter a Raft vote

findings.observation: Three voters and one configured non-voter joined a local cluster. With DNS-SRV discovery, all four status responses on 8.14.0 listed the fourth member as Voter. Version 8.14.1 listed it as Nonvoter. All four nodes read back the same SQL row in both versions.
findings.interpretation: The DNS-SRV join path in 8.14.0 supplied a constant Voter flag. The leader received true and recorded AddVoter. The fixed code forwarded the configuration flag and recorded AddNonvoter. Runtime events matched the leader’s join handler to the exact goroutine created by the cluster service for the connection.
findings.limits: The local cluster used four real processes and DNS SRV/A queries on loopback. It did not recreate the reporter’s Kubernetes, TLS or authentication setup. The matched goroutine is the leader-side connection handler; the replica’s sending stack was observed in a separate process.

cases.title: Raft commit indexes arrived as strings in the rqlite status API

findings.observation: Three healthy nodes committed writes and reported indexes 9 and 12. The affected status endpoint returned both as JSON strings. Taking their maximum with jq returned "9". With the upstream fix it returned the number 12. Across 24 responses per build, the parent sent all 216 selected numeric field values as strings. The fixed build sent all 216 as numbers.
findings.interpretation: The Go stack linked the status handler to Store.Stats. The returned Raft map already held the strings seen in the HTTP response. The fix converted numeric entries before JSON encoding. We independently decoded each node’s durable log and replayed the SQL. The on-disk snapshot at index 32 contained the same 24 rows on all three nodes.
findings.limits: The report describes the field type and provides no reproduction script. The replay used the upstream command examples and the exact parent and fix revisions. The three-node workload, snapshot threshold of 32 and jq check are local controls. The recorded call stacks identify the status path. A goroutine creation site was not established.

cases.title: A successful rqlite insert returned year 1 for the current timestamp

findings.observation: The posted INSERT combined CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and strftime in two DATETIME columns. The reported release acknowledged one inserted row, but the first column stored the text CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. Its typed API value was 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z and its Unix epoch was NULL. All three healthy voters in the parent cluster returned those values. At the fixed revision in UTC, all three returned a timestamp matching the HTTP response clock.
findings.interpretation: The parent parser classified CURRENT_TIMESTAMP as an identifier. Visiting strftime marked the statement for serialization, which put double quotes around the identifier. SQLite accepted that unbound quoted name as text. The fix recognized a timestamp literal and emitted datetime with a numeric Julian day. The HTTP peer, Go creation event, visitor stack and returned Raft index identify one request goroutine. All three Bolt stores contain the same replicated command bytes for that index. Local backups independently confirm the resulting value.
findings.limits: The six posted curl requests use loopback port remapping and one fresh connection each. The three-voter runs, parameterized insert, Unix-epoch reads and timezone comparison are local controls. Each process run has its own wall-clock timestamp. UTC results are checked against that request’s time window. With the fixed server explicitly set to Asia/Shanghai, the mixed insert returned an epoch 28,800 seconds ahead of its HTTP Date in this run. The origin evidence identifies the leader’s HTTP connection goroutine.

cases.title: RxPY’s AsyncIOScheduler reports dates in 1970

findings.observation: The reporter’s print_now returned a 1970 date, and a supplemental stream timestamped all three readings incorrectly and dropped them all at a cutoff set to yesterday.
findings.interpretation: The task graph located the clock read and conversion, and comparisons across two builds and two clock bases confirmed the effect on timestamps and absolute-time filtering.
findings.limits: The report demonstrated only now. The stream was an additional Linux test on Python 3.12.3, versus the reporter’s 3.12.10.

cases.title: RxPY zip completes before it pairs two four-item sources

findings.observation: Rx 3.2.0 and the fix parent printed no rows for the upstream example, while the fix produced 2, 4, 12 and 16 in order.
findings.interpretation: The first source directly invoked the downstream completion callback with four values still queued and the second queue empty. The fix delayed completion until the finished source’s queue was exhausted.
