findings.limits: Ran the reported Rx release on Python 3.9.25 instead of 3.9.6. The example used a synchronous scheduler.

cases.title: SciPy returned a negative median for two positive pixel values

findings.observation: The report asked for the median of one labelled region. With int8 pixels 65 and 70, SciPy 1.5.1 and 1.5.2 returned −60.5. With two true pixels they returned 0.5. SciPy 1.5.3 returned 67.5 and 1.0. Omitting labels or widening the pixels gave the expected values on every release.
findings.interpretation: The synchronous call reached _select from ndimage.median. The live operand stack showed an int8 sum of −121 before division on the affected release. The fixed release converted both middle pixels to float64 before adding them, giving 135.0. Boolean addition likewise produced True in the old build and 2.0 in the fixed build.
findings.limits: The original report supplies two small arrays. On the bundled Ascent photograph, three of 64 regional medians were low by exactly 128. The exhaustive table counts ordered two-pixel regions once per release. The two backport module runs share the SciPy 1.5.3 binaries. The historical runs use CPython 3.8.20 and the reported NumPy 1.19.1.

cases.title: BayesianRidge reports the wrong predictive uncertainty for uncentered inputs

findings.observation: For training inputs from 80 to 100, version 1.8.0 reported standard deviations of 7.7532, 43.6024 and 48.3014 at x=0, 90 and 100. The corrected values were 43.6024, 7.7532 and 9.1017.
findings.interpretation: Replacing only _bayes.py in 1.8.0 with the centering fix brought the entire curve into agreement with the posterior formula. Version 1.9.0 agreed, and both upstream regression checks passed.
findings.limits: Dense floating-point inputs on a single CPU thread. ARDRegression was covered only by the shared upstream regression test.

cases.title: scikit-learn awarded a perfect F1 score to two swapped predictions

findings.observation: The two reported labels were 0 and 1. Predicting 1 and 0 missed both. With zero_division=1, scikit-learn 1.3.0 and the fix parent returned F1 = 1.0. Version 1.2.2 and the fixed commit returned 0.0. All builds agreed on the other three reported examples, including the genuinely undefined all-negative case.
findings.interpretation: The live Python stack reached precision_recall_fscore_support through f1_score and fbeta_score. It recorded zero true positives, one predicted positive and one actual positive. The parent's intermediate denominator, precision plus recall, was zero, so it selected the configured fallback of one. The fixed implementation used the count denominator of two and returned zero.
findings.limits: The report supplied four label arrays. The Iris predictions are a separate control using the same train/test split on six builds or runs. The nearest-centroid model scored 0.906629 macro-F1 on all 75 held-out flowers. The error-only comparison selects the 7 misclassified flowers from that holdout. The physical stack capture covers synchronous scoring of the first reported input.

cases.title: Why did a three-component MDS fit return two coordinates?

findings.observation: The reporter requested three coordinates for each of 20 observations. With classical initialization, scikit-learn 1.8.0 returned a 20 × 2 array. Version 1.9.0 returned 20 × 3. Each build also ran with two shared input seeds. Every traced result matched the plain process on every coordinate.
findings.interpretation: The outer estimator requested three components on both releases. Segment 2 shows that the 1.8.0 ClassicalMDS initializer received its default of two. Its 20 × 2 result in segment 3 was the array passed to smacof. The low-level solver entered with a request for three components, then took the width of the initializer array, two, in segment 6. MDS returned the resulting two-column array. In 1.9.0 the initializer received three and the solver retained three. On a tetrahedron, the summed squared error in the six pairwise distances fell from 0.075765 to below 1e-16.
findings.limits: The releases ran on Linux x86-64 CPU with NumPy 2.2.6 and SciPy 1.15.0. The reporter used macOS arm64. The geometry controls use a tetrahedron and 15 observations from the Iris dataset. The table rounds distance error to six decimals. The four physical captures contain synchronous Python calls and zero matched coroutine origins.

cases.title: Why did a converted max normalizer turn negative values positive on CPU?

findings.observation: On the four rows from the landed regression test, the skl2onnx 1.20.0 wheel and the immediate fix parent each produced six wrong float32 values in ONNX Runtime (ORT) CPU. For [-1, -2, -4], ORT returned [1, 2, 4]. Scikit-learn and independent division by the row’s largest absolute value gave [-0.25, -0.5, -1]. The zero row and the positive-dominant row matched on every build. L1 matched scikit-learn exactly, and the largest L2 difference was 5.96 × 10⁻⁸. The source fix reproduced all 12 expected max-normalized values.
findings.interpretation: The converter stack shows apply_normalizer selecting ai.onnx.ml.Normalizer(MAX) and add_node inserting it into the serialized model. ORT’s CPU profile records that operator executing. Its output fits division by the signed maximum. In the separate seven-row pipeline, ORT CPU and ONNX ReferenceEvaluator loaded the same bytes for each build. For the parent model, the converter and both executors recorded SHA-256 a6c929a45f8e85fc1844ab7c3acb8e1de513bb2dc743af51027ac3b83203d4fa. On both older models, ReferenceEvaluator’s _run called norm_max. Its recorded row divisors were [4, 4, 4, 4, 0, 8, 8], and all seven outputs matched scikit-learn. For [-4, -2, -1], ORT returned [4, 2, 1] and ReferenceEvaluator returned [-1, -0.5, -0.25]. The fixed converter emitted Abs, ReduceMax, Div, Less and Where. Both engines matched all seven rows, and ReferenceEvaluator bypassed norm_max.
findings.limits: The reporter described a sign discrepancy and later identified a one-step scikit-learn Pipeline. Neither post provided the numeric input or exact versions. The first table uses the four-row fixture from PR #1271. The second uses a separate seven-row pipeline inspired by the comment. These runs used float32, opset 18, scikit-learn 1.8.0, ORT CPU 1.24.4 and ONNX ReferenceEvaluator 1.20.1. The parent and fix were measured from source. The sealed release index listed 1.20.0 as the latest wheel. Converter stacks establish which nodes were emitted. The ORT trace covers Python dispatch, CPU kernel events and returned tensors. Its internal divisor is inferred from the numeric outputs. The reference executor exposed its divisor directly. All captured stacks were synchronous.

cases.title: OneHotEncoder discarded the low-frequency feature for an unseen category

findings.observation: On scikit-learn 1.7.2 the reporter’s unseen building type, casino, encoded as [0, 0] under warn. The same encoder settings with infrequent_if_exist returned [0, 1]. Both modes returned [0, 1] on 1.8.0.
findings.interpretation: At the call to _map_infrequent_categories, the caller had already selected the effective policy infrequent_if_exist. With the instance policy still set to warn, the old function assigned code 2 and left the row masked out. The fix kept that code and marked it valid. With a fitted linear model on separate CSV data, that single feature changed the prediction for an unseen building use from 10 to 38.
findings.limits: The local Linux run matched the report’s CPython 3.13.3 and numerical package versions. The reporter used Windows. The parent and fix comparisons used their exact encoder module on the same 1.8.0 wheel. The CSV rates are controlled inputs. This synchronous path has no coroutine origin.

cases.title: Warm-starting Newton–Cholesky changes multiclass predictions

findings.observation: On Iris with 1.7.1, two one-step fits matched the feature coefficients of one two-step fit, yet 49 of 150 predicted classes differed and the first five rows had a maximum probability difference of 0.071784.
findings.interpretation: The fix subtracted the last intercept from all three to preserve relative log odds; both the patch alone and 1.7.2 matched the two-step reference, improving regression checks from 5/8 to 8/8.
findings.limits: The CPU test used three classes and L2 regularization. All builds warned about nonconvergence because the step count was deliberately limited.

cases.title: MessagePack binary events and acknowledgments get the wrong packet type

findings.observation: The JavaScript client received all three bytes of bar, but its parser reported an invalid packet type and delivered neither the event nor the acknowledgment to the application.
findings.interpretation: The sending task assigned the wrong type, and tracing matched the queued buffer to the received bytes; skipping binary-type conversion for MessagePack restored both callbacks.
findings.limits: The report gave steps but no version or full app. A warm-up ensured the tested acknowledgment used ID 1, isolating a separate ID 0 behavior.

cases.title: An async Socket.IO server dropped messages addressed to a list of rooms

findings.observation: The posted server emits twice to one client. With python-socketio 5.7.2, the client received the message addressed by its session ID. Wrapping that same ID in a list raised TypeError. Release 5.8.0 delivered both messages. In a separate four-client test, the two target rooms had three distinct members. On 5.7.2 none received the joint notification. On 5.8.0 each of the three received it once, including the member in both rooms.
findings.interpretation: The Engine.IO task factory trace identifies the coroutine allocated for AsyncServer._handle_event_internal. That same coroutine and frame were executing when AsyncManager.emit tried to look up the list as a room dictionary key. The exception occurred before get_participants yielded any session. The closing commit removed the single room-key check. On the fixed revision, the three distinct session IDs yielded by get_participants match the three receiving clients. The synchronous control already delivered to all three on 5.7.2.
findings.limits: The original client ran on an ephemeral loopback port with a listener to count receipts and a bounded shutdown. Its original transport negotiation upgraded to WebSocket. The four-client workloads use local room memberships chosen for this experiment. Async clients used WebSocket, and the separate synchronous controls used HTTP polling. The matched origin belongs to the incoming event handler.

cases.title: AsyncResult.freeze stores an unawaited fetchall coroutine

findings.observation: In three runs on 2.1.5, reading the frozen Core result raised TypeError, while freezing an ORM result raised AttributeError. The fix replayed both Core rows and froze the ORM result.
findings.interpretation: FrozenResult saved the async fetchall return object directly, and its creation, cache read and unawaited warning matched by identity. The ORM path requested a missing _raw_row_iterator.
findings.limits: Tested on real SQLite. The fetchall coroutine never executed. Task creation and execution were verified for the cache writer and reader.

cases.title: Rows.Err can block after a RawBytes scan and query cancellation

findings.observation: Rows.Err stalled in 7 of 20 runs of the posted program and 9 of 20 runs of the reporter’s repository example, while all 18 control runs returned.
findings.interpretation: Four traces showed a writer queued before Err requested its read lock, and GDB confirmed on three instances that the earlier RawBytes scan still held a read lock on the same Rows object.
findings.limits: Local Linux/amd64 replaced the reporter’s arm64 host and private database endpoint. Lock identities and scheduling traces came from separate runs.

cases.title: Chained selectinload waits until attribute access

findings.observation: Both releases returned foo with two SELECTs, but 2.0.48 issued the second on access to bar.top.foo, while 2.0.49 completed it inside q.one().
findings.interpretation: The older loader rejected the Top-to-Bar path and fell back to lazy loading; the fix also checked inheritance in the reverse direction and registered the Bar.foo loader.
findings.limits: The report specified only 2.0.x. The comparison used adjacent releases and synchronous Python queries.

cases.title: Async SQLAlchemy result views lose column and uniqueness settings

findings.observation: On 2.1.5, async deduplication yielded [1,1,2], selecting column b returned values from a or exposed both columns, and an ORM query still demanded unique(), while synchronous results were correct.
findings.interpretation: scalars() and mappings() inherited the underlying result’s columns and uniqueness policy instead of the wrapper’s state. Reversing the deduplication order worked, and both upstream test suites improved from one of six passing to all six. The separate coroutine replay matches that same all() allocation and return frame. The affected instance returns the a column where the caller selected b.
findings.limits: The workload uses the original SQLite example. The allocation probe wraps the call to all() and returns the existing coroutine object. Stock and traced results agree on every build.

cases.title: Casting a timestamp to a date made the optimizer drop matching rows

findings.observation: On the reporter’s DuckDB example, two distinct timestamps fell on October 30. The original query returned October 30 twice and October 31 once. The reported commit and the parent of the fix returned October 30 only once after optimization. The fix and release v30.28.0 preserved all three rows.
findings.interpretation: The recorded stack leads from eliminate_joins through _should_eliminate_join to _is_joined_on_all_unique_outputs. A Cast node reported the name of the timestamp column. The affected check accepted that name as proof of uniqueness and authorized removing the join. The fixed check requires a Column node. With the same flight data, the fixed query preserved all 39 matches on February 28. Joining directly on an already unique date remained safe in every build.
findings.limits: The additional calendar workload uses 2,000 public flight records, 1,920 distinct minute-level timestamps and one added day with no flights. Each result was checked against an independent per-day timestamp count. All four builds ran on CPython 3.12.4 and DuckDB 2.0.0. The optimizer runs synchronously. The function stacks were imported from CPython return events, with local values and SQL results recorded separately.

cases.title: SQLGlot loses a join source when USING follows an ON clause

findings.observation: The reporter’s query raised “Cannot automatically join: c_id” three times each on 25.21.1 and the fix parent. The original SQL returned seven PostgreSQL rows, and both fixed builds emitted the exact expected SQL.
findings.interpretation: After skipping the first ON clause, _expand_using knew only a.b_id and could not resolve b.c_id. Registering b first yielded the correct join condition and the same rows as PostgreSQL.
findings.limits: The report did not pin a version. Adjacent releases and commits were checked against locally constructed data in a synchronous optimizer.

cases.title: SQLGlot mishandles a correlated scalar subquery during optimization

findings.observation: Full optimization of the reported SQL raised AttributeError on two 29.x releases and the pre-fix commit, while the posted single-rule script exited normally but discarded invalid SQL that PostgreSQL rejected with 42601.
findings.interpretation: The full optimizer tried to replace a missing predicate, while the single rule took a faulty grouping path. The fix preserved this subquery in both cases and still rewrote eligible projections as LEFT JOINs.
findings.limits: Execution was synchronous. Probes inspected the expression tree and grouping keys, and PostgreSQL results were read independently.

cases.title: Moving a filter inside a right join returned excluded flights

findings.observation: The reported predicate-pushdown rule moved y.flag = 1 from WHERE into the join condition. Both DuckDB and SQLite then returned one extra row, with flag 0 and a null left key. On 2,000 public flight records, the same rewrite returned every flight for a query that requested the 424 flights delayed by at least 15 minutes.
findings.interpretation: In the affected stack, nodes_for_predicate selected the RIGHT JOIN as the target. Its caller put the filter into ON and replaced the outer WHERE condition with TRUE. A right join still emits a right-hand row when the match condition fails, so the flight survived with a null airport column. The fixed rule kept the outer filter, restoring every expected result including duplicate counts.
findings.limits: This report used the standalone pushdown_predicates rule. The complete optimizer filtered a derived table and preserved the correct result on every tested build. The two database engines agreed across 720 query executions, including inner-join, duplicate-key and null-key controls. These were synchronous SQL transformations.

cases.title: SQLite translation changes how GREATEST and LEAST handle NULL

findings.observation: For (NULL, 1), old SQLGlot output returned (NULL, NULL) in SQLite, while the original SQL returned (1, 1) in PostgreSQL and DuckDB. The merge and 30.19.0 restored agreement.
findings.interpretation: Both generator functions received ignore_nulls=True but emitted bare MAX and MIN. The fix used the flag to build COALESCE expressions over rotated arguments.
findings.limits: Checked constants, columns and deterministic integer expressions. MySQL was a generator-only control. The measured Python stack was synchronous.

cases.title: Where did the two-hour shift go in generated SQLite SQL?

findings.observation: SQLGlot 30.32.0 translated the reporter’s MySQL timestamp plus two hours into SQLite DATE. SQLite returned 2024-01-01. The landed source and 30.33.0 returned noon on that date. The four-row control also crossed midnight and leap day. The affected builds returned the correct dates but lost the times on all three non-null rows.
findings.interpretation: The physical capture follows the affected call on one thread. Segment 1 records DATE as the generator’s actual function argument for HOUR. Segment 2 contains the emitted fragment. Segment 3 records the statement received by SQLite. The fixed capture shows DATETIME at each step. The unchanged landed test’s four literal subtests fail before the change and pass afterwards.
findings.limits: The tracker supplies a SQL statement and omits the installed version. The two release wheels and immediate source pair were exercised with real SQLite and a Python datetime oracle. The trace captures synchronous Python frames and SQLite’s statement callback. The original MySQL server was not required to validate the stated arithmetic.

cases.title: SQLite counts two rows in a UNION ALL subquery that returns three

findings.observation: The reporter inserted a and b into the left table and c into the right. SELECT DISTINCT on the left followed by UNION ALL returned a, b and c on all six builds. An outer COUNT(1) returned 2 on SQLite 3.42.0, 3.43.0 and the fix parent. The fixing commit restored the count to 3. Disabling the unused-column optimization on the parent also restored it to 3.
findings.interpretation: In the parent trace, the planner treated the projected values as unused because the outer query counted a constant. It replaced both branches’ column reads with NULL, even though the left branch needed its values for DISTINCT. The duplicate check accepted the first NULL and discarded the second. Only one left row and the right row reached the counter. The fix checked each branch for DISTINCT and preserved the column reads. The debugger then saw two distinct keys, a and b, and three calls to the counter.
findings.limits: The native trace follows one prepared COUNT(1) statement through compilation and execution on a single thread. It establishes no application coroutine origin. Both adjacent development builds identify themselves as SQLite 3.44.0, so the table labels them by Fossil check-in. The independent PostgreSQL 14.13 replay added the derived-table alias that version requires.

cases.title: A sliding group_concat window cut digits off a surviving value

findings.observation: The original query returned 24 rows. SQLite 3.36.0 and the parent of the fix returned 17 incorrect strings. The eighth began with 50. A fresh aggregation of the same window began with 4450. Both the fixing commit and 3.37.0 returned all 24 expected rows.
findings.interpretation: GDB followed one statement from groupConcatInverse to the next result. The parent removed ten bytes, using the length of George for the separator after the outgoing value. The stored separator at that position was John. The fix removed eight bytes and preserved the next value. PostgreSQL string_agg and an independent Python calculation confirmed the expected output.
findings.limits: The Linux CLI included SQLite’s generate_series implementation. The original query ordered by name alone. Adding a numeric tie-breaker reproduced the same discrepancy. The captured native stacks cover synchronous C execution.

cases.title: An upsert can leave lastrowid pointing to another project

findings.observation: Each run used one SQLite connection for 24 concurrent upserts. Twelve new projects got their own row IDs. Of the twelve updates, one read zero and eleven read a positive ID belonging to another project. Reopening the database confirmed the row actually updated in every case.
findings.interpretation: The capture joins each asyncio task created by gather in measure to its lastrowid getter and the value it returned. For example, project 12 returned 0 and committed to row 12. The original database controls explain how that can happen. A conflict update preserves the connection’s last successful insert ID, which CPython copies into the cursor at execution time.
findings.limits: Task identities come from the local concurrent workload that used the published SQL. The upstream comment used synchronous sqlite3. Two traced runs each matched all 24 tasks. Diagnosing the stale ID also required the insert history and the committed rows.

cases.title: An SSE heartbeat after an event ID produces an empty message

findings.observation: The synchronous example yielded three events with IDs, including an extra empty message after the heartbeat, and just two when the IDs were removed.
findings.interpretation: The decoder ignored the comment but retained the prior ID, so the next blank line emitted an event from an empty buffer; both proposed changes preserved a genuine empty data field.
findings.limits: The report gave no version. The original iterator was synchronous, and task creation was observed only in an additional Uvicorn request.

cases.title: A Unicode line separator truncated a server-sent event

findings.observation: A successful HTTP response carried one SSE event with U+2028 inside its JSON string. Version 0.4.1 delivered a string ending at Hello. Chromium EventSource, the fixing commit and release 0.4.2 delivered the complete JSON document.
findings.interpretation: The client gave SSEDecoder.decode two lines for a single data field. The suffix beginning with World was ignored and the next blank line dispatched the truncated event. The repaired line splitter kept U+2028 within that field. The task created in main was the one that ran decode and received the returned event object.
findings.limits: The original example uses a synchronous in-memory stream. The task-origin evidence comes from a local async HTTP client reading the exact same response bytes over loopback. Chromium closed after receiving the first event. The Python client read to the end of the stream.

cases.title: Scalar quantization wraps values outside the calibration range

findings.observation: Two out-of-range coordinates yielded int8 [-42, 42, -112] instead of [-128, 42, 127], and uint8 also mapped both extremes to interior bins.
findings.interpretation: The merged fix and 5.7.0 rounded and clipped before conversion, correcting all 1,226 uint8 discrepancies among 3,072 held-out coordinates.
findings.limits: The original version was unspecified. The separate retrieval check used eight local documents and a four-sentence calibration set.

cases.title: Left padding changed weighted-mean sentence embeddings

findings.observation: The reporter pooled the same two token vectors twice. On the reported commit, the fix parent and release 6.1.0, the unpadded call printed 2.3333 and the left-padded call printed 2.2000. The fixing commit and release 6.2.0 printed 2.3333 both times. In SentenceTransformer.encode, three of four STS Benchmark sentences changed when batched with a longer sentence. The largest absolute change in any embedding coordinate fell from 1.6583939 on the parent to 1.1444092e-05 on the fix. Right-padded batches matched singleton outputs exactly on all five builds.
findings.interpretation: A physical stack from encode reached Pooling._forward_padded. Its recorded mask and effective weights explain the two-token result. With left padding, the parent gave the real tokens weights 2 and 3, producing (2 × 1 + 3 × 3) / 5. The fix subtracted the leading padding length and gave them weights 1 and 2, producing (1 × 1 + 2 × 3) / 3. An independent sum over the actual token vectors used each token’s position within its sequence. Across all four fixed-batch embeddings, the largest coordinate difference from this calculation was 1.0146234e-06.
findings.limits: The corpus check used four published test sentences, the SmolLM2-135M-Instruct checkpoint with its chat formatting, and an explicitly configured weighted-mean head. Token counts include the chat template. The measurements cover embedding consistency on CPU in float32. The local environment used Linux, Python 3.12.4, PyTorch 2.11.0 and Transformers 5.14.1. The pooling calls ran synchronously.

cases.title: A cached Kafka Streams scan returns a deleted key

findings.observation: After cache eviction, the processor that deleted B scanned both A and B from a shared RocksDB store, even though a subsequent lookup of B returned null.
findings.interpretation: In 3.9.1 the iterator returns A before consuming the matching store and cache entries for B. Swapping just that class between versions reversed the result.
findings.limits: Local single-node KRaft, one partition and stream thread, and a 1 KiB cache. Bytecode probes supplied key comparisons. Production frequency is unknown.

cases.title: Streamz reuses the first dictionary event across ten Dask submissions

findings.observation: In two uninstrumented runs, inputs numbered 0–9 printed 0 ten times, the scheduler ran one map task, and the ten outputs took 27.8 and 28.1 ms.
findings.interpretation: Ten distinct scatter tasks returned the same key i, so nine submissions reused the first map result, while hashing the whole dictionary produced ten keys and ten correct worker results.
findings.limits: The local TCP cluster used two single-threaded workers. Creation evidence identifies client scatter tasks. Scheduler keys linked them to worker threads.

cases.title: Flushing a collection leaves async sink callbacks unawaited

findings.observation: Two releases and the fix’s parent created ten callback coroutines without starting any, producing ten warnings. The merged version printed all ten single-item tuples in order.
findings.interpretation: sink.update created each coroutine and _emit returned it, but flush cleared the buffer without awaiting it. The merged fix clears first so a value of 13 emitted by a callback survives for the next batch. The transparent CoroPerf launch identified all ten allocations in each affected run. The stock warning showed the point where the coroutine was discarded. The captured allocation stack included sink.update, _emit and flush.
findings.limits: The report omitted a version. CPython creation records identify the unstarted coroutines separately from scheduled tasks.

cases.title: A repeated stream value cancelled a new Dask task

findings.observation: On Streamz 0.6.1, the reporter's program printed one random number and raised CancelledError. Two stock runs on the parent of PR 399 did the same. The merged fix and release 0.6.2 printed 1,000 distinct values in each run. With 1,000 distinct input strings, the old release also completed. A separate 32-input public-sink control kept only the first scattered Future alive. On 0.6.1 all 32 calls then reached workers despite sharing one scatter key. Releasing that Future after eight results made the ninth emission fail in both runs.
findings.interpretation: The random map received a fresh task key on every call. On the old build each repeated 'd' had the same scatter key. The scheduler received a release for that key, forgot it, and found the dependency absent when it processed the new map task. Its cancelled-key message named the same future that raised in Client._gather. The graph links that exception frame to the creation of the same coroutine in Client.sync. The fix disables scatter hashing and gives each emission its own dependency. The lifetime control isolates the effect of retaining a scheduler reference while leaving the non-pure map in place. Worker PIDs, addresses and distinct invocation UUIDs confirm that the 32 delivered replies came from separate calls.
findings.limits: The report lists Python 3.8.5, Dask 2.30.0 and Streamz 0.6.1. We selected matching Distributed 2.30.0 and ran each local cluster on two CPUs. Trace collection changed the cancellation point: the 0.6.1 traced runs printed four and three values. Random numbers and task IDs vary per process. The 32-emission control uses a worker-identifying function in place of random.random and tests the lifetime of a single strong reference.

cases.title: Streamz consumed the first generator item and delivered none

findings.observation: A generator containing the integers 0 through 9 produced no downstream values on 0.6.4. After the exception, 1 through 9 were still in the generator. The merged fix and 0.6.5 delivered all ten. In a separate SQLite pipeline, each fixed input path delivered all 344 Palmer Penguins records in the expected order.
findings.interpretation: The exception stack stopped at flatten.update after it read item 0. The next expression called len(x) to decide whether this was the last item. A generator has no length. A SQLite cursor reached the same line while a list of the identical rows passed. The fix reads one item ahead to identify the last one. In one- and three-record batches, the fixed generator path attached the year marker to the last record of each batch.
findings.limits: The posted program uses a synchronous Stream. The task-origin evidence comes from a separate pipeline using the built-in asynchronous from_iterable source. Source.start registered its run callback. Tornado scheduled the task that later reached flatten.update. The capture identified the generator, cursor and list source tasks separately. The reporter’s traceback identified Python 3.10 and did not specify a Streamz release.

cases.title: tikv-ctl omits the state of a healthy Raft region

findings.observation: After one RawPut to region 10, tikv-ctl 7.5.1 showed region metadata on the leader and both followers but omitted state from all three responses.
findings.interpretation: Independent RegionInfo reads decoded Normal on every replica, and the corrected CLI emitted it; the client source change adds get_state() to the JSON field at region_local_state.region.state.
findings.limits: Normal is the protobuf zero value and may be omitted on the wire. The fix-side CLI identified itself as 7.5.3 inside the 7.5.2 TiUP bundle.

cases.title: A tokenizer counted a real leading space as part of the first word

findings.observation: With prefix insertion disabled and offset trimming enabled, the first token in “ My name is John” covered characters 0–3 and included the space. Setting add_prefix_space=False on the post-processor moved the start to 1. The four token IDs stayed the same across both configurations on all five builds.
findings.interpretation: The native stack follows Python encode() to the Rust process_offsets branch. The default post-processor treated the first leading space as an inserted prefix and reduced the trim count from one to zero. Matching the pre-tokenizer setting kept the trim count at one. The cited revision already accepted this keyword. The closing change documented it and added tests.
findings.limits: The report gave the configuration and a source revision. The local experiment used RoBERTa vocabulary files and examined character offsets. In 697 SQuAD answer windows beginning with one real space, the aligned configuration recovered all 697 annotated starts and 694 complete answer strings. Three annotations ended inside a token. The native samples cover synchronous encoding.

cases.title: Left padding assigns tokens to the wrong input sequence

findings.observation: With ABC and DEF padded to three tokens, both builds emitted IDs [50257, 24694, 32988]. The old build assigned sequence IDs [0, 1, None], so selecting the second sequence returned ABC. The fixed build assigned [None, 0, 1] and returned DEF.
findings.interpretation: The native Encoding kept its original sequence ranges after left padding. The fix moved both ends of each range by the padding length, and the upstream Rust regression passed. Right padding and unpadded inputs were correct.
findings.limits: The report did not specify a release. Official builds and the Encoding component bracket the fix. GDB sampled synchronous Rust calls.

cases.title: A second MetricCollection read can return another metric’s cached result

findings.observation: After ten updates on four samples, recall changed from 0.5 to 0.6667 on the second read, and three four-element ROC arrays became the scalar 0.625.
findings.interpretation: Grouped metrics shared the first metric’s computed cache. Disabling grouping or caching restored the readings, and the fix passed all 64 combinations versus 16 before.
findings.limits: This was synchronous CPU evaluation in one process. Scores and labels independently verified the scalar and curve results.

cases.title: A perfect classifier received a macro accuracy of two thirds

findings.observation: The reporter’s predictions matched all six targets. After excluding target class 0, TorchMetrics 0.11.4 reported a macro accuracy of 0.6667. The fixed implementation returned 1. On held-out Iris measurements, the two retained species had recalls of 0.90 and 1.00. The affected metric reported 0.6333 and the fix returned their mean of 0.95.
findings.interpretation: The confusion matrix and per-class counts were already correct when they reached _accuracy_reduce. The affected average gave equal weight to three classes, including an absent class with a score of zero. The fix gave zero weight to the class with no true positives, false positives or false negatives. The predictions and the other two scores stayed the same.
findings.limits: A nearest-centroid classifier trained on 120 public Iris measurements produced the 30 held-out predictions. A separate calculation checked every prediction, and a scikit-learn reference checked the scores. The same results held in one batch and four interleaved batches. When a retained example was predicted as an excluded target class, that class still had a false positive and remained in the macro average. Evaluation ran synchronously on CPU.

cases.title: TorchMetrics summed per-batch segmentation IoU at validation epoch end

findings.observation: On 56 labeled images, the released MeanIoU metric returned 18.811829 for a pixel-count mean of 0.335926. On two Gloo ranks the fix parent returned 9.405914 on each rank. The fixed code returned 0.335926. With the reference masks as perfect predictions, the single-process release returned 56, the two-rank parent returned 28 and the fix returned 1.
findings.interpretation: The parent added each image batch's mean IoU to its local score. At compute time it averaged the two rank sums and returned that value directly. The fixed metric sums both scores and batch counts across ranks, then divides. A forward call per image and one repacked update per rank both agreed with the independent oracle. The physical stack samples expose the local and synchronized states inside Lightning's validation hooks.
findings.limits: The issue describes epoch-end validation but supplies no dataset or weights. The local image workload uses public Penn-Fudan photos and pedestrian annotations with a fixed brightness predictor. The 56 images are divided evenly across the two ranks. The separate issue-comment replay uses its four index-mask tests, including the target retained on the last step. The observed compute frames belong to synchronous CPU workers.

cases.title: A failed compute leaves the metric synchronized

findings.observation: After the expected no-positive-sample error, adding one positive sample per rank still produced an already-synchronized error in three runs on 1.9.0; the proposed fix returned MRR 1/3 on both ranks.
findings.interpretation: The first error skipped unsync, leaving stale global state active; restoring each rank’s local cache in finally allowed the next call to gather the updated samples.
findings.limits: The comparison used two local CPU/Gloo processes and an unmerged fix proposal.

cases.title: Weighted Dice scores exceed one when foreground is absent

findings.observation: The old implementation returned 2 for the author’s four foreground-free samples and 1.34 for a valid mixed batch, whether updated together or separately.
findings.interpretation: The fix and release 1.6.2 returned 0 and 0.34 on the same inputs and passed all four upstream regression assertions. The fix’s parent retained the inflated scores.
findings.limits: Zero for an empty foreground is the upstream convention. The replay used the default single-process DiceScore on Linux CPU. The reporter used macOS.

cases.title: Tornado drops the Allow header from a 204 OPTIONS response

findings.observation: The original handler tells clients it supports GET and OPTIONS. Tornado 6.0.3, 6.0.4 and the immediate source parent dropped Allow from the 204 response. All five builds transmitted the reporter’s custom Alloww header. Changing only the status to 200 preserved both headers on every build.
findings.interpretation: The affected filter received both headers. Its clear_header call took the argument Allow, deleted that entry on the live handler and returned to finish. The HTTP writer then received only the custom header of the two. The landed filter preserves Allow, and curl received it on both the merged revision and Tornado 6.1. The archived source change removes Allow from the list of headers the filter clears.
findings.limits: The two trials used the reporter’s entire server and curl command on loopback with CPython 3.9.15. The reporter gave the Tornado version only. The coroutine witness belongs to the framework’s RequestHandler._execute. The application method options and the header filter both ran synchronously inside it. The comparison covers the posted 204 response, the 200 status control and a GET.

cases.title: Concurrent update_or_create returns the other caller’s value

findings.observation: Two tasks supplied different defaults for the same missing PostgreSQL row. On the observed parent run, the first task created the row with a. The caller that requested b also received a, and an independent database read found a. No UPDATE ran. With the fix, the second caller received b, one UPDATE ran, and the committed row contained b.
findings.interpretation: The original gather call created the task that lost its defaults. Its return sample in update_or_create led through _create_or_get after a conflicting INSERT. That path fetched the existing row and returned it with the creator’s value. The corrected path applies the waiting caller’s defaults. Aligning the two initial reads let the opposite caller win and produced the same role-dependent behavior.
findings.limits: The missing-row race depends on scheduling. In the default-pool runs the second caller saw the existing row and updated it normally. PostgreSQL readbacks and statement logs establish the committed value and write count. The Python stack identifies the caller and ORM branch.

cases.title: SQLite wrote a timestamp that the ORM could not find

findings.observation: The original create call committed its row. The subsequent get call with the same Python datetime raised DoesNotExist on 0.11.9. The database still contained the row. Across 354 invoice dates, the affected client missed all 412 expected invoices on equality lookup. Its one-day range queries also included 118 invoices from the following day. Version 0.11.10 returned every expected invoice on both query paths.
findings.interpretation: On the SQLite worker thread, the bound INSERT passed through adapt_datetime, which separated the date and time with a space. QuerySet.__await__ created a QuerySet._execute coroutine. Inside that same live instance, ValueWrapper.get_value_sql rendered the filter datetime with a T. SQLite compared the two stored and supplied strings. Converting only the filter input restored every result. Converting only the write input left the mismatch intact.
findings.limits: The original Python, SQLite, ORM and aiosqlite versions ran locally on Linux. The additional invoice workload used 412 midnight timestamps from the Chinook sample database. Two explicit timestamps also exercise subsecond precision. SQLite DATETIME() truncated the fractional timestamp and selected the whole-second neighbour. The tests use timezone-naive datetimes.

cases.title: SQLite sorted a decimal bill of 27.27 before 9.99

findings.observation: The reporter inserted 0, 27.27 and 9.99 and ordered the resulting objects by their decimal field. Both affected builds returned the values in that insertion order. The fix and release 0.15.5 returned 0, 9.99 and 27.27.
findings.interpretation: The planner passed the bare column to ORDER BY. SQLite had stored the values as text, and its execution trace confirmed the comparison used that column. In an independent check, changing only the ORDER BY expression to CAST the column AS NUMERIC recovered every expected bill and tip position. The fix generated that cast. The local relation-prefetch example links the task that returned the misordered bills to BaseExecutor._execute_prefetch_queries. The tip query used a separate prefetch task.
findings.limits: The original report supplied model and query fragments. The local wrapper supplied initialization and invoked the reported operations. Release 0.15.4 is the release immediately before the confirmed fix release. The coroutine-origin evidence comes from an additional reverse-relation query on 244 restaurant checks, grouped by service day. All reference rankings used exact decimal values from the CSV and row ID to break ties.

cases.title: Why did an HTTP response turn 200.00 into 2E+2?

findings.observation: A view created a record with a two-place DecimalField and serialized it with the Pydantic model generated by Tortoise. On 0.20.0 and 1.1.8, six of eight amounts lost their declared scale in the creation response on both databases. A later GET returned 2E+2 from SQLite and 200.00 from PostgreSQL for the same posted amount.
findings.interpretation: The request stack reached Model.create and DecimalField.to_python_value. In that frame the native normalize method received an already quantized 200.00, and the field returned 2E+2. Pydantic emitted that value in the response. PostgreSQL stored 200.00 in a numeric(12,2) column and later returned a native Decimal. SQLite stored text and ran field conversion on each read. The two upstream regression tests failed at their scale assertions on the parent commit and passed on the merge.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied steps and a screenshot. We rebuilt the HTTP view with the specified ORM and serializer. Two batches each made 368 loopback requests using 26 service processes. Numeric equality held for every amount. The origin match identifies the measured ASGI endpoint coroutine. The Decimal operand came from a targeted CPython callback while its field frame was running.

cases.title: A directory page returned two distinct users and a total of three

findings.observation: The reporter’s query returned users 101 and 102 on Tortoise ORM 0.25.3, but reported a total of three. One user matched both selected roles. The fix and release 1.1.9 returned the same two users and a total of two.
findings.interpretation: QuerySet.count received a distinct queryset. In the affected build the new CountQuery lacked its distinct flag, and PostgreSQL executed COUNT(*) over the joined role rows. The fix passed the flag through and counted distinct user IDs. Replaying the logged statements with one role membership removed, restored and then added to the second user moved the old count from 3 to 2 to 3 to 4. The fixed count stayed at 2.
findings.limits: The report supplied the query body, Python version, ORM version and driver. The local run supplied the missing models and records. The creation stack belongs to a request in our asyncio Unix-socket service. The same query was also run directly on PostgreSQL. The upstream regression used SQLite.

cases.title: A reverse foreign-key lookup uses the primary key instead of to_field

findings.observation: The database contained row 101 referencing the UUID, but 1.1.7 and the fix’s parent returned an empty list, while the fix and 1.1.9 returned [101].
findings.interpretation: Both queries used app_id, but the old ORM bound the integer primary key as text and the fixed ORM bound the UUID named by to_field, as confirmed by SQLite and an independent join.
findings.limits: SQLite and the fixture rows were supplied locally. Task creation was verified only for an additional reverse-prefetch query.

cases.title: Which book does first() return when a subclass inherits its ordering?

findings.observation: The abstract base model requests newest-first order. Its Book subclass specifies the table name. On the three posted books, Tortoise ORM 1.1.8 and the immediate fix parent returned IDs 1, 2, 3. first() selected the oldest book, ID 1. The fixing commit and 1.1.9 returned IDs 3, 2, 1 and selected ID 3. Sorting the original timestamps in Python and reading the saved SQLite files with explicit descending order both put ID 3 first.
findings.interpretation:
The metaclass samples show the base model’s descending ordering and the child’s empty ordering in the affected build. The query resolver used that same child metadata object, and SQLite received a SELECT without ORDER BY. The fix copies the base ordering when the child omits it. With the repaired metadata, the resolver emitted ORDER BY on created_at descending. Explicit ordering worked on every build.

On the affected wheel, segment 4 records the unstarted QuerySet._execute coroutine created by QuerySet.__await__ at queryset.py line 1294. Segment 6 includes its pinned frame while the SQLite client returns the three IDs. At segment 7 that same instance returns the list received by the public caller. Segments 1–3 sample the earlier synchronous decision that determined the order.
findings.limits: The issue supplied the model definitions and three rows without identifying a database engine or release. This replay uses SQLite, preserves the timestamp strings and awaits the two posted query alternatives separately. The sequence of an unordered SQL query depends on the database and plan. The coroutine match covers query execution on the event-loop thread.

cases.title: Updating a Shanghai timestamp moved 09:00 to 17:00

findings.observation: On SQLite in WAL mode, creating a model with the reported local time of 09:00 and reading it back returned 09:00 in every build. In 1.1.8, assigning that same naive time to an existing model and saving it returned 17:00. A QuerySet update also returned 17:00. Both operations returned 09:00 after the fix. On insertion, automatic timestamps used a UTC offset in the old build and the Shanghai offset in the fixed build. Both represented the correct instant.
findings.interpretation: The creation path converted the input to a Python field value first and attached the configured Shanghai zone. The update path entered DatetimeField.to_db_value with a naive value and called make_aware with UTC. The SQL executed by SQLite contained 09:00+00:00, which became 17:00 on reload in Shanghai. The fix attached the configured zone during writes. In the hourly meter import, the creation stack and the make_aware sample identify the specific task that wrote the naive timestamps.
findings.limits: The issue supplied a timestamp, configuration and steps. The local program implemented those steps on CPython 3.11 and SQLite WAL. The supplementary import used German load readings from two weeks spanning both 2019 clock changes. The published UTC column distinguishes the two occurrences of 02:00 on October 27. With the fixed build, dropping that distinction still misplaced one reading. Preserving the Python fold flag or supplying an explicit UTC offset recovered all 336 instants. The matched child task belongs to this local import.

cases.title: Two many-to-many filters incorrectly share one JOIN alias

findings.observation: After supplying a missing reverse-relation name, the posted query returned no rows on either database, while independent aliased SQL, the fix and 1.0.0 all returned 101, 105, 105.
findings.interpretation: resolve_filters deduplicated the two category joins by table identity, putting both name predicates on one column. Separate aliases restored the rows, including the duplicate.
findings.limits: The report omitted a version and its model definitions conflicted at startup. Task origins cover local prefetch controls. The posted query ran in its caller’s task.

cases.title: A tournament participant count used the joins in reverse order

findings.observation: On Tortoise ORM 0.16.1, the reported Count over events__participants raised JoinException before SQLite received a SELECT. The database contained one event and two teams in the populated tournament. Raw SQL returned two for that tournament and zero for the empty one. Releases 0.16.0 and 0.16.2 returned both counts, and the direct event-participant count returned two on all three releases. Each result repeated in a second run. The report also tried to print the annotation on a list. That raised AttributeError after a successful await on the two working releases. The upstream regression reads the value from the first returned model.
findings.interpretation: The resolver in 0.16.1 produced events followed by participants, then reversed that list. The first attempted join referenced event before that table had been joined to tournament. The physical stack follows PyPika validation through the join builder and QuerySet.__await__ to the failing await in the upstream regression. The test runner’s creation call and the propagation of the same exception into the running test are linked by the CPython coroutine object, its frame, the current asyncio task and its root frame. The filtered QuerySet also matches from allocation through the throw. PR 328 removed the extra reversal. Its parent and merge differ in just one ORM package file.
findings.limits: The origin edge belongs to TestAggregation.test_nested_aggregation_in_annotation, the caller that awaits the reported query. On 0.16.1 synchronous query construction failed before the ORM created its _execute coroutine. The traceback identifies Python 3.7.6. We selected PyPika 0.36.0 from the traceback source lines and used SQLite 3.31.1 for every build. The public-data controls import every game and team from the frozen 1930 and 2018 World Cup schedules. All ten saved databases matched the same 164 source memberships. Both nested counts failed before SQL on the affected release and exact parent. The exact merge returned 36 entries and 13 distinct teams for 1930, and 128 and 32 for 2018.

cases.title: Tortoise resolves a nested ordering field on the wrong model

findings.observation: The reported SQLite query failed before returning a row because Tournament did not recognize teamname on two old releases and the pre-fix commit, while both fixed releases and the fix commit succeeded.
findings.interpretation: Tracing showed that Team had the field and the root model did not, while the fix resolved the TextField on Team and submitted the final team-name sort to SQLite.
findings.limits: The original example had one tournament and printed no rows. Multirow ordering and worker-task attribution came from a separate file-backed control.

cases.title: Why did a non-null filter return the only NULL row?

findings.observation:
The reporter inserted two names in SQLite, 'a' and NULL. On the reported revision, the 1.1.9 wheel and the immediate fix parent, awaiting name__not=None printed [None]. Both the SQL reference and a Python check on the two stored values selected ['a']. The landed source returned ['a'].

A separate check on the same connection added an empty string, a second 'a', 'b' and another NULL. Four rows had non-null names. The affected builds selected the two NULL rows, IDs 2 and 6. The fix selected IDs 1, 3, 4 and 5, including the empty string. Explicit null checks and comparisons with 'a' agreed across all four builds.
findings.interpretation:
The affected filter function received None and returned an inequality with NULL joined by OR to IS NULL. The resolver received the same criterion object. SQLite evaluated the resulting expression as unknown on 'a' and true on NULL, so only the NULL row survived. The landed source returned field.notnull() for the same argument. The emitted SQL spelled this as NOT "name" IS NULL.

On the reported revision, segments 1 and 2 record synchronous predicate construction. Segment 3 records ValuesListQuery.__await__ creating the unstarted _execute coroutine at queryset.py line 1859. Segment 5 samples the live instance while the SQLite client returns the projected row. At segment 6 the same coroutine object and frame return [None], which the original application prints. The corresponding fixed trace returns ['a'].
findings.limits: The original program uses an in-memory SQLite database and a nullable character column. The four additional inserts and control queries follow the original print calls. The fixed comparison ran the merged source commit. Coroutine identity was measured in the query on the event-loop thread. SQLite’s truth values were checked by running SQL on backups of the original connection.

cases.title: Projecting book IDs dropped the join needed to order by the author

findings.observation: The reporter’s full-object query included the author join. On 0.25.1, 1.1.9 and the proposal parent, selecting just the book ID removed that join but kept the author column in ORDER BY. PostgreSQL returned SQLSTATE 42P01. SQLite reported a missing column when the same calculation used a portable CAST.
findings.interpretation: The recorded values() call began with author in the requested relations. Its returned ValuesQuery had an empty relation list, and _make_query built zero joins. The submitted patch carried the relation into the projection, producing one join. PostgreSQL and SQLite then returned the same six ordered catalog IDs for dictionary and flat projections.
findings.limits: The posted module printed SQL. The launcher supplied the omitted RawSQL import and called the published main(). The database runs added six GITenberg catalog entries and used the difference between death year and birth year as the integer sort input. The proposed fix was open at collection time. The recorded stacks cover query construction and database execution.

cases.title: Related-field CASE and filtered COUNT queries lose a required join

findings.observation: On the reported revision, fix parent and 1.1.9, CASE failed on a missing e__t.name and filtered COUNT returned zero for one matching child. Both queries returned one on the fix commit.
findings.interpretation: The old COUNT queried only the parent table, and this SQLite build treated the unknown quoted column “n” as text. Propagating the join produced a LEFT OUTER JOIN and counted the child.
findings.limits: SQLite only, using the report’s two rows. The verified Task origin belongs to a separate related-object prefetch.

cases.title: The audio pipeline applies softmax to regression and multi-label scores

findings.observation: With the reporter’s two public checkpoints and silence inputs, the regression model produced a raw score of −1.053481. The affected pipeline returned 1. On three music clips it also changed 11 of 30 multi-label decisions at a threshold of 0.5. All 30 decisions matched the independently calculated scores on the fixed build.
findings.interpretation: The affected parameter sanitizer filled in softmax when the caller omitted an activation. The same logits passed intact from the model forward call into postprocessing. After the fix, postprocessing read the checkpoint’s task type and returned the raw regression value or applied sigmoid separately to each label. Explicit activation controls on the affected release produced the expected values.
findings.limits: The original report used a T4. These runs used an A100 with both original checkpoints, five builds, and three two-second music clips. The checks compare scores to the output layer and use an absolute tolerance of 0.001 for the batched music scores. Classification accuracy against human labels was outside this comparison. All recorded pipeline calls were synchronous.

cases.title: Beam scores include prompt tokens in the length denominator

findings.observation: For GPT-2 prompts of 4 and 413 tokens, the old code divided each one-token generation’s log probability by 5 and 414. A three-token control used 8 instead of 3.
findings.interpretation: With identical weights and returned tokens, the merged change normalized by generated length, correcting all five candidate scores for each prompt and the three-token control.
findings.limits: The replay used CPU instead of CUDA and evaluated returned scores. Early EOS and ranking across different completion lengths were not tested.

cases.title: The Transformers pipeline squeezed a regression score onto a probability scale

findings.observation: On 40 held-out sentence pairs with human similarity ratings from 0 to 5, the regression head produced 38 scores above 1. Transformers 4.45.2 passed all outputs through a sigmoid. Its largest raw score, 4.4564, became 0.9885. With the same learned weights and inputs, 4.46.3 preserved 40 of 40 raw scores. The tables distinguish agreement with the model from agreement with the human ratings.
findings.interpretation: For the same input, the physical stack contains the final Linear.forward and the classification pipeline. The head value matches an independent dot product of its frozen weights and the recorded pooled vector. In TextClassificationPipeline.postprocess, 4.45.2 takes the single-output branch and executes scores = sigmoid(outputs). Passing function_to_apply="none" on that release returns the continuous score. The merge tests the explicit regression setting first. Unspecified and multi-label configurations still select sigmoid on both releases.
findings.limits: Upstream classified this as a requested change to the default. Its own regression test configures a two-output DistilBERT fixture. That fixture takes softmax on the parent revision and returns the raw top score on the merge. The single-output experiment uses a locally fine-tuned BERT and a held-out sample of STS Benchmark image-caption pairs. Its scores measure this model on those inputs. The captured CPU inference functions are synchronous.

cases.title: Treelite changed the order of search results on sparse ranking features

findings.observation: Treelite 0.93 changed six of ten scores in the maintainer’s LambdaRank regression, including a score of 2.0 that became −1.095265. Those six changes produced zero strict pair inversions in that fixture. On an additional workload with signed feature hashing, 658 of 768 held-out scores changed, reversing 1,181 candidate pairs across all 50 queries. For 19 queries, the returned and reference top sets had no common candidate. The original LightGBM example features passed on all four builds.
findings.interpretation: GDB stopped in the generated predictor at the split on feature 25416. The sparse row omitted the feature. Treelite 0.93 entered leaf 0 and the running score became −1.095265. The fix continued to leaf 5 and produced 2.0, matching native LightGBM and the dense control. An independent walk of the archived trees counted 2,339 changed leaves across the hashed sparse queries in 0.93. The source parent produced 1,180 strict inversions and the fixed builds produced zero.
findings.limits: The reporter’s trained model and validation matrix were unavailable. The public ranking comparison uses LightGBM’s distributed train/test split and a separate signed-hash transformation. Strict inversions exclude near ties within 1e−6 on either ranking. A separate dense observation concerns only the source parent. In row 702 both physical predictors read present feature 64 as 0.49999999999999994 and its low word as −1. The parent reached a leaf worth -0.0925675473, and the fix reached one worth -0.0028503143. That single dense score change produced zero strict inversions. The captured execution is synchronous.
