cases.title: Manual iteration shifts a centered xarray rolling window

findings.observation: For the values 1 through 9 with a centered three-point window, the built-in mean placed 2 at the second position. In 2022.3.0 and the fix parent, manual iteration placed 2 at the third position and returned 8 at the last position. The fixed commit and both later releases matched the built-in mean.
findings.interpretation: With center enabled, DataArrayRolling.__iter__ passed slice(0, 2) into DataArray.isel at the second label. Those two values failed the minimum of three. The fix passed slice(0, 3) and averaged 1, 2 and 3. An independent check of the window members on NetCDF data found six failing configurations per backend before the fix and zero afterwards.
findings.limits: The reporter did not specify a platform or release. The local comparisons use a shared Linux dependency environment. The Dask controls use its synchronous scheduler; the reported iterator is a synchronous generator.

cases.title: Descending sort moves missing values to the front

findings.observation: The reported version and the fix’s parent put both NaNs first for [3, NaN, 4, 2, NaN], while the fix and 2026.2.0 returned [4, 3, 2, NaN, NaN].
findings.interpretation: Dataset.sortby reversed the entire ascending index [3,0,2,1,4] before isel, bringing NaNs forward. The fix also used the nonmissing mask when sorting.
findings.limits: Checked values, missing positions and label alignment on synchronous NumPy arrays using live CPython frames.

cases.title: A missing-temperature marker survived xarray decoding

findings.observation: The reported example stores six missing values as float32 and supplies the marker as a Python float. With xarray 2024.7.0 and NumPy 2.0.1 all six remained in the output. For the Elgin 5 S station in Arizona, 3 of the 29 daily minimum temperatures in February 2012 were missing. Counting their markers as temperatures gave a monthly mean of -12.328 °C. The fixed decoder returned -2.223 °C, matching the original station record.
findings.interpretation: The physical stacks identify two points in decoding. CFMaskCoder.decode prepares the missing-value marker in _check_fill_values. Materializing the variable reaches _apply_mask, where the reported build compares the float32 data with a float64 marker. The merged fix passes a float32 marker to that comparison. Testing the immediately adjacent representable numbers confirmed that both valid neighbors survive.
findings.limits: The reporter used a dataset constructed in memory. For the station comparison we mapped the original missing entries to the reported float32 storage convention and read the marker from JSON. The data archive retains the original file, encoding step and daily outputs. Both measured paths are synchronous.

cases.title: Rolling argmax and argmin counted days from the wrong end of the window

findings.observation: In the posted increasing series, the maximum is the last of three values. The affected accelerated path returned position 0 for all eight full windows. On 1,461 daily Seattle temperature records, it selected a day without the highest temperature in 1,254 of 1,455 seven-day windows. For the lowest temperature it selected a wrong day in 1,255 windows. Both counts fell to zero after the fix.
findings.interpretation: The recorded stack reaches DataArrayRolling._bottleneck_reduce. Its backend counts positions from the right edge of a window. The old wrapper returned that offset directly. The fixed wrapper subtracts the offset from the window width minus one. For the week ending January 7, 2012, the highest temperature was 12.8 °C on the first day. The affected wrapper pointed to the seventh day.
findings.limits: Tests covered in-memory arrays with complete trailing windows. Ties were accepted whenever the selected day had the actual extreme temperature. Python reference calculations, a separate SQLite query, the NumPy reduction and the backend-disabled path were checked. The local interpreter was CPython 3.12.4 and the report used 3.12.0. The stack covers the Python wrapper and the return from Bottleneck 1.3.7.

cases.title: Seasonal resampling changed the timestamp unit of passenger totals

findings.observation: The original program returned 10 for January through May and changed its time coordinate from seconds to microseconds. Using 144 monthly passenger counts, we reopened two Arrow files covering six years each. Strict concatenation failed for second, millisecond and nanosecond input. The merged repair preserved all four units and joined all twelve annual totals.
findings.interpretation: The stacks follow DataArray.resample into SeasonResampler.factorize and both calls to pandas DatetimeIndex.__new__. The old constructor received plain Python datetime labels built from year, month and day. Its returned index used microseconds even when the source used seconds. The fixed constructor received NumPy datetime64 labels carrying the source unit. We independently checked all output dates and counts, including the 1949 January–May total of 612 thousand passengers.
findings.limits: The original report used macOS arm64. These Linux x86-64 runs matched its xarray commit, Python, pandas and NumPy versions. The two-file Arrow operation is a downstream test added for this study. A safe explicit cast also restored the twelve annual records in these data. The captured resampling path is synchronous.

cases.title: Time weights aligned with latitude in a three-dimensional fit

findings.observation: The original 10 × 20 fit succeeded. Adding a third dimension produced the reported broadcasting error on xarray 2024.11.0. When time and latitude had equal lengths, the fit completed and silently returned incorrect trends at all 24 locations in an NMC air-temperature sample with nonuniform weights.
findings.interpretation: Dataset.polyfit passed a weight array of shape (10, 1) into the multiplication of a (10, 20, 30) response. NumPy aligns these shapes from the right, placing the time weights on the middle axis. The fix supplied (10, 1, 1). With eight samples and eight latitudes, the affected release gave −1.208087 K/h at 75° N, 200° E. The independent weighted fit and the fixed release both gave +0.050764 K/h.
findings.limits: The seeded public example ran on Linux x86-64 with the reporter’s Python, NumPy, pandas and xarray versions. The original used macOS arm64. The gridded temperatures come from the public NMC reanalysis example. We selected the sample and varied its weights as a diagnostic control. The NumPy fits ran synchronously.

cases.title: XGBoost returns raw margins as binary probabilities

findings.observation: On 3.0.0 and 3.4.1, 103 of 104 predictions were outside the probability range and the remaining prediction was also wrong, although every pair summed to one within rounding error.
findings.interpretation: The wrapper returned [1−m, m] for raw margin m, and applying the merged sigmoid change to the same model and CPU library made all 104 rows match the independent tree-by-tree reference.
findings.limits: The reporter did not specify a version. Coverage was limited to finite CPU inputs and binary gbtree predict_proba.

cases.title: Unsigned indices select an invalid row within a Zarr chunk

findings.observation: On a 4×2 array, indices [3,0] worked as int64 but failed as uint8 by selecting row 3 within a two-row chunk, while sorted uint64 indices also failed.
findings.interpretation: The graph identified the failing chunk-read task, and a separate probe showed a uint8 difference wrapping to 253 and falsely marking the indices as increasing, while subtracting a chunk offset from uint64 produced float64.
findings.limits: Linux x86-64 replaced macOS ARM with matching Python, NumPy, and numcodecs versions. Separate value traces and fix controls established the numerical cause.

cases.title: Go’s CommandContext can keep waiting for an inherited pipe

findings.observation: Both historical builds took about 5 seconds to return from the original program. In a paired diagnostic run, setting WaitDelay reduced the wait from 903 ms to 271 ms.
findings.interpretation: The Go dump separated the parent waiting for copying to finish from the writerDescriptor copy goroutine. An independent /proc check showed that a descendant still held the pipe’s write end.
findings.limits: The graph comes from the paired Go 1.23 diagnostic program. The two original runs and the descriptor evidence were recorded separately.

cases.title: Go’s goroutine profile omits workload labels

findings.observation: The reporter’s unchanged HTTP server started one labeled goroutine. Go 1.9.2 and 1.14.7 produced a binary profile sample for the worker with zero labels. Go 1.15 and 1.23.0 put a-label=a-value on that worker’s sample. Each release ran the original program, a two-worker control, and a control that exchanged the two label arguments. Two batches launched 24 separate server processes.
findings.interpretation: The binary profile describes the aggregation problem. In the old pair runs, two workers in main.waitForWork collapsed into one sample with a count of two. The runtime dump kept separate goroutine IDs and creation sites at main.startImport and main.startRefresh. The released Go 1.15 profile contained two labeled worker samples and the profile writer stack included the label-aware runtime entry point. Two timed Go 1.9.2 runs link GoCreate at main.main to GoStop at main.Func by goroutine ID. Their creation-to-park intervals are 200.422 µs and 91.712 µs.
findings.limits: The timed intervals use the Go runtime trace clock from creation to the first park at select {}. The text dump supplies a retrospective check of goroutine ID and creation site. Binary pprof records aggregate stacks and labels. Each control worker separately read its runtime label and printed its ID. Swapping labels preserved each worker’s creator and changed the label it reported. This experiment measured goroutine profiles on Linux amd64.

cases.title: An SDK cleanup Task can outlive its event loop

findings.observation: In SDK 1.50.1, manually closing the loop destroyed a still-pending BaseApiClient.aclose Task. Draining the loop first removed the warning.
findings.interpretation: The Task’s creation traced to the SDK destructor, and its identity matched the object named by the destruction warning.
findings.limits: The replay exercised local client cleanup only. Garbage collection and shutdown order affect the warning.

cases.title: An uniterated inference stream leaves a client warning

findings.observation: Two streams requested from the same loopback endpoint and left uniterated produced one client warning on the affected build and none after the fix.
findings.interpretation: Session and response identities tied the warning to submit_alpha and matched the independently recorded release order, and the shared URL and warning text could not distinguish the callers.
findings.limits: The test used aiohttp 3.10.5, controlled the release order, and triggered garbage collection. Production frequency was not measured.

cases.title: Video polling blocks the async client’s event loop

findings.observation: During 1.5 seconds of mock polling the timer ticked zero times on the old SDK and 29 times after the fix. With a real local TCP queue the counts were zero and 31.
findings.interpretation: The request task made three status queries and one result query inside nested get_response calls before downloading the video, while the fixed task yielded at to_thread.
findings.limits: All variants returned the same 1,099-byte, eight-frame video. The test covered local client polling without contacting a hosted model.

cases.title: A synchronous checkpoint read waits on its own event loop

findings.observation: The reported in-memory SQLite get_tuple call exceeded two seconds, while its async counterpart completed and the fixed synchronous entry point raised InvalidStateError immediately.
findings.interpretation: The loop thread scheduled the coroutine back onto itself and then blocked in Future.result(), preventing the callback from running.
findings.limits: The replay used the reported framework and storage packages with a newer Python patch release and covered one checkpoint read.

cases.title: Synchronous history listing waits on its own event loop

findings.observation: The synchronous SQLite history list exceeded two seconds, while the async entry point worked and the fixed synchronous path immediately raised InvalidStateError.
findings.interpretation: The Future returned by run_coroutine_threadsafe was the same object on which result() blocked, showing that the calling thread was waiting on its own loop.
findings.limits: Only in-memory history enumeration was checked, using the reported packages and a newer Python patch release.

cases.title: A busy default executor delays DNS until an HTTP request times out

findings.observation: With two default-executor threads occupied by synchronous reads, all three uninstrumented localhost requests raised ConnectTimeout in getaddrinfo and never reached the server.
findings.interpretation: All three traced requests reached the resolver submission stack. Their Futures were cancelled before the resolver ran, after a median of 241 ms. All nine uninstrumented control requests returned HTTP 200 across the private-pool, one-free-worker, and idle runs.
findings.limits: The report omitted the application and production concurrency. The local asgiref pipe reads established this mechanism on Linux CPython 3.11.

cases.title: A slow Future wakeup warning hides the identity of its Task

findings.observation: With the same roughly 85 ms wakeup callback, one historical CPython 3.8 build printed only TaskWakeupMethWrapper, while the fixed build identified the actual Task.
findings.interpretation: Matching the Handle and C callback across dispatch, the wait and warning formatting distinguished the two local Tasks. The slow callback is the worker whose task and coroutine were recorded at start_pair.
findings.limits: The delay was introduced locally to exercise the native warning. Periodic sampling missed the wait itself.

cases.title: Garbage collection destroys a pending task waiting on an isolated Future

findings.observation: A task waiting on an isolated Future produced a destruction diagnostic after garbage collection, while keeping a strong reference suppressed it.
findings.interpretation: GDB identified the pending task passed to TaskObj_finalize, and the Python graph supplied its creation identity, consistent with collection of an unreachable cycle.
findings.limits: The original app was unpublished. The local test covers the lifecycle mechanism, and GDB supplied the internal GC path.

cases.title: An asyncio semaphore releaser can repeatedly reacquire ahead of waiters

findings.observation: In the same bounded 20-worker workload without cancellation, only five workers acquired a permit on CPython 3.10.3, versus all 20 on 3.10.4.
findings.interpretation: The releasing task woke a distinct waiter but immediately reacquired the permit synchronously, whereas the fixed version yielded at that point. The task created by submit_batch released and reacquired the semaphore. The blocked waiter had a separate Task identity.
findings.limits: This checks the upstream workload without cancellation and establishes no general fairness guarantee.

cases.title: A WebSocket sender delays the server heartbeat

findings.observation: The websockets 8.1 loopback transfer completed, but the longest gap between server heartbeats was 20.035 seconds versus 1.002 seconds with cooperative sending.
findings.interpretation: A separate diagnostic send traced immediate returns through send, write_frame, _drain and _drain_helper, explaining how the synchronous generator could retain the event loop.
findings.limits: Heartbeats were measured independently in the original program. The stack came from a control run, and no production ping disconnect was observed.

cases.title: A large upsert pauses the event loop during request serialization

findings.observation: Writing 1,000 points took 1,567 ms in one batch with a maximum event-loop gap of 1,079 ms, versus 1,592 ms in batches of 64 with a maximum gap of 76.8 ms.
findings.interpretation: The upsert task entered model_dump_json before sending HTTP, and smaller batches reduced the longest pause with the same point count, implicating synchronous serialization.
findings.limits: Client and server were 1.17.1 with dense and sparse vectors, integer IDs and a 128 MB HTTP limit. Wall times were measured without probes.

cases.title: Synchronous retrieval delays async LlamaIndex routing tasks

findings.observation: In the posted script the background wait fell from 111 ms to 11 ms with the proposal, and the two-query Qdrant run fell from 416 ms to about 260 ms with identical results.
findings.interpretation: Each router task read its HTTP response synchronously, delaying an already-created downstream task. The proposal let both queries wait concurrently on async sockets.
findings.limits: Local fixed embeddings and real vector retrieval, with 200 ms of controlled relay delay per response. The proposal was unmerged.

cases.title: Some SGLang multimodal responses arrive seconds after the first token ID is ready

findings.observation: All five Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct runs completed 100 three-image requests each. The baseline and instrumented high-concurrency runs peaked at 100 in flight, with median times to first text of 28.071 and 27.550 seconds.
findings.interpretation: At high concurrency the median gap from tokenization to the first scheduler ID was 23.987 s, versus 4.166 ms from ID to text. Five of 100 latter gaps exceeded 1 s, and 4.513 s of the longest fell between detokenizer send and frontend Future completion.
findings.limits: One run per condition on one A100 with Triton and overlap disabled. The original FA3 deployment and inputs were unavailable, and the production cause remains unconfirmed.

cases.title: Synchronous tokenization delays SGLang health checks in an ASGI test

findings.observation: The baseline failed the proposal’s health-check assertion in 1.040 s and the proposed code passed in 0.039 s, and a separate chat conversion test measured 117.2 ms and 16.8 ms.
findings.interpretation: The baseline health task entered its handler only after synchronous tokenization returned, while the proposed handler ran during the tokenizer task’s suspension.
findings.limits: The unmerged PR used in-process ASGI, a controlled tokenizer, and a substitute generation manager. The production workload, GPU inference, and container restarts were outside the reproduction.

cases.title: Pause and continue time out before a worker starts receiving

findings.observation: In the reporter’s minimal example, pause and continue each timed out at 0.5 seconds on a cold worker and left one broadcast queued. Both completed with no backlog once the receiver started.
findings.interpretation: In both warm controls, the waiting control task and the receive handler referenced the same Future, while the cold worker had no event_loop at that boundary.
findings.limits: The example bypassed worker construction and used an in-memory queue, simplified receiver and scheduler. It did not establish a production service deadlock.

cases.title: Per-chunk polling reduces SGLang streaming throughput

findings.observation: At concurrency 48 on one A100, median output throughput was 13,534 tokens/s on the parent, 9,419 on the affected commit and 13,500 with only the polling limit applied in windows with no other GPU process observed.
findings.interpretation: For 96 requests of 96 tokens, direct polls fell from 9,120 to 96 per run, frontend CPU time fell from 97.7 to 65.1 µs/token and throughput recovered by 43.3%.
findings.limits: The short local runs used a 135M model. One-second GPU sampling and different hardware and concurrency limit comparison with the upstream 120B run.

cases.title: A local vLLM stream did not reproduce the reported burst of late tokens

findings.observation: The historical CUDA worker and HTTP client produced 150 and 384 tokens. In three ordinary long-stream runs, the last 192 items arrived over 658.1–675.7 ms, with no observed AsyncStream backlog.
findings.interpretation: Pausing client reads for 0.7 s compressed parsing of the remaining items into 3.9 ms. Pausing only display compressed refreshes into 2.6 ms while parsing still spanned 678.2 ms, distinguishing two possible locations for a visible burst.
findings.limits: Serial loopback requests with OPT-125M on one sometimes-shared A100. The original prompts, model, client and load were unknown, so the production cause remains open.

cases.title: A vLLM worker exits after a reported NCCL broadcast timeout

findings.observation: Upstream logs showed a rank-0 NCCL broadcast timeout and a Ray worker exit. A healthy vLLM 0.3.3 control on two A100s completed six tokens with OPT-125M.
findings.interpretation: The published stack placed _run_workers_async waiting for a worker, but the two stacks lacked a shared timeline or task identity to establish causation.
findings.limits: The incident input and missing rank’s state were unavailable. The graph uses upstream logs, and the two-GPU run validates only healthy inference.

cases.title: Streaming detokenization runs on the vLLM renderer’s event loop

findings.observation: With 20 streams of 2,048 chunks, stock and fixed builds both reconstructed all text. Throughput was 1,993 versus 1,753 tokens/s, while concurrent /tokenize p95 fell from 155 to 57 ms.
findings.interpretation: Both stock request Tasks ran incremental detokenization on the loop despite four renderer workers, while the paired fix submitted that work to an executor.
findings.limits: Each build had one unprobed GPU-less run with a local tokenizer. HTTP timings include client and logging costs and do not establish production inference throughput.

cases.title: Async v2 stack recovery depends on how the task is awaited

findings.observation: After resumption, both traditional async and verified v2 methods on .NET 11.0.0 omitted OuterMethod. The PR build showed MiddleMethod → OuterMethod on all five direct v2 runs and none in physical-stack mode.
findings.interpretation: In the PR build, Main remained absent in all five runs through NonAsyncHelper even after the outer task suspended, while directly awaiting AsyncHelper restored it in all five.
findings.limits: This tests draft diagnostic behavior. The public API lacks a per-frame continuation flag, and the full IL-mapping experiment was outside the replay.

frames.function: System.Threading.ExecutionContext.RunFromThreadPoolDispatchLoop(Thread threadPoolThread, ExecutionContext executionContext, ContextCallback callback, Object state)

cases.title: Main disappears from the physical stack after Foo resumes

findings.observation: In the original .NET program, a stack captured inside A’s constructor after Foo resumed no longer showed Main.
findings.interpretation: Comparing the original and instrumented assemblies, the async state-machine identity linked A’s constructor diagnostic to the call in Main that created Foo.
findings.limits: The trace identifies the origin of this invocation only.

cases.title: Synchronous SQL on Drogon’s database loop times out the profile request

findings.observation: A PostgreSQL-backed HTTP request timed out when the profile path ran synchronous SQL on Drogon’s database event loop.
findings.interpretation: The blocked stack and the shared coroutine’s creation record pointed to profile_entry, and moving execution to a different loop allowed the request to finish.
findings.limits: The Drogon 1.9.9 app recreated the reported mechanism. The original ORM project was unavailable.

cases.title: Express error forwarding reaches middleware after an empty database lookup

findings.observation: When MongoDB returned zero users, Express 4 with explicit next(err) and Express 5 with native forwarding both returned HTTP 200 with JSON code 404, while an unmatched route returned HTTP 404.
findings.interpretation: The same Mongoose Query and route Promise linked the empty lookup to middleware, and Express 5 recorded the router’s then continuation.
findings.limits: The tested error came from the detail controller. The original unhandled rejection, stalled connection and process exit were not reproduced.

cases.title: A WebSocket subscription task remains pending at shutdown

findings.observation: In the original WebSocket example, notifications_handler was still waiting in subscribe during shutdown.
findings.interpretation: The sampled stack and cancellation point both identified the outstanding subscription task.
findings.limits: The replay used the first public example and an external WebSocket client. The later implementation’s suggested close(1001) handshake was not observed.

cases.title: Identical Go sender stacks can have different leak status

findings.observation: Two senders blocked at the same doubleSend line, but goroutineleak marked only the sender whose channel the main goroutine no longer retained.
findings.interpretation: Swapping the retained channel swapped the flagged goroutine. Dropping the remaining reference raised the count from one to two, consistent with Go’s reachability check.
findings.limits: coroPerf correlated the runtime’s labels with goroutine IDs. Reachability leaves future communication possible and does not establish intent or diagnose every deadlock.

cases.title: A goroutine dump omits creators that have already exited

findings.observation: The original Go program left its last goroutine blocked on a channel, with exited ancestors absent from the ordinary stack dump.
findings.interpretation: Runtime trace creator IDs linked the blocked bar back through foo and an earlier bar to main.
findings.limits: The upstream issue concerned diagnostic visibility in this example.

cases.title: A gRPC health check stalls with the observability plugin enabled

findings.observation: The original Health/Check workload stalled when the observability plugin was enabled.
findings.interpretation: A native wait graph showed a circular dependency between the event loop and a mutex owner involving the GIL, and plugin controls distinguished a separate shutdown stall.
findings.limits: Some Cython symbols were stripped. An independent native debugger supplied the lock relationships.

cases.title: A restarting Raft follower blocks while replaying committed logs

findings.observation: The original test timed out after 130 submissions. In a new three-node group, a follower reopening a database at commit 135 stalled in NewRaft while the other two nodes still committed new values.
findings.interpretation: The follower blocked on a queue send in restoreFromCommittedLogs → processLogs before replay wrote anything. With proposed change #730 it applied all 135 writes and caught up.
findings.limits: Tested on v1.8.0 with real Bolt storage and a clean shutdown. The wrapper persisted the commit position after logging. Power-loss atomicity was outside scope, and #730 was unmerged.

cases.title: Starlette cancels a background task after the client disconnects

findings.observation: In the reporter’s Starlette app, a client disconnect cancelled a background task that was still running.
findings.interpretation: The affected task ran through BaseHTTPMiddleware into the background _sleep call, where it received cancellation. The linked fix removed that downstream cancellation.
findings.limits: Verified with the supplied middleware and a local connection.

cases.title: A Kotlin exception after delay omits secondCall from the JVM stack

findings.observation: In the reporter’s JUnit method, the exception stack showed crashCall after resumption but omitted secondCall, so the original assertion failed.
findings.interpretation: The same Job’s continuation chain retained secondCall and firstCall. Using the reporter’s scoped crashCall restored both callers in the ordinary exception stack and made the assertion pass. The throwing continuation belongs to the same BlockingCoroutine Job created by the test’s runBlocking call.
findings.limits: Ran the public test on Kotlin 1.4.31 and kotlinx.coroutines 1.4.3. The original versions and production futures chain were unspecified.

cases.title: Optimized Android builds lose the coroutine await site

findings.observation: The D8 debug build showed worker.await() at line 27, while the optimized build retained only the I/O-side throw and scheduling frames.
findings.interpretation: With debugging on, line 27 returned only when both the forced-false getter rules were removed and continuation metadata and label fields were preserved.
findings.limits: This feature request supplied no production APK or rules. The local Android test establishes the behavior of that configuration.

cases.title: Kotlin’s recovered coroutine stack can omit a caller after suspension

findings.observation: The 2017 example lost the call site for xxx() after delay(100). A separate 2020 Android test omitted a, which tail-called b.
findings.interpretation: Adding an unreached yield() after b(x) restored a at line 18 in the Android debug stack, supporting the maintainer’s tail-call explanation for the 2020 case. Neither release build showed a recovery boundary.
findings.limits: Two public examples with incomplete device and build details. The earlier issue closure confirmed only the named throwing function in the 2017 example.

cases.title: Optimized Clang builds omit coroutine-frame debug information

findings.observation: Clang 18.1.8 emitted four __coro_frame variables and one frame type at -O0, but the variable was absent from both IR and ELF at -O1, -O2 and -O3.
findings.interpretation: At -O2 the promise had only dbg.assign and both declaration lookups failed. Disabling assignment tracking yielded a dbg.declare match and restored the ELF frame type, with identical machine code at each paired optimization level.
findings.limits: The closing patch addressed debugger access inside a resume function. Its parent already emitted the type, unlike Clang 18.

cases.title: Optimized coroutine code reuses the thread ID from before suspension

findings.observation: After cross-thread resumption, all six -O0 runs read the current thread and all six runs at each of -O1, -O2, and -O3 printed the original thread ID. All 24 same-thread controls were correct.
findings.interpretation: Early CSE reused the first pthread_self() value for the second call, and the final binary saved that value in the coroutine frame and reloaded it on resumption.
findings.limits: The Linux test used an equivalent program with a joined worker and an independently held frame. Logs, GDB, IR, and the binary supplied distinct pieces of evidence.

cases.title: A Nest TCP event error reaches a Subject with no subscribers

findings.observation: The original TCP event program sent its exception to a Subject with zero observers.
findings.interpretation: The trace followed evtRpc through the exception filter to Subject.error, where the subscriber count explained why no observer reported it.
findings.limits: Used a local port. The Kafka branch of the related PR was untested.

cases.title: An async error stack omits the caller shown by the generator

findings.observation: On Node 7.7.3 the reporter’s async error stack contained only functionOne, while the corresponding generator stack also showed functionTwo.
findings.interpretation: At the same throw site, both V8 debugger runs with async tracking recovered functionTwo at line 9, and both runs without tracking omitted it.
findings.limits: Linux x64 replaced the reporter’s Windows 7 x64 system. The async parent frames came from V8 and did not identify the originating Promise object.

cases.title: A stack captured after sleep omits the function that started sub

findings.observation: In the original Node 18 example, sub printed a stack after sleep that omitted main.
findings.interpretation: The creation stack for the same Promise recovered the line in main that started sub.
findings.limits: This identifies the initiator of one call. main did not await sub.

cases.title: An empty stdout write adds a tick frame to an assertion stack

findings.observation: The original program showed processTicksAndRejections between test and assert in the assertion stack.
findings.interpretation: The empty stdout write created a TickObject, and removing the write changed that async boundary.
findings.limits: Tested with the report’s first code sample on Node 18.20.8.

cases.title: An indirect call hides the async caller in Node’s default stack

findings.observation: The original Node program lost its higher-level async caller after an indirect call.
findings.interpretation: Promise creation records recovered main → indirectCall → foo, identifying the application call path that the default stack omitted.
findings.limits: The V8 issue did not establish an internal cause, and the recorded chain does not identify an optimizer mechanism.

cases.title: A Node DNS error omits the awaiting read call

findings.observation: On Node 22.2.0, all three ordinary runs and all three runs with native async stacks enabled reported ENOTFOUND without the application’s read call on line 10.
findings.interpretation: In all three traced runs, CoroPerf matched the socket error to the rejection of the same read Promise and recovered its application call on line 10. In all three wrapped controls, AggregateError printed the same line.
findings.limits: The report used Windows x64. The Linux x64 run used the same Node release, the local resolver, and a probe that returned the original Promise.

cases.title: An instrumented Spring/MySQL request stalls on the affected JDK

findings.observation: The original Spring/JPA, MySQL and OpenTelemetry application stalled on the affected JDK and returned HTTP 200 on the fixed JDK.
findings.interpretation: A core dump linked the MySQL read to the virtual thread’s onPinned path and a native thread in transition, while uninstrumented HTTP requests independently confirmed the stall.
findings.limits: Identifying the VM transition required a HotSpot core dump and Serviceability Agent inspection.

cases.title: A Quarkus request pinned in Hibernate while waiting on PostgreSQL

findings.observation: Three delayed REST inserts pinned a Quarkus virtual thread with the pooled-lo optimizer, and the paired none controls recorded no pins. Every request returned 201 and a separate SQL query confirmed the row. PostgreSQL reported a nextval relation-lock wait in all six runs.
findings.interpretation: The selected probe wrapped Quarkus's existing factory, recording the child JDK thread ID before start and the real request dispatch stack. The same thread ID owned the JFR pin sample through PooledLoOptimizer.generate and the JDBC read. Retaining the original factory preserved the virtual-thread name. Disabling the optimizer removed the pin.
findings.limits: This restores the creation stack for the Quarkus example published after the specific Hibernate report. The reporter's production deployment was unavailable. The optimizer comparison holds the same driver, JVM and database constant.

cases.title: Asyncio shutdown stalls during subprocess cleanup

findings.observation: After a subprocess started normally, immediate asyncio shutdown failed to finish within the observation window.
findings.interpretation: Shutdown cancelled a Task during pipe setup, leaving the whoami subprocess path waiting in transport cleanup, consistent with the upstream duplicate.
findings.limits: The replay used the simplified upstream program and ended the process at a bounded timeout.

cases.title: Recovering the creator and the current waiter of a sleeping asyncio task

findings.observation: The four functions in the upstream example returned 42 after a ten-second wait on CPython 3.12.4 and 3.14.3. At entry to f4, the physical stack included f4 and f3. The parent task was waiting in f2. In a second experiment, two consumers awaited each other’s submitted tasks. Both children ran the same code and returned 42.
findings.interpretation: coroPerf matched two suspended samples of each child to its creation by task generation and coroutine object. In the original example the creation points to f2, where ensure_future schedules f3. In the crossed experiment, from_west created the child that read_east awaited. The other child had the reverse pairing. CPython 3.14 independently reported each current waiter and its frames.
findings.limits: The issue requests an async call graph. The crossed-task experiment is a local control. Current waiting relationships came from CPython’s task waiter pointers and, on 3.14, asyncio.capture_call_graph. The coroPerf creation records identify who scheduled each task.

cases.title: A Ray Serve request stays pending after a lock is released

findings.observation: With the reporter’s await order, a Ray 2.47.1 request remained pending after another event loop released the lock.
findings.interpretation: The lock, ActorReplicaResult and loop identities located the cross-loop release, with reversed await order and a newer release as controls.
findings.limits: Local Ray Serve deployment. The comparison did not measure general throughput.

cases.title: Cancelling release leaves Redis and its client disagreeing about a lock

findings.observation: After release was cancelled, Redis still held the lock although the original client considered its ownership lost.
findings.interpretation: The client cleared the token before the actual release. Comparing lock state and retry outcomes on the affected and fixed versions distinguished the two steps.
findings.limits: The replay used the upstream function snippet and a private Redis instance.

cases.title: A Tokio trace exposes a task’s lifecycle

findings.observation: The Tokio example recorded task creation, polling and exit.
findings.interpretation: The trace illustrates the task visibility requested in the proposal.
findings.limits: The upstream observability user story supplied no incident program.

cases.title: A Seastar generator’s waiter chain leads back to the same task

findings.observation: The upstream generator regression encountered the same task again while traversing waiters, and the fixed test completed.
findings.interpretation: The affected getter returned its own task pointer. The fixed getter returned a different task. The affected reference and stripped runs timed out, while the affected queue-control run and both fixed runs completed.
findings.limits: Only the waiter-chain cycle was checked. The separate early-yield initialization path was not tested.

cases.title: A nested-JAR initialization stack also occurs on healthy requests

findings.observation: The reported dump showed one virtual thread waiting for the JAR monitor and another for class initialization, while all four sets of sequential HTTP requests succeeded in the local static-resource app.
findings.interpretation: The local virtual thread returned normally through MediaTypeFactory initialization and NestedJarFile.hasEntry. The sole JAR address in the original dump did not identify a lock owner.
findings.limits: The production app was unavailable and entered through an MVC converter. The static-resource replay does not establish a deadlock.

cases.title: Cancellation during async connection cleanup leaves a pool checkout outstanding

findings.observation: On SQLAlchemy 1.4.37, cancelling the original async exit path left a real PostgreSQL connection checked out.
findings.interpretation: Pool checkout and return records placed cancellation between __aexit__ and close and provided a comparison with the shielded fix. The same Task created by main borrowed the connection and received cancellation during close. The pool recording identifies its checked-out connection.
findings.limits: The only change to the original workload was the private PostgreSQL address.

cases.title: A local activity queued at the heartbeat deadline can leave a workflow waiting

findings.observation: In all five old-SDK runs, the workflow waited on its second Promise, the service history recorded only the first local activity, and the workflow eventually timed out.
findings.interpretation: The handler reported one pending activity, none outstanding and no follow-up task. Applying only the #1295 handler patch to 1.13.0 reversed those counts, requested another task and completed all five runs.
findings.limits: The upstream JUnit case used the official test service’s virtual clock. Run IDs linked stacks and histories. The CLI did not automatically flag the long wait.

cases.title: A spawned task remains in the local LIFO slot when its worker blocks

findings.observation: In the eager-dispatch workload, another worker did not steal the task from the LIFO slot, and the task timed out after its spawning worker blocked.
findings.interpretation: Scheduler records linked schedule_local, slot placement, the blocked worker and the child’s first poll, with normal scheduling and a disabled LIFO slot as controls.
findings.limits: The bounded replay used Tokio source probes. It covered the scheduler mechanism rather than the full production workload.

cases.title: A Next.js render error hides the App Router component hierarchy

findings.observation: After the original development app threw, its physical render stack omitted the parent App Router components.
findings.interpretation: CoroPerf recovered the React owner chain Home → AsyncComponent → ThrowingComponent in all six throws across three instrumented runs. The control with owner links disabled recovered zero complete chains across six throws. Source observations independently checked each ownership link.
findings.limits: The comparison measures JSX ownership in the React development renderer. The original application and dependencies are pinned to Next.js 15.1.4 and React 19.0.0.

cases.title: Mongoose validation errors lose the caller across nextTick

findings.observation: Reading length on a missing nickname produced a stack beginning in the nextTick callback, while a valid nickname passed validation.
findings.interpretation: The old stack reached validateNickname from _tickCallback but omitted the code that called doc.validate. The longjohn control showed additional asynchronous history.
findings.limits: Node 0.10 callback stacks only. The run did not access a database or link the native stack to the caller.

cases.title: Awaiting a Mongoose query can hide the Express caller

findings.observation: An invalid ObjectId produced a CastError without the getCat route frame when the handler awaited the query directly, while explicit exec() restored the frame.
findings.interpretation: The graph linked getCat’s await to the Query.then → Query.exec casting path, and a valid ObjectId on the same route returned an empty result.
findings.limits: MongoDB 6.0.3 was connected, but the cast failed on the client.

cases.title: Mongoose validation errors lose the application’s save call

findings.observation: The original ValidationError on 8.12.1 omitted runDemo’s doc.save line, while 9.0.0 retained it and passed all 15 upstream stack assertions versus 3 on the older version.
findings.interpretation: The creation stack connected runDemo line 22 to validation through model.save and its pre-save hooks, although the error itself had only four frames and began at Document.invalidate.
findings.limits: The old printer could already show the caller. Tests used a separate database and a 20-frame limit. The version comparison spans multiple changes.

cases.title: A Mongoose validation error omits the application call site

findings.observation: Creating a document with a field below its minimum raised ValidationError without the application call site in its ordinary stack.
findings.interpretation: On 8.17.1, the same Promise linked createUnit’s model.create call to the failed minimum check in Document.invalidate, while a valid document was written successfully.
findings.limits: The error came from model validation. The successful write only checked the MongoDB data path.

cases.title: A MongoDB write error loses its application call site

findings.observation: An uninstrumented local duplicate-key write showed only driver and receive frames, matching the report’s 14 file positions in order on two historical Node versions.
findings.interpretation: Moving the conflict to the other write moved the error reply from request 1 to request 2. Wire IDs and callback identity traced the latter to writeFromImport at line 11.
findings.limits: The report omitted the operation, error code and caller. Per-request attribution required local protocol and queue probes. The generic agent saw only the shared socket.

cases.title: Awaiting a Mongoose query hides the ObjectId cast caller

findings.observation: Directly awaiting a query with an invalid ObjectId produced a cast error whose stack omitted the application call site.
findings.interpretation: The promise creation stack showed Query.then calling exec internally, while calling exec explicitly on the same input exposed the application stack.
findings.limits: Casting happened before the driver could send a database query.

cases.title: Axios drops the caller when V8 limits the stack to two frames

findings.observation: With the V8 stack limit set to two, Axios captured requestFromNamedCaller but omitted it from the reported error. Version 1.21.1 preserved it in the same script.
findings.interpretation: A debugger showed that short-stack deduplication treated an empty suffix as a duplicate and discarded the captured caller.
findings.limits: Used the report’s custom adapter. The debugger supplied the key observation, and the graph contains no Promise parent edge for that breakpoint.

cases.title: Axios errors hide which application call issued a request

findings.observation: Two awaited GETs to the same local billing route returned HTTP 500, and both errors matched the report’s seven frames while omitting both application callers.
findings.interpretation: The creation stacks at axios.get, matched through Promise, Error, and ClientRequest identities to the server receipts, distinguished the two callers.
findings.limits: Axios 0.19.0 and Node 12.6.0 were inferred from frame locations. A separate probe established object identity.

cases.title: AxiosError instances lack a stack property in 0.27.0

findings.observation: Two real HTTP 400 responses produced errors without a stack property in 0.27.0, while the same input produced stacks in 0.26.1 and 0.28.0.
findings.interpretation: V8 showed the property was already missing immediately after Error.call(this) in the AxiosError constructor, consistent with the upstream diagnosis.
findings.limits: Checked on Node/V8 using constructor breakpoints and application observations.

cases.title: Axios omits the awaiting caller from a connection error

findings.observation: In the reporter’s script, Axios 1.0.0 serialized the loopback connection refusal without line 4 of main, while 1.21.1 retained that line.
findings.interpretation: The affected Promise’s creation stack contained line 4, but the error sample’s direct identity link led to the catch registered on line 8.
findings.limits: The closing comment covered HTTP status errors. The first release to fix this connection-refusal case was not established.

cases.title: Axios reports a generic browser network error

findings.observation: The XHR error object said Network Error, while the browser’s separate network event recorded ERR_EMPTY_RESPONSE. HTTP 404 and 200 were also tested.
findings.interpretation: The exception stack ended at XMLHttpRequest.handleError, consistent with the browser withholding the underlying connection failure from XHR.
findings.limits: The original Sentry session was unavailable, and the browser network event was an independent observation.

cases.title: A failed Knex migration omits the migration filename

findings.observation: migrate:latest printed the reported warning with a stack starting at TableBuilder.toSQL, and after rollback, the devices table was absent and the migration ledger was empty.
findings.interpretation: The graph traced the error from SchemaCompiler.createTable to TableBuilder.toSQL, and V8 breakpoints read an undefined callback both in exports.up and when the same table was compiled.
findings.limits: The test used the maintainer’s invalid argument and PostgreSQL. The original migration and dialect were unpublished. The graph identifies the Bluebird task that logged the error.

cases.title: Await and catch expose different Knex query stacks

findings.observation: With Bluebird long stacks enabled, both missing-table queries returned 42P01, but only the chained catch and rethrow preserved its application query line.
findings.interpretation: The logged continuations traced to test1 line 5 and test2 line 13. The directly awaited error stopped at Builder.Target.then and process._tickCallback, while the catch path retained test2.
findings.limits: Upstream did not confirm a cause. The Linux replay establishes stack visibility, not deliberate truncation by Knex or the maintainer’s Bluebird settings.

cases.title: Awaiting a Knex query drops the caller from its error stack

findings.observation: For the same missing userss table, Bluebird’s then stack retained line 18 of test, while await retained three previous-event sections and lost test.
findings.interpretation: The Promise delivered to unhandledRejection matched its async_hooks creation in test. A separate configuration control restored both caller stacks when the builder’s wrapper also enabled asyncStackTraces.
findings.limits: The graph identified the function entry only. The later commenter’s application was unavailable.

cases.title: A misspelled Knex option hides the application call site

findings.observation: With asyncStackTrace set in Knex 0.16.5, a PostgreSQL conversion error omitted the caller. The same 22P02 error showed requestFromApplication with asyncStackTraces, and a valid ID returned data.
findings.interpretation: At saveAsyncStack, V8 showed the singular option was true but the plural option Knex actually reads was undefined.
findings.limits: The breakpoint verified 0.16.5. Another user’s 0.16.3 environment was not tested.

cases.title: An undefined binding hides the Knex query-builder call site

findings.observation: The public route lost its caller during query compilation on both MySQL and PostgreSQL, while wrapper tracing recovered the builder call on line 22 of the published callback.
findings.interpretation: Each rejection mapped to a promise created on line 21 and passed through its dialect’s QueryCompiler.toSQL; valid bindings read back row 17, while invalid bindings sent no target SELECT.
findings.limits: The published SQLite callback used replacement database factories. The private helper and exact PostgreSQL version were unavailable, and replication was not tested.

cases.title: Knex query errors omit the application call site when tracing is off

findings.observation: Two PostgreSQL calls on a public Knex release returned 42P01 without their query call sites when tracing was off. Enabling tracing added the SELECT and ALTER call sites at lines 1317 and 1326.
findings.interpretation: The await continuations and their catch samples identified both callers. Tracing retained the driver stack in originalStack, and changing the pool from 2–10 connections to one left the result unchanged.
findings.limits: The reporter’s SQL, app and tracing settings were unavailable. These calls do not establish a Tarn connection-pool cause.

cases.title: A duplicate-key error loses its caller on Sequelize’s create path

findings.observation: In the reporter’s duplicate-username example, create showed only Query.formatError, Query.run and microtasks, while findOrCreate retained model.save, findOrCreate and the test line.
findings.interpretation: The second create’s task linked the application call at line 9 to the catch at line 11. Plain INSERT formatted the driver error there, while findOrCreate returned it through a SQL wrapper.
findings.limits: This covers the public PostgreSQL example with a minimal local model. The opening post’s length-validation model was unavailable.

cases.title: A foreign-key update error loses the Sequelize model call site

findings.observation: Assigning device 7 to missing user 102 reproduced the foreign-key error and 21 consecutive framework and runtime frames, but the stack showed only the transaction entry and omitted Device.update.
findings.interpretation: MySQL reported 1452/23000 on UPDATE before rollback; adding user 102 allowed commit and readback, while separate promise and error-identity checks distinguished two otherwise identical caller stacks.
findings.limits: The private SQL, route and dependency lock were unavailable. The maintainer’s suggested failure at COMMIT did not occur in this transaction.

cases.title: The callback query API omits the application line from driver errors

findings.observation: A callback-based pool.query returned MySQL error 1054 with only packet-processing frames. The Promise API showed promiseFromApplication for the same query, and SELECT 1 succeeded.
findings.interpretation: The error traveled through Query.execute to Packet.asError. The callback API retained the socket’s allocation site but did not save the individual query call site.
findings.limits: The first query opened the socket. Its creator cannot identify arbitrary later queries on a reused connection.

cases.title: A MySQL query error loses its async caller

findings.observation: Two entry points queried a missing table through the same helper, and neither caller appeared in the affected driver’s native error stack.
findings.interpretation: Separate query promises linked the errors to readAccount and readInvoice, and capturing an Error at query time preserved both callers in the 1.4.0 stacks.
findings.limits: The test used direct promise queries against MySQL 8. The pooled-connection variant was not traced.

cases.title: Got’s HTTPError stack omits the application caller

findings.observation: The public Got test read “ok” with a 200 and then “not found” with a 404. The HTTPError contained only the response callback and Node’s task queue, matching the reported frames.
findings.interpretation: Runtime object matches linked each GET, request, response body and error to its catch. Even on a shared socket, the two calls could be traced separately to viewInvoice and printInvoice.
findings.limits: The reporter supplied a Node 13 stack but no app or command. Cross-stage matches used additional hooks and WeakMap comparisons.

cases.title: Got’s connection timeout stack omits the downloader’s application caller

findings.observation: Across two runs, only the download with the 200 ms connection budget failed, and all 13 error frames matched the report after path normalization while omitting the SDK and application callers.
findings.interpretation: Promise identities and the active timer identified the local caller and connect-phase abort, and switching the 200 ms and 2,000 ms budgets moved the failure to the other caller.
findings.limits: The test used a published Electron downloader with locally chosen call sites. The original dependencies, domain setup, and timeout source were unavailable.

cases.title: A refused Got request omits the top-level await call site

findings.observation: The reporter’s compiled top-level await program exited with code 1, and the refusal stack pointed to Got core/index.js:792 without an application line.
findings.interpretation: The request creation stack retained compiled line 2, corresponding to source line 3, while Node reported the uncaught error through the ESM loader’s task.
findings.limits: The public example ran locally. No direct Promise edge linked request creation to the exit diagnostic, and the private service was unavailable.

cases.title: MySQL’s duplicate-key error loses the TypeORM insert caller

findings.observation: When MySQL rejected a second insert with the same primary key, the old QueryFailedError stack began at Query.onResult and omitted myNamedFunction1234.
findings.interpretation: The upstream regression linked the error to the named function’s returned promise, and throwing from query’s catch restored InsertQueryBuilder.execute and the second insert’s call site. The sampled stack is the rejected Promise’s saved error stack, read in Chai’s callback. The callback’s execution ID is separate from the Promise ID.
findings.limits: The public regression used a duplicate key. Both builds returned 1062/23000 and retained the original row; promise identity was verified for the test function.

cases.title: TypeORM’s SQL Server error stack starts in the query runner

findings.observation: On TypeORM 0.3.24, a NULL for a required integer column returned SQL Server error 515 (EREQUEST) with a stack starting at SqlServerQueryRunner.js:204. A valid write was independently read back.
findings.interpretation: Promise identities connected each runner.query rejection and its await continuation to the originating importOrders or refreshCatalog call, even though both used the same SQL and produced the same error.
findings.limits: The reporter’s Nest app and schema were unavailable. Two local callers exercised the reported versions, driver, query pattern and constraint. The intervals use V8’s Promise init and settlement notifications on the same Node clock. A second hook captured the rethrow stack during the settlement notification.

cases.title: A TypeORM query error stack ends at the Promise wrapper

findings.observation: The TypeORM error stack stopped at the wrapper when PostgreSQL rejected “select * foo” with SQLSTATE 42601 on that connection. The control query “select 1 as ok” returned 1.
findings.interpretation: Breakpoints showed the application query entering PostgresQueryRunner.query’s __awaiter and the error returning through the generator’s rejection branch, consistent with the upstream explanation.
findings.limits: The breakpoints captured the Promise wrapper but supplied no async parent edge.

cases.title: Objection’s QueryBuilder loses application callers from async error stacks

findings.observation: Two application callers disappeared from native exceptions raised by failing QueryBuilder queries. Healthy queries against the same PostgreSQL server each returned one row.
findings.interpretation: At the custom thenable boundary, the identities of the two query objects linked their application creation sites to the corresponding rejections in handleExecuteError.
findings.limits: The links came from a dedicated WeakMap probe and establish query-object identity only.

cases.title: Protractor’s async wait loses the helper’s call site

findings.observation: With Selenium’s promise manager disabled, the 10-second wait failed without the helper in its stack, while skipping the wait exposed the helper in the failed click.
findings.interpretation: The helper was visible when the wait was registered, the condition was still false after 10 seconds, and enabling the promise manager restored the helper frame.
findings.limits: The report omitted the full configuration and lockfile. The test used ES5, ts-node 3.3.0 and a locally proxied page.

cases.title: The async test macro changes wrapper line numbers

findings.observation: Both outer wrapper frames pointed to line 1 in the macro test, compared with lines 4 and 3 in its expanded equivalent.
findings.interpretation: Closer to the panic, the full traces still identified the assertion at 4:5 and 5:9 respectively, so the wrapper excerpt alone did not establish a lost assertion site.
findings.limits: The original application was unavailable, and its author withdrew the macro-specific attribution. Both should_panic tests passed as expected.

cases.title: Recovering suspended Asio callers after a timer resumes

findings.observation: When a timer resumed async_c, the physical stack ran through the scheduler, but GDB could still follow caller_ from async_c through async_b to co_spawn_entry_point.
findings.interpretation: The saved caller chain recovered the suspended calls, and a detached boundary would require a separate creation record.
findings.limits: The timer experiment did not run Silkworm. Its original message stream, cancellation order, exact revision, and macOS arm64 build were unavailable.

cases.title: Async Zod validation errors omit the caller

findings.observation: Both 3.5.0 and 3.5.1 reproduced the full invalid_arguments result and all six reported file positions without the caller, while each release passed its 12 function tests.
findings.interpretation: A debugger showed the caller in the async parent stack. The proposed fork also restored the test line in the captured error for the same validation test.
findings.limits: The report omitted the caller and lockfile. Both releases match, and the fork was tested only as a comparison.

cases.title: A second async assertion loses the TestCafe caller

findings.observation: In a browser, failing the helper’s second assertion omitted the test-body call site, while failing its first assertion kept it.
findings.interpretation: The promise creation stack still contained myHelper and the test body before the first suspension, locating a point where the caller was observable.
findings.limits: The second assertion’s error could not be linked uniquely to a promise, and upstream did not establish why the frame was lost.

cases.title: NativeAOT omits a non-inlined Task forwarder from an exception stack

findings.observation: After the public program suspended and resumed, NativeAOT printed ThrowAfterResume, Outer and Main, while CoreCLR included Forwarder in both runs.
findings.interpretation: External symbols mapped RVA 0xce097 to Forwarder at line 31 despite hidden ILC metadata. Making the method explicitly async restored its name in the exception text.
findings.limits: The address required external symbolization. No Task identity was recorded, and upstream has not confirmed a root cause or fix.

cases.title: A reverted contract call loses its application call site

findings.observation: Calling f on the reporter’s bytecode on a loopback chain produced an eth_estimateGas revert with reason boom and a CALL_EXCEPTION without the contract call line.
findings.interpretation: The Promise stack showed sendTransaction, sendUncheckedTransaction and estimateGas, matching the failed RPC method. The control bytecode deployed successfully.
findings.limits: Ganache replaced the remote chain. The outermost call was not uniquely linked to the error, and upstream did not confirm why the frame was missing.

cases.title: A dispatch callback’s stack omits the code that submitted it

findings.observation: The async main-queue callback’s physical stack omitted submitFromApplication, which remained visible in the synchronous control.
findings.interpretation: The same block address at dispatch_async submission and callback execution identified the submitter.
findings.limits: The capture used Linux libdispatch. The original UIKit action, Apple build and matching dSYM were unavailable.

cases.title: Panel reports different callback stacks for the same exception

findings.observation: Clicking the original async and sync buttons in a real browser raised the same ValueError through different server callback paths.
findings.interpretation: The async wrapper led to async_on_click at line 7, while the synchronous callback reached sync_on_click at line 10. The affected Task was created as Tornado scheduled Panel’s async wrapper. The same Task produced the async_on_click exception stack.
findings.limits: Server logs already identified both lines. No cross-process Task creation link or final upstream root cause was established.

cases.title: Jest loses the original error stack for an unhandled VM rejection

findings.observation: A test rejected an Error inside the VM, but strict mode ultimately reported only ERR_UNHANDLED_REJECTION, and handling the same rejection avoided a fatal process error.
findings.interpretation: The rejection probe retained the test’s original stack, while the host realm’s instanceof check failed and the fatal listener later saw Node’s replacement error.
findings.limits: The result is specific to the tested Node and Jest versions. VM setup and the fatal-error listener were additional probes.

cases.title: Jest reports stackFormatter instead of the failing request

findings.observation: The reporter’s unmodified spec and locked dependencies printed only “Failed: SyntaxError” and stackFormatter, and the loopback service received no request.
findings.interpretation: XMLHttpRequest.open failed to resolve a relative URL against about:blank, leaving Jasmine without options.error. Changing only testURL made the POST succeed.
findings.limits: The public reproduction used a local service. A separate Jest alpha.7 run identified XMLHttpRequest.open but still omitted the spec line.

cases.title: Jest’s resolves and rejects matchers omit the test line

findings.observation: Two failing async matchers omitted their test locations, while equivalent assertions after a direct await showed the lines.
findings.interpretation: The debugger’s async parent stacks for throwingMatcher led back to test lines 3 and 11, locating the loss at the matcher boundary.
findings.limits: Stacks were sampled at those matchers. Upstream tracked the location fix in #5104.

cases.title: Async Jest assertion errors omit the test line

findings.observation: All three posted examples—resolves, hasAssertions and assertions—failed without showing the user’s test line.
findings.interpretation: The debugger recovered line 16 for resolves. The two count errors were constructed during teardown in extractExpectedAssertionsErrors, while a directly awaited assertion retained its location.
findings.limits: The original registration lines for the two assertion-count checks could not be recovered.

cases.title: Async logger creation shortens the component mounting stack

findings.observation: The old async and new compatibility paths logged three frames each, versus 27 on the synchronous path, but all three retained connectedCallback.
findings.interpretation: Only the synchronous recipe preserved mounting frames such as runConnectedCallback; the reported disappearance of connectedCallback did not recur locally.
findings.limits: Released LWC components ran in Jest/jsdom with an Apex save stub, outside hosted Aura. Two newer recipe tests also failed on an undefined logger.

cases.title: Nested Playwright steps lose the outer page-object method from an assertion stack

findings.observation: The original test failed its color assertion in a real browser, but the ordinary error omitted the outer shouldBeCorrect call.
findings.interpretation: Matching the actual step Promises across three error observations recovered the nested methods, and the upstream await change in raceAgainstDeadline restored the outer call in the native stack. The two inner steps had identical error stacks. The native IDs of their returned Promises identify separate calls on lines 18 and 19.
findings.limits: The page response was deterministic and local. Step ownership was recorded separately from physical callback stacks.

cases.title: A compiled async error omits the calling TypeScript function

findings.observation: Running the upstream ES6 output made fun2 throw “miau,” but the ordinary stack lacked the full fun1 calling context.
findings.interpretation: A debugger captured physical and async parent frames at the generated __awaiter boundary. A separate Bluebird example exposed that boundary through a previous-event stack.
findings.limits: The Bluebird example threw a different error. Its frames and wrapper-construction frequency were not established for the original program.

cases.title: FastOpenAPI returns a 500 without logging the route exception

findings.observation: A loopback request to /2 returned HTTP 500 on both builds, but only rc2 logged the ZeroDivisionError.
findings.interpretation: Samples captured the exception in root_fastopenapi and handle_request_async under _starlette_view, locating the change in the adapter’s error handling. Uvicorn’s handle_events created the ASGI request Task whose sampled stack includes root_fastopenapi.
findings.limits: A single local route tested whether the server logged the exception.

cases.title: Dispatching a PromiseKit callback hides its registration frame

findings.observation: With then on the main queue, the physical stack showed only the closure symbol, while inline execution retained registerFromApplication.
findings.interpretation: The same block was observed at dispatch_async and at callback execution, linking it to a submission stack containing PromiseKit.then and the registration function.
findings.limits: The historical implementation was inspected, but the available run used Linux Swift and PromiseKit 6.18.1. The original iOS project and build settings were unavailable.

cases.title: Errors created in a Node-API completion callback lack the application stack

findings.observation: An Error created in a native async completion callback showed only its message, while the same addon’s synchronous entry showed callFromApplication.
findings.interpretation: async_hooks preserved the application site where the work was created, distinguishing it from the later callback where the Error was constructed.
findings.limits: The original addon variants, inputs, and revision were unavailable. The closing comment still requested a reproducer.

cases.title: Asynchronous file errors omit the JavaScript readFile caller

findings.observation: Callback and Promise reads of a missing file both returned ENOENT without the initiating JavaScript frame, while the synchronous read showed its origin.
findings.interpretation: GDB observed native error construction with execution ID zero, and libuv request addresses and V8 objects linked subsequent delivery to the actual requests.
findings.limits: The reported Node version ran on Linux. No active JavaScript parent was observed at native error creation.

cases.title: Compiled async structlog calls lose the active traceback

findings.observation: The original workload loses the async traceback in the Nuitka 4.1 binary. Nuitka 4.1.1 and interpreted CPython both render the traceback. Passing the active exception explicitly restores it in a separate 4.1 control.
findings.interpretation: At the call on line 115, the exception handler still holds the RuntimeError from line 113. CoroPerf matches the created aexception object and frame to the pre-executor stack. The affected run passes empty exception info. The fixed and explicit controls pass the original RuntimeError.
findings.limits: The trace covers the logger call and executor boundary. The original report used macOS and 4.2rc1. The local comparison uses Linux and the 4.1 release line.

cases.title: An unstarted async generator loses the injected exception’s original traceback

findings.observation: After athrow into an unstarted generator, all three 4.2.2 runs lost make_exception, while all three 4.3 runs retained it.
findings.interpretation: Observing the same exception object and Task at creation and receipt narrowed the loss to the interval between injection and receipt.
findings.limits: Two read-only application probes supplied the enhanced graph. The compiler’s internal branch was not observed.

cases.title: pygls logs an empty traceback for an async notification error

findings.observation: Opening a real JSON file against the v0.10.3 example server produced a diagnostic notification but an empty server traceback for the injected exception in did_open.
findings.interpretation: The completion callback had no current exception, though the Future held did_open’s ZeroDivisionError. Version 0.11.0 logged the handler on the same input, and the original example worked without the injected error. The Task created by _execute_notification threw in did_open. The completion callback received that Task and its coroutine object.
findings.limits: A local LSP client drove the extension server. The VS Code interface was untested.

cases.title: A forgotten-return warning prints without its available stack

findings.observation: The original example printed only the warning message to stderr by default and included call frames with --trace-warnings.
findings.interpretation: The warning event already held an Error stack containing checkForgottenReturns, locating the difference in how Node displayed the warning.
findings.limits: The reported package version ran on Linux rather than Windows. Native Node 6 warning observations did not establish promise ancestry.

cases.title: A Bluebird warning omits the origin of a nested Promise.delay

findings.observation: The reporter’s nested-delay warning omitted its creation site, while 3.4.7 included an additional origin segment.
findings.interpretation: The Promise returned by delay had no _trace, and _warn received that same object. The revised release exposed the delay creation site in the original program.
findings.limits: Node 4 lacked async_hooks. Object matches came from an observer’s WeakMap.

cases.title: Bluebird’s done() changes how a browser reports a rejection

findings.observation: Calling .done() produced an uncaught browser pageerror, while removing it produced an unhandled-rejection console diagnostic with the source.
findings.interpretation: A breakpoint showed the final Promise taking rejectUnchecked’s deferred rethrow branch, and the browser event still contained applicationOrigin.
findings.limits: Chromium 159 reproduced the rethrow. The original page and Chrome build were unavailable, so the 2014 DevTools display could not be verified.

cases.title: A forgotten-return warning loses the fromCallback creation stack

findings.observation: Nested fromCallback calls produced a forgotten-return warning without the corresponding creation stack, while the Promise-constructor control preserved more origin frames.
findings.interpretation: The returned Promise had no _trace, and its identity matched the object later seen in _warn, locating the missing trace on the fromCallback path.
findings.limits: The constructor was a separate control. Imported native stacks did not establish coroutine identity.

cases.title: Puppeteer’s Target closed error omits the application caller

findings.observation: Across four repetitions, the selector-timeout stack included the user function, while evaluate after an explicit browser close produced a Target closed stack without it.
findings.interpretation: In both instrumented runs, the same Error object led back to the Promise returned by Page.evaluate, whose creation stack identified puppeteerTargetClosedError at line 5.
findings.limits: Used the original script with a Linux headless launcher. The match relied on object identity, and upstream did not confirm a mechanism.

cases.title: Puppeteer’s selector timeout shows only timer frames

findings.observation: After successful HTTP navigation, a missing selector timed out at 500 ms and the reporter’s handler exited with status 1, while the matching local page printed Done.
findings.interpretation: At the timeout, V8’s immediate async parent stack contained waitForSelector and main on line 21, recovering the application caller missing from the error.
findings.limits: The test used Puppeteer 0.10.1 and local pages. The 2017 external page and the reporter’s macOS build were unavailable.

cases.title: Awaiting wait_closed rewrites the original read traceback

findings.observation: After a loopback connection reset interrupted readexactly, awaiting wait_closed in the exception handler made the final log point to cleanup.
findings.interpretation: The application confirmed that both awaits raised the same exception object, and skipping only the cleanup await preserved the read traceback.
findings.limits: One connection and one reset sequence were tested. No released framework fix was evaluated.

cases.title: Resuming a coroutine with throw() shortens its traceback

findings.observation: CPython 3.10.4 showed four frames on normal entry but only two while handling throw(). 3.14.3 showed four in both cases.
findings.interpretation: Matching the same live c frame before and after injection showed the call chain change from a → b → c to b → c at that resumption.
findings.limits: The coroutines were driven directly, outside asyncio tasks. Upstream did not confirm an interpreter-level cause.

cases.title: Identical Trio socket-read frames obscure which child was cancelled

findings.observation: Three runs of the original single-task example retained Cancelled’s implicit context. With two readers at the same line, a parent nursery timeout surfaced at fail_at.
findings.interpretation: Matching each Task and coroutine to its cancellation and creation site identified start_profile or start_catalog correctly in all six captures when the nonresponding side was swapped.
findings.limits: The public issue was a diagnostics discussion. The two-socket nursery was a local extension on historical Trio and Python 3.6.2.

cases.title: Compressed SQLx debug information leaves Rust backtrace frames unresolved

findings.observation: On the reported nightly and mold version, two runs with standard zlib-compressed SQLx debug sections produced “Error: foo” with 21 of 22 frames unknown. Lld and the fixed linker left only one unknown.
findings.interpretation: One sqlx_rt object had outer alignment 8 but declared alignment 1. The old linker inserted two extra bytes before DWARF unit 119, and the runtime resolved the same application address only after the fix.
findings.limits: The source and lockfile were public, but the original linker-input archive returned HTTP 410. The compressed input was rebuilt locally with a different OS and LLD version.
