cases.title: The browser reports a closed connection for a page served with HTTP 200

findings.observation: Both documents in the original project returned 200, yet a real browser reported “Connection closed”. Correcting one HTML delimiter removed the error.
findings.interpretation: The production renderer linked four unexpected HTML values to the h component and request, and response-body and browser parsing checks corroborated the input change.
findings.limits: This was an application-input issue. Browser and server observations were matched by document, and the lockfile differed from the reported React version.

cases.title: Soft async assertions lose their source locations

findings.observation: All ten assertions in the original gist failed as intended, but only five reported source locations on the affected build, compared with all ten after the change.
findings.interpretation: For soft resolves.toEqual, the stack ran from the internal catch to handleTestError. The Promise.then parent repeats at generated position 31:72. The loaded source map from that repeat resolves it to repro.test.ts:40:50 on the soft assertion. Ordinary resolves reports its source line directly.
findings.limits: The full suite established the counts. The execution graph covered one soft assertion.

cases.title: A GopherLua coroutine error omits the Go stack

findings.observation: With IncludeGoStackTrace enabled, coroutine.resume returned only the diagnostic marker, while a direct call included a Go stack.
findings.interpretation: At the VM’s threadRun recovery branch, the debugger showed coResume, callGFunction and diagnosticMarker, locating the Go call before the error became text.
findings.limits: Used a benign diagnostic marker. The original embedded host and Lua script were unavailable, and the #539 change was reviewed.

cases.title: Dartium reports a two-frame error when opening a WAV file

findings.observation: The original app on Dartium r34591 reported “Error must not be null” with exactly two frames for a valid GSM 6.10 WAV, while PCM and A-law versions of the same tone played.
findings.interpretation: The entry stack showed onFileRead calling parseArrayBuffer, but the later error showed only an AudioContext callback and _AsyncCompleter.completeError; the single submission linked the observations.
findings.limits: The original WAV and Editor screenshot were unavailable. Its encoding is unknown, and no cross-callback edge was captured.

cases.title: Dart compiler stack loss remains unexplained

findings.observation: The original package compiled system.dart and hello_test.dart into 23 and seven commands, and a healthy VM breakpoint showed both reported code-generation lines.
findings.interpretation: The VM debugger recovered codegenFunction:113 and its caller codegen:96, and a controlled unsupported-function error retained the generator stack both with and without catchError.
findings.limits: The original noSuchMethod input, checkout, and VM build were unknown. Generated Fletch code was not executed.

cases.title: An awaited socket error loses its source line and column

findings.observation: The upstream loopback Socket.connect regression failed on 1.21.1 with no location in its first frame and passed on 1.24.0 with main:12:5.
findings.interpretation: A refused connection in the related socket test likewise had no location on 1.21.1 and pointed to 108:19 on 1.24.0, isolating the source-location change.
findings.limits: The unmodified test from #28315 passed on both versions. Its intermittent SIMMIPS connection failure was not observed on local x64.

cases.title: DDC loses an error from an async generator

findings.observation: DDC 1.24.0 failed to deliver the async* error to its caller while an independent timer kept running, while ordinary async and DDC 2.2.0 async* delivered it.
findings.interpretation: The Node 8 debugger observed onError, throwError and addError, followed by the cancellation callback.
findings.limits: The replay used compiled output from the original example. Cancellation and error delivery were separate breakpoint observations.

cases.title: Dart’s debugger pauses at the wrong await under optimization

findings.observation: At optimization threshold 5, the original Observatory test paused at caught line 29 instead of uncaught line 34 in all three runs on each of two development builds.
findings.interpretation: The VM Service stack led through doThrow and asyncThrower to testeeMain at line 29. The default threshold stopped at line 34, and Dart 2.1.0 passed all three low-threshold runs.
findings.limits: The parent and child VMs ran together. The inlining explanation comes from the upstream fix. The original CI build and failure rate are unknown.

cases.title: A Dart AOT error trace yields two frames instead of ten

findings.observation: With the reporter’s initial review patch, the Linux x64 AOT test on 2.8.1 reported “Expected 10 frames, found 2.”
findings.interpretation: The lone DWARF instruction address resolved to throwSync and inlined allYield3, while symbolic output included allYield2; the final upstream regression failed on 2.8.1 and passed on 2.9.3.
findings.limits: Upstream gave no commit hash. The fix was verified with the merged regression because other assertions in the initial test also differed.

cases.title: A Dart timer callback disappears from the stack after an await

findings.observation: In the reporter’s console example, the synchronous stack showed handleTimeout calling nonAsyncFunc. After resumption it showed only func1 or func1 and func2.
findings.interpretation: Sampling before and after resumption narrowed down where handleTimeout disappeared from the visible stack.
findings.limits: The two console snapshots could not be linked to a single Flutter click.

cases.title: Dart’s browser error stack omits two awaiting callers

findings.observation: In the browser, the DDC-compiled program’s error stack omitted test1 and main even though each awaited the next call.
findings.interpretation: At the same Chromium exception pause, the debugger’s async parent stack recovered both callers, and ordinary page output and the Dart VM showed different caller coverage.
findings.limits: The run used cached DDC 2.18.2 output and explicitly enabled browser debugging.

cases.title: Pausing a Flutter startup wait yields no Dart frames

findings.observation: On Android API 34, the reporter’s Kotlin Activity reached the controlled Dart main, but manual pauses showed zero frames with either one or two Futures waiting.
findings.interpretation: Registration logs linked waitAlpha and waitBeta to main. Releasing A left B pending, and releasing B allowed the first frame to render.
findings.limits: Only part of the Dart app was public. The reported intermittent startup failure lacked the main-entry log seen here, so its blocking point remains unknown.

cases.title: A missing-file stream error omits its caller

findings.observation: When file aaa was absent, the stack from openRead().listen().asFuture() omitted the first user call, while the read succeeded when the file existed.
findings.interpretation: VM Service captured the same execution in _FileStream._start.openFailed, StreamController.addError and the asFuture error handler.
findings.limits: The original read ran on 3.5.3 and 3.14.0. The internal breakpoint graph came from 3.14.0.

cases.title: A Dart interceptor stack cannot distinguish two feature callers

findings.observation: In 3.5.3, both featureA and featureB produced an interceptor stack showing the testFuture closure without identifying which feature called it.
findings.interpretation: The stack reached the closure through CInterceptor.onRequest, Future.forEach and doWhile. 3.14.0 restored a separate testFuture await frame but still omitted both feature entry points.
findings.limits: The two features ran separately. The affected stack identifies the Future boundary only.

cases.title: Optimized Dart Wasm omits the throwing async function

findings.observation: In a real browser, the Wasm exception stack omitted the original async function at -O2 and retained it at -O0.
findings.interpretation: The loaded binary’s source map resolved the -O2 offset 0x4878 to the SDK’s async_patch, while -O0 and dart2js retained application source locations.
findings.limits: The test used a Dart 3.14.0 sample and did not identify the optimization pass responsible.

cases.title: A Flutter integration test loses the test caller after a delay

findings.observation: The unmodified integration test and host driver both reported err1 with only throwErr1:8 in the stack.
findings.interpretation: Removing the delay on the same Flutter 2.2.3 engine restored the test closure at line 15. Removing the throw made the same test pass.
findings.limits: Ran the public driver and app on Flutter’s Linux test device. The reporter used an iOS 14.5 simulator.

cases.title: Bun’s error stack omits the module awaiting a rejected Promise

findings.observation: When the original module’s closure threw, the ordinary stack omitted its top-level awaiter, and a split-line control on 1.2.22 retained two named awaiters.
findings.interpretation: One debugger pause showed where the work was created, and another caught the module executing await pending, distinguishing creation from consumption.
findings.limits: The split-line program was an attribution control. The two sites came from separate pauses. The original also ran on 1.1.2.

cases.title: An error thrown by throwIfAborted lacks a stack

findings.observation: On Bun 1.2.4 the exception from AbortSignal.throwIfAborted() had no stack. On 1.4.4 its public stack showed throwIfAborted and application line 3.
findings.interpretation: The Inspector retained the module call site when AbortError was thrown, even on the affected version.
findings.limits: The original script ran on Linux rather than Darwin. The graph contains no internal C++ wrapper frames.

cases.title: Bun drops the caller from a stack after await

findings.observation: In Bun 1.2.4, an ordinary exception stack stopped at the throw after await, while 1.2.22 included the caller.
findings.interpretation: Pausing on the exception showed run in the async parent stack even in the affected version.
findings.limits: Only the reported suspended branch was exercised. Repeated synchronous lines are a separate issue.

cases.title: Reading .stack changes how Bun displays a Redis callback error

findings.observation: With the reporter’s error class on Bun 1.2.19, four real Redis messages alternated between 10 and 1 displayed frames. 1.4.4 showed 10 each time.
findings.interpretation: The same error’s .stack string had 10 frames, but Bun.inspect showed only the constructor after that read. Without it, handleMessageReply and the Redis decoder remained visible.
findings.limits: The original app, messages and lockfile were unavailable. The replay did not identify the intermittent reader or reproduce the reported change of error name.

cases.title: A Bun timeout can leave the caught error’s stack empty

findings.observation: A related attachment produced an empty stack with a 1 ms deadline in both source and standalone builds, while the same loopback request returned HTTP 200 with two seconds.
findings.interpretation: A separate stack taken in catch identified only src/Main.ts:11:68, and the Kubernetes client succeeded twice without an explicit deadline, leaving the original intermittent timeout unexplained.
findings.limits: The original CLI, source map, request and dependencies were unavailable. The attachment came from a different issue.

cases.title: Bun’s PostgreSQL syntax error has no stack in the affected release

findings.observation: Bun 1.2.20 passed its own syntax-error test on PostgreSQL 14. A valid query returned 1, while the invalid query returned SQLSTATE 42601 with an undefined stack.
findings.interpretation: A separate Promise catch exposed its callback stack, and the earlier graph showed onRejectPostgresQuery. Version 1.4.4 supplied a one-line message but failed the old test’s SyntaxError type assertion.
findings.limits: The reporter’s query, schema and application code were unavailable. The test’s error location differed from the reported VALUES position.

cases.title: Bun omits the awaiting module when a then callback throws

findings.observation: On Bun 1.3.0, a throw inside a then callback produced an error stack without the module awaiting the Promise.
findings.interpretation: An exception pause in the same execution showed unwrap, promiseReactionJob, and the module’s then call site.
findings.limits: The linked PR ran this example and supplied the explanation, but it was never merged.

cases.title: AsyncLocalStorage.run hides callers in Bun’s error stack

findings.observation: Bun 1.3.1 printed only fn3 inside AsyncLocalStorage.run, while the same program retained more frames outside it.
findings.interpretation: Pausing on the second exception recovered fn2, fn1 and the callback inside the store, locating the visibility change at the context boundary alongside the 1.3.14 control.
findings.limits: The debugger supplied the JavaScript parent stack. The context-wrapper explanation comes from upstream source.

cases.title: A fetch timeout produces an empty error stack

findings.observation: With a one-millisecond timeout on Bun 1.3.3, TimeoutError.stack was an empty string, while a healthy request to the same service returned 204.
findings.interpretation: Pausing on the exception located the rejection of the suspended fetch, but did not reveal where the timer allocated the DOMException.
findings.limits: A private HTTP service with a fixed delay replaced the original Google request.

cases.title: Bun drops a caller when an error is thrown after await

findings.observation: In Bun 0.5.9, throwing after await omitted the caller of bBroken from the error stack.
findings.interpretation: On affected version 1.2.4, pausing at the exception recovered cBroken and main. The same script included a synchronous throw for comparison.
findings.limits: The original baseline used 0.5.9. The Inspector graph came from 1.2.4, with 1.4.4 as a version control.

cases.title: Bun’s error stack omits the module-level await

findings.observation: Bun 1.4.4 retained the stack from baz through main but omitted the module’s await main() call.
findings.interpretation: Pausing on the same exception exposed the module through the active and async parent frames, and ordinary Node 24.19.0 output included that location.
findings.limits: The report used a 1.4.0 canary. The missing module frame also overlaps with issue #10483.

cases.title: Bun omits the application stack from a missing-path lstat error

findings.observation: On Bun 0.7.3 and 1.2.20, lstat on a missing path produced an error without an application stack.
findings.interpretation: Pausing at rejection on 1.2.20 showed native lstat, its Promise wrapper and the awaiting main. Version 1.4.4 showed the application line, and creating the directory made 1.2.20 succeed.
findings.limits: Used a local test path, with separate working directories for the existence control and the Inspector run.

cases.title: Bun loses an earlier error stack after a timer wait in catch

findings.observation: On Bun 1.0.0, printing an error after awaiting a timer in catch omitted the original synchronous throw frames, and printing without the delay retained them.
findings.interpretation: Separate debugger pauses captured the throw and the timer ancestry at print time, locating the two events independently.
findings.limits: The pauses do not establish how the Error object lost its stack internally.

cases.title: A shell error omits the line that created the command

findings.observation: Bun 1.0.29 reported #run and then for the posted ShellError but omitted the application line that created the command. 1.1.2 restored line 5.
findings.interpretation: Constructor probes distinguished the ShellPromise created at submission from the ShellError created at consumption. 1.1.2 allocated the error when the command was created.
findings.limits: The main graph uses an additional constructor probe. The uninstrumented script invoked only a nonexistent local program.

cases.title: Which Kotlin caller received the gRPC status exception?

findings.observation: Two separate coroutine Jobs invoked the same generated unary method on one stub. In the simultaneous-failure trial the server received identical protobuf bytes, and both RPCs returned UNAVAILABLE with the description “io exception”. Both original throwables had callback stacks ending at the gRPC client and omitted the application call. Two batches sent 64 real RPCs.
findings.interpretation: The continuation handed to GreeterCoroutineStub.sayHello contained the actual Kotlin Job. Its identity joined the application coroutine’s creation site to the failure at ClientCalls.kt line 295. The independent await checks used JVM reference equality for the throwable. This separated the profile call at MatchedCalls.kt line 11 from the inventory call at line 15, including when both calls carried the same message and the server reversed its reply order.
findings.limits: The service deliberately emitted the reported status over a real localhost HTTP/2 connection. The report supplied no application or version lock. These traces answer the caller and generated-method questions. Determining the underlying cause of a production network failure requires additional transport or server evidence.

cases.title: A suspending tail call disappears after a dispatcher switch

findings.observation: After switching dispatchers, the exception stack omitted callThrowableSuspendFun in the affected tail-call example.
findings.interpretation: The method was observed calling changeContextAndThrow before the switch, consistent with upstream’s explanation that tail-call optimization removes its state machine.
findings.limits: Tested with Kotlin 1.3.50 and coroutines 1.3.3, using tail and non-tail calls with debugging on and off.

cases.title: Two awaiters receive the producer’s exception stack

findings.observation: Two coroutines awaiting the same CompletableDeferred received the same producer-created exception with identical producer frames and neither await site.
findings.interpretation: The actual Job distinguished the two consumers and linked them to importOrders line 15 and refreshCatalog line 18 even when startup order was reversed.
findings.limits: The reporter had omitted debug mode and supplied no application or versions. The two-waiter scenario was a local control.

cases.title: Kotlin Future bridges lose the caller of a failed request

findings.observation: Two of the six original JUnit tests failed both with and without capture. All six passed after DebugProbes was installed.
findings.interpretation: Job creation and completion records tied the two requestSuspend failures to their respective async and launch callers, the locations DebugProbes recovered. The collector and an independent continuation probe agreed on each failed Job and throwable for the async and launch cases.
findings.limits: The replay used the original compiled test classpath and covered these two Future bridges.

cases.title: Sending to a closed callbackFlow can yield a frameless cancellation

findings.observation: After flatMapLatest switched flows, sending through the old wrapper produced a zero-frame ChildCancelledException with debug off, while the new wrapper delivered 9 to the active channel.
findings.interpretation: ART traced the stale send to Closed.getSendException; with debug on, removing just two R8 rules changed the trace from zero to 24 frames and exposed the coroutine name.
findings.limits: The Android Activity used version 1.4.2 and locally controlled callback timing. The original app and effective shrinker rules were unavailable.

cases.title: Reported iOS coroutine stack loss does not reproduce on Linux

findings.observation: On Linux, both immediate throws and throws after suspension retained 18 frames on versions 1.5.0 and 1.5.2.
findings.interpretation: The Service throw frame survived suspension in all four controls, leaving the reported iOS version difference unexplained.
findings.limits: The attachment had an Xcode project and an arm64 framework but no launchable app. This Linux host lacked an iOS toolchain.

cases.title: Android omits the fatal stack for UnknownHostException

findings.observation: All four UnknownHostException runs logged just two fatal lines, while all eight NullPointerException and IOException controls logged 27 frames pointing back to MainActivity.kt.
findings.interpretation: The platform logger took the early exit at Log.java:447 for UnknownHostException and reached printStackTrace at line 457 for both controls. System records independently confirmed process death.
findings.limits: Tested on the author’s demo and an API 31 image. The reporter’s device build was unknown, and debugger breakpoints paused the main thread.

cases.title: Stack recovery misses a suspend API’s await site

findings.observation: With assertions and debug off, the maintainer’s JVM example showed doWork at line 6 and the worker at line 15, but omitted the API await at line 18 and runBlocking at line 27.
findings.interpretation: The worker belonged to the API singleton’s Job while runBlocking awaited it. Adding code after await produced an API state machine, allowing debug recovery to show line 18.
findings.limits: The reporter’s Android snippet omitted two functions, and no original APK or mapping was available. Job ownership was verified in the maintainer’s JVM example.

cases.title: Nested suspend callers disappear from the exception stack

findings.observation: The uncaught exception in the JVM example omitted the nested callers f1 and f.
findings.interpretation: Following the continuation from the resumed f2 recovered both missing callers, independently of the separate Deferred.await exception-identity question.
findings.limits: The original nested-suspension example was tested. The separate concurrent Flow case was outside scope.

cases.title: Ktor loses the bar caller when a pipeline resumes

findings.observation: The reporter’s JUnit test omitted bar on a direct call but retained it with withContext(IO) on both 1.2.4 and 1.3.0, and both paths threw as intended.
findings.interpretation: The direct call still showed bar on first entering barInternal, but only the continuation remained on resumption, and both releases passed their two official stack-walking tests.
findings.limits: The report named master, and the closing comment identified no fix commit or fixed release.

cases.title: Enhanced exceptions filter out the application’s require call

findings.observation: Enabling enhanced exceptions in Cats Effect 2.2.0 removed the application origin of a failed require.
findings.interpretation: IORunLoop.dropRunLoopFrames received 20 frames starting with Predef.require and the application’s foo but returned an empty array, consistent with upstream’s finding that the filter included the entire scala package.
findings.limits: The same program ran with enhancement on and off in 2.2.0 and 2.3.1. The probe captured the actual input and returned frames.

cases.title: Four waiting Cats Effect fibers have no application frames

findings.observation: The real Play service’s /dump/fibers endpoint returned four WAITING system fibers without business frames.
findings.interpretation: All four traced to tasks that Dispatcher launched through GenSpawn.background, supporting the upstream system-fiber hypothesis.
findings.limits: The replay used Play 2.8.11 and Cats Effect 3.3.0. The rule that omitted the frames remains unconfirmed.

cases.title: A second timeout points to the first timeout’s source line

findings.observation: With cached tracing, the one-second timeout on line 9 was reported at line 8.
findings.interpretation: Both calls reused the same trace record because their internal flatMap shared a cache key, matching the upstream explanation.
findings.limits: The replay compared cached and full tracing on the final upstream two-timeout example in 3.5.0-RC5.

cases.title: A ZIO failure trace loses the application’s unsafeRun entry point

findings.observation: On 1.0-RC5, two calls entered unsafeRun on different threads, but after work resumed on a pool thread both ZIO.trace and the failure Cause omitted the initiating method and line.
findings.interpretation: Matching FiberContext identity in the debugger recovered the application line for the failing fiber, and switching which call failed switched the recovered line.
findings.limits: The original app was unavailable. A local two-entry program and external JDI probes identified the root fiber’s entry point. No parent fiber was observed.

cases.title: Five historical stack-trace assertions fail when ZIO yields at every step

findings.observation: Forcing a yield after each operation made 5 of 21 StackTracesSpec assertions fail.
findings.interpretation: The failing runs reached FiberContext.captureTrace, but upstream closed the issue without identifying which scheduling step lost a frame.
findings.limits: The historical suite reproduced the failures. Each probed method had a sampling limit.

cases.title: ZIO logs lose callers at a non-ZIO runtime boundary

findings.observation: In 1.0.12, a Cause logged inside an effect showed the parse failure but omitted externalRequestHandler. In 2.0.18, the internal log likewise omitted foo and bar without propagated context.
findings.interpretation: In two runs of the proposed example, ZLogger retrieved the StackTrace captured by fromJava from FiberRefs and passed that same object to Cause.traced, restoring foo and bar.
findings.limits: The original logging APIs were private. The controls cover one runtime boundary and an unmerged proposal, PR #8509.

cases.title: Cause.prettyPrint omits the fiber ID and source location

findings.observation: The affected Cause.prettyPrint printed an exception without a fiber ID or source location even though the original test passed.
findings.interpretation: The old unifyFail received FiberId.None and an empty Chunk, while the fix retrieved the fiber ID and stack from each failure node.
findings.limits: Both classpaths came from the same historical tree, with the pre-fix Cause.class substituted for comparison.

cases.title: Publishing before a ZIO Hub subscription leaves the reader waiting

findings.observation: Publishing before subscribing caused the read to time out. Reversing the order delivered the same element to map, where the expected exception was thrown.
findings.interpretation: The result matched the reporter’s explanation that the earlier publication never reached map. The upstream test waited for subscription, and the maintainer’s delayed publisher also reached map.
findings.limits: The complete failing program was unavailable. The upstream examples and local publish-first control were recorded separately.

cases.title: ZIO prints an interruption message without a fiber number

findings.observation: The RC2 parallel-failure example printed zio-fiber- with no numeric suffix in the interruption message.
findings.interpretation: unifyInterrupt had the actual interrupt.fiberId but called threadName on FiberId.None, producing the incomplete name addressed by the upstream fix.
findings.limits: The reporter’s MainApp and a 2.0.0 control were rerun, with the formatter’s input inspected directly.

cases.title: A typed ZIO failure logs the stream endpoint instead of the parser line

findings.observation: On 2.0.0-RC6, a CSV quantity error at line 10 logged only runDrain at line 23 as a typed failure, while orDie and a throw from map showed the parser line.
findings.interpretation: The formatter took Cause.unifyFail, which rendered only the fiber stack. UnifyDie included the Throwable stack, and changing the terminal operation to runCollect moved the lone location to line 27.
findings.limits: The report supplied no version, code, input or stack. This reproduces the logging symptom in a local component without establishing the reporter’s cause.

cases.title: ZIO.attempt drops the Java call site from the printed failure

findings.observation: The maintainer’s program printed only effect and run on 2.0.0, while 2.0.1 also printed POJOService.foo and something.
findings.interpretation: Both missing methods were still visible on entry to Cause.fail, matching PR #7016’s finding that ZIO.attempt omitted the exception’s Java stack from Cause.Fail.
findings.limits: The same example from the upstream comment was compiled and run against both released dependencies.

cases.title: A ZIO map failure loses the application line that called Nil.head

findings.observation: The original ZIO 2.0.0 example failed in Nil.head, but its printed trace omitted the map call at Main.scala:4.
findings.interpretation: The affected capture showed line 4 calling Nil.head and the path into Cause.die. The upstream fix retained lastTrace when FiberRuntime.runLoop handled the unexpected exception.
findings.limits: Versions 2.0.1 and 2.0.2 were also replayed. Patch-release differences alone do not isolate one PR’s contribution.

cases.title: Exhausted retries replace the original failure location

findings.observation: When retries ran out on ZIO 2.0.4, the output pointed to retry and omitted the original failure site in foo.
findings.interpretation: The callback still received an exception carrying foo at line 14, but called ZIO.fail again at retry line 11; PR #7590 changed this to rethrow the original Cause.
findings.limits: The published program was rerun on 2.0.5, with samples attributed separately to each attempt.

cases.title: An exception on the right side of ZIO flatMap loses caller context

findings.observation: In the original Scala 3 program, the exception on the right side of flatMap printed only c, while the left-side control retained more call sites.
findings.interpretation: Separate observations showed a’s callback calling b and b’s callback calling c, consistent with the contributor’s account of where caller context is lost.
findings.limits: No sample captured a write to lastTrace, and there was no confirmed fix.

cases.title: ZIO’s getOrThrow error stack omits the outer caller

findings.observation: On 2.1.7, the FiberFailure printed at getOrThrow omitted Test.call.
findings.interpretation: The JVM stack still contained getOrThrowFiberFailure, Test.subcall, and Test.call when the exception was constructed, and PR #9386 added the JVM call stack at that boundary.
findings.limits: The original app and a 2.1.19 control used the same input. The application frames were captured during exception construction.
